This game is fun, I will say. It's very unwinding and a relaxing game involving racing on amazing and awesome jumps and loops and well, stunts. STUNTMANIA Reloaded is a basic free-roaming racer involving several gigantic maps that have all sorts of hidden and secret areas to explore. Each of the ~10 maps feature hundreds of jumps and stunts, complete with large amounts of green, yellow, and red collectables to gather in each level. Also in each stage, there are 3 types of coins that need to be gathered in-order to unlock certain parts of the game. Some coins need to be gathered in 3 pieces, which will be spread around the map. These include the first coin, a "car coin", which is used to unlock different cars. Second, a "level coin", which is used to unlock different levels. And the only coin that comes in whole, the "gamemode coin", which is used to unlock gamemodes. Finally, in each level there will be a set of powerups. These powerups include Super Jump, Nitro, Antigravity, Teleport, and more. These little parts of gameplay make this game a very fun and relaxing racer/explorer, leaving you taking a long breath at the ramps, loops, and obstacles of each map.
"Wait, if this is 'very fun', then why did you rate it badly?" You may be asking.
The biggest and most dreaded downfall of all players' experiences is the giant number of glitches and bugs that there are in this game. Let me explain. So, you crash your car into a wall, and you wait around 2 seconds for it to respawn. Around 1/7 of the time your car will respawn being shot up into the air like a cannon and stay airborne for a good 40 seconds, leaving you with nothing to do but wait. Once that car comes crashing down again, unless you've picked up the "Mega Health" powerup, there's a 50/50 chance that you won't survive the fall, with the possibility of respawning shot up into the air once more. However, I have come to a slight realization of the glitch and it is if you've crashed with your car's nose tipped mildly upwards, it seems to bring up the glitch. An easy way to stabilize your car is holding down SPACE, but this is still unconfirmed as far as I know. In the game I guarantee that you'll find your car glitching through the map either fully, or just partially, even if you can make it out with a small hop. And, I've also taken note that you can literally drive up a flat wall, whether it be land, or a building, without any powerups or any help or tricks.
Now, I will say that this game is relaxing, fun, and enjoyable, but the glitches that this game possesses just seem to ruin the fun for most people. The price just doesn't seem like it's worth it's value if it's possessed by such bugs and broken mechanics, even if it's only $5. However, this game demonstrated to me amazing levels, and breathtaking and cool stunts and jumps and loops; This game is its own rollercoaster. But, even all of this doesn't top for the game's value. The only time I would recommend to buy this game is when it's on sale, or in Humble Bundle or other such sorts.

As you probably know, Dark Souls II is a hard game. Unfair even. But few modern games give the same rush when you beat that hard boss you've been trying the last couple of hours. I would say you can compare this game to more old school games, and one that specifically comes to mind is Super Mario 64. This game is in a way very similar; the game doesn't really tell you much about how you're supposed to proceed, and the levels get trickier and trickier, requiring more precision from you. This game is just like that.
If this is your first time playing Dark Souls you will probably die a lot, and be frustrated in the beginning, but after a while you will learn the timings of the enemy, and suddenly you have won your first boss battle. What's special with this game is not really that it's hard, but that it's mostly YOU that get better at the game, not just your character that getting better gear.
On top of this the game is stunningly beautiful, with truly great environments and enemies.
This is a game I find my self putting down with "no more for today", and then an hour later I'm there playing again.
A 5, out of 5.
That said I have some recommendations if you're going to play this:
* Play with a hand controller
* Use a wiki/guide. The game doesn't tell you much, and without a guide you will most probably be hopelessly lost.

本作是一款fans向的作品，小时候就看了圣斗士看到有游戏果断入了！
首先是画面，单看背景绝对是会认为本作画面很惊艳，不过人物模型和剧情过场就显得格格不入，甚至有些突兀，特别是剧情模式中过场的老年童虎，真的很想让人砸显示器了。不过战斗中人物的动作和场景还是很流畅的，整体的打击感也让人满意，如果能添加场景破坏之类的，会更加让玩家喜爱。
音乐应该不会有太多的挑剔，格斗类型的音乐本身只要够燃就好。
可用的圣斗士很多，从黄金十二宫到极乐净土中所有重要的圣斗士神斗士海斗士和冥斗士悉数登场，几位神级别的人物也拿起武器参战，应该能让多数人满足吧。还有不满足的？那么去挑战一下黄金之战，让十二宫的神圣衣登场来满足自己的收集癖吧。楼主只是打完所有的剧情，因为没有达到全s和全挑战，可能有些没收集齐，比如除了星矢以外的四小强神衣版。而且雅典娜之后还有两个空位，不知道是哪两个人物的，有待发掘。
上手方面应该没有难度，操作方△攻击，×跳，o小招，L1防御，L2积攒小宇宙，r1特殊移动，r2+方，△，o是各种特殊攻击，r3觉醒第七感。轻重攻击比较流畅，招式也还原了动画片中的动作，因为没有玩过前作，不做对比，不过从整体的连击和绝招的释放都不会让新手觉得难以驾驭，当然，个别圣斗士操作可能不是那么轻松，仙女座的瞬算是代表，很多时候连击和追击的节奏不好找，需要多练习。唯一要吐槽的就是抓投，硬直过大而且范围因人而异，是很头痛的东西，具体下面会讲。有些人物的攻击模型很类似，最明显的就是童虎和紫龙，不乏给人偷工的感觉。
剧情模式主要是解锁人物，称号和各种辅助的道具，应该是大家最优先的完成的东西。因为我现在只通过了一周目的剧情模式，重点说明一下这里，剧情可谓是完整的复述了五小强从黄金十二宫的战斗史，对于喜欢回味剧情的玩家是很过瘾，战斗前后都有动画衔接剧情，全程战斗和过场都有语音，而且是那些我们熟悉的日文语音，不仅不会感到枯燥，还会觉得很亲切，当然前面吐槽过过场动画，此处不再累赘，但是大部分战斗都需要连续打几场，会容易积累游戏疲劳，电脑本身的水平并不高，很多时候都是因为有额外的伤害加成容易导致重战，而站起来的时候你要听着雅典娜不停的啰嗦还要疯狂的按x键，这就是更大的煎熬。只是单纯打一遍就想完成所有的挑战会很困难，很多时候需要你防御15次或者20次（难主要体现在某些对手破防太容易，不小心就会被打的很惨，比如海皇篇的加隆），或者抓投对方5次，更有要求不能被打倒的挑战，会让全挑战完成变得是一种折磨（不过去做全挑战本身就是折磨自己，诶）。好在如果是连续战斗，只要有一个拿到s，这个小节就算s，可以省不少力气。在剧情模式更需要注意的是大招，剧情模式中每个小节的战斗，绝招是固定的，每个人却有好几个绝招，圣衣不同，敌人不同都会影响。当你兴冲冲的用大招却发现不是你之前一节使用的，而且还被电脑追着打了一套，内心的伤痛可想而知。
接着上面的再说一下新的黄金之战模式，这个主要是解锁黄金十二宫的神衣，每个人物有基础的3场战斗，完成第一场就可以用神衣参战，三个全s会出现额外挑战，就是自己打自己，当然，这几场战斗都不难，多尝试就好，不过神衣的基础3场战斗都需要用特殊道具火把解锁，1个火把解锁一场，解锁过的重复挑战不会使用火把。火把可以在商店购买，2000一个。新作黄金魂的奥丁狮子没有，差评。
线上对战模式和其他的辅助道具还没过多的尝试，暂时不多评价。最后总结其实很多人都心里有数，主要是冲着粉丝怀旧圈钱。粉丝向的玩家可以不用犹豫，如果在观望的建议考虑。

If you are a newbie, it's quite hard to win although you select "easy". AI sometimes hits hard and moves fast but if you observe the AI movements about 3-4 games, you will know how to win. Practice in training mode or vs mode and remember all of moves is the best way to success.
In brief, if you are a big fan of Saint Seiya. This game surely never disappoints you.
Pros:
- Easy to use combos and moves.
- Exquisite graphic.
- System requirements are not too high.
- Any controllers supported.
- Easy to understand the story especially, if you are the fan of Saint seiya.
- Many characters available. There are 48 characters with more than 100 costumes.
- Many items to unlock.
- God cloths from Soul of Gold available.
- BBA cutscenes never bore me.
- Many modes to play besides the story mode (The legend of Cosmo); VS mode, Galaxian wars tournament, Survival mode and Battle of Gold.
Cons:
- Hades chapter is too short. There are only 3 judges of underworld and Hades available to use.
- There are only 3 silver saint characters (Marin, Shaina and Orphee)
- Abilities of some characters are not balanced even though all of them are based on the animation.
9/10

StuntMANIA Reloaded is a fun and charming do what you want, car game. Sure it's got some bugs, camera issues, respawning issues, textures not loading, but for $5 it really isn't a bad game. The music for the game is very interesting and is fun to listen to, and the ideas for the levels are really cool (Mini Golf is probably my favorite). There is a nice small selection of cars to choose from and having to collect coins to unlock them, levels, and game modes let's you search every nook and cranny on the map. Some pieces are difficult to find, but it shouldn't take long to get all the coins on every level. Go Crazy is a neat feature, no time pressure or objective really, you can go nuts and drive to your hearts desire, blowing up your car as many times as you want. One thing I really wish that would have been added were nice backdrops. It gets boring looking out into the gray/black outside of the arena, though this is a smaller issue. All in all, this is a good game for $5, even if it was $10. It's not the game of the year, but the developer clearly had a great idea in their head, and did a great job of making a fun game.

Similar gameplay to Dark Souls with a few changes both positive and negative. Overall, if you enjoyed Dark Souls, you should absolutely pick this up.
I'm going to be writing this aimed at people who played Dark Souls. If you are completely new to the Souls series, this probably won't mean much to you, but in that case, you should probably look at another review, or perhaps my review of Dark Souls, first.
--
Perhaps the most important thing to note, if you played Dark Souls on PC, is that this time, we have actual keyboard/mouse support (at least for the most part - more on that to come), and 1080p resolution. We're still stuck on DirectX 9, but once again the community comes to the rescue and there's a very nice graphical enhancement mod available if you feel it's not pretty enough for you.
A few major changes from Dark Souls 1, which you may embrace or dislike:
-You start with a single estus flask, which is upgraded by consuming items you find as you play. To compensate for this, Demon's Souls-style consumable healing items are back, and while they aren't as strong as the Flask, they're a workable holdover if you run out of flasks.
-Weapons degrade much (Much!) faster, to the point that you will need to carry more than one weapon lest your weapon breaks in the middle of a fight. Fortunately, equipment that isn't fully broken is repaired, for free, every time you rest at a bonfire (or die, or successfully assist someone as a white/gold phantom). Repairing is no longer an unavoidable soul-sink, but equipment degradation is something you need to be keeping a close eye on.
-A new mechanic, called Soul Memory, tracks the total number of souls you've earned (including those spent at shops, to level up, to upgrade equipment, to repair equipment, and even lost due to deaths). This number dictates who you can and can't interact with in PvP or Co-op. Soul Level is still a factor pre-NG+, as well, so it's important to make sure you're keeping both in mind if you have a friend you want to play with regularly. Luckily there are a few ways the game makes playing with your friends easier, the most notable of which is a ring you can purchase right from the start of the game for a nominal fee that lets you filter whose summon signs you're seeing while also extending the Soul Memory range you can summon within, making it much easier to arrange to play with someone specific.
-While Dark Souls started with a single path and opened up into multiple paths as the game progressed, Dark Souls 2 is the opposite, and starts with a lot of options, then narrows into a single path later in the game. This works well in my opinion, but some disagree.
-The ability to warp between bonfires is available from the start of the game, and you can warp to and from any bonfire you've lit. This certainly makes some aspects of the game easier (especially since the world is somewhat less interconnected than it was in Dark Souls), but something about it just feels... off. It certainly makes it easier to miss things that're changing in areas you've already visited as you progress in the game, since you aren't moving through those areas as often.
-NG+ adds a number of changes into the game, including new items (and new boss souls) and new enemies. To my knowledge there is new content up through NG++. Additionally, a new item, Bonfire Ascetics, can be burned at bonfires to raise the difficulty in the area around the bonfire, effectively moving that area into one NG+ level higher than it previously was. This respawns single-kill enemies, chest loot and corpse loot in that area only, and this 'upgrade' persists into 'actual' NG+ playthroughs. For instance, burning a bonfire ascetic in NG will boost an area to NG+ difficulty; restarting in NG+ will mean that area is now NG++ equivalent, and so on.
-A lot of the covenants will feel familiar (the Heirs to the Sun, for instance, and the dragon covenant function more or less exactly as they did in Dark Souls), but there's some new ones that have some fun new mechanics - for instance, one that can be accessed almost immediately after starting the game severely increases the difficulty of the game and rewards the player for killing new, difficult enemies which don't exist for non-covenant members. Fans of the Forest Defenders may enjoy two new covenants with similar mechanics.
-It's now possible to be invaded when you're not human. There is, however, the option to burn a Human Effigy, the new equivalent to Humanity, to prevent all invasions (and friendly summons) for 30 minutes, even persisting through death, so if you're really not wanting to deal with that, you have options.
-The most jarring change to me is that now, enemies will respawn a maximum of 15 times. If you're doing well, this won't be noticeable, but if you're getting stomped in an area, you'll soon notice enemies missing when you return. This has the effect of making difficult areas beatable through sheer persistence alone - as long as you're killing at least 1 enemy each time you respawn, you're making permanent progress - but the downside is that everything is now finite. Souls are no longer an infinite resource, nor are any item, even those with unlimited supply on merchants, since eventually, you'll run out of enemies to kill for souls. Note that the game is far larger than Dark Souls, and actually running out of enemies to kill would take a very, very long time, but it feels like an ever-present threat all the same.
-You now lose max hp when you die. It's not as jarring as it was in Demon's Souls - you lose a small amount after each death, with the max penalty being 50% of your normal maximum, and the effect can be removed at any time by using a Human Effigy to regain humanity (which does not require a bonfire anymore). Like Demon's Souls, there's a ring which halves this penalty when worn.
Aside from these changes, expect very similar gameplay to Dark Souls; if you enjoyed Dark Souls, you will most likely enjoy Dark Souls 2.

A year later, so how does the game hold up in its current state (without the new DLC)
Positives:
- potential for several playthoughs due to new game + and 2 characters
- some things were added to make life easier, including a stats page you can check during missions to see deaths or if you were spotted, the ability to deny powers right in the beginning as part of the story, and more non-lethal combat moves
- great looking areas for each mission with different mechanics (sometimes suprisingly complex) introduced every time
- a great and unique stealth game with multiple play styles
- where the main plot lacks, it picks up interest in small dialogue, reading journals or notes, and learning the backstory to wherever you are
- the powers Emily and Corvo have can be used in a crazy number of ways, allowing for a high skill cap which keeps veterans from being bored (the new difficulty added can help with that as well)
Negatives:
- once again story isn't very complex or super compelling, and doesn't change as much as it should have when playing a different character
- gameplay feels less fluid and quick, which may be a problem for big fans or the first game
- optimization isn't great, it should run much better than it does and a lot of people report technical issuees to this day (personally it was unplayable until a few patches in)
While it wasn't everything I hoped it would be, the game is definitely still good and worth a purchase especially if on sale. I may be over critical/ biased from being such a big fanboy of the first game, and there were a lot of changes made here including the engine, so keep that in mind when looking at the negatives. Try getting the demo and double check the requirements to make sure it will run good enough to play on your system.

Well what a surprise, this is actually a pretty neat little game. It has native Xbox 360 controller support, although there's nothing in the options or menus telling you what does what... it's not hard to figure out.
The controls feel a little touchy at first. Okay, a lot touchy. You have to make corrections quickly and there's not much margin for error, but you're controlling what's basically an R/C car that can take a lot of punishment, so it's okay.
The game starts out with nothing but an open world type map with all these powerups and collectibles scattered around everywhere. You have to build coins out of fragments to unlock more maps, vehicles, and game modes, but starting out you have access to 3-4 different vehicles so it's not bad. As you go through the level you also collect upgrades for your current car - things like nitro, super jump, low gravity, extra health, etc. The challenge is to figure out how to jump or climb up to the hard to reach spots to get your goodies. There's no penalty for dying, you just respawn at a random location, sometimes way up in the air.
Like other reviewers have mentioned, you have full control over your pitch and roll while in the air, so you're basically like a cat in that way. If you're good at being a cat, you'll always land on your feet... err... tires. If not, if you land on your nose or roof, you'll probably go boom if you're high enough.
You can switch camera angles. I found it's easiest to control spin from the bumper cam, but the disadvantage is it's harder to see where the roads, ramps, and hills lead off to. There's no way to adjust where you're looking, it's always straight ahead, except in third person, then the camera faces whatever direction you're going. There's a button to do a full 180 reverse, and another button to do a quick stop. It's not like a handbrake, it's to stop completely. This is useful for planting yourself on hard to reach ledges after you had to take a running jump to get to it. I keep forgetting that's what it's for but there it is.
So, this game is cheap, it's goofy, it's fun, and with so many things to unlock and maps to explore, I think it's well worth it for the price. Thumbs up! A solid 7/10 at least. Good fun.

First game to make me physically feel ill while playing. No, it's not an "insane" stunt game. It's just a poorly designed one. The physics are terrible, the smallest bump in the road will send you flying or 180ing. The controls suck, no matter how you tweak them and doing stunts, what few there are, is ridiculously easy. Now to the physically ill part; I can't really understand why this is literally the ONLY game to do it but I suspect it's because when you control the vehicle in 3rd person it appears the terrain, not the car, shifts. It looks ridiculous and it's a bit messed up.
Even if I am the only that perceives the camera as such you're still left with a poorly made game that's too easy, despite itself, and not fun. There was definite potential here but it was wasted.

The Short Version: 7/10, but keep in mind this is a driving exploration game, not a racing game. You'll be disappointed if you expect Mario Cart. Think Spyro's hub worlds in a car, and graphics like the original Spyro.
Long Version: I'm two levels in and I have to say this game is exactly what I wanted. You drive an RC car around a large area collecting hidden things and doing tricks. I have a couple of complaints, however. Doing tricks doesn't seem to do anything but flash some text; It'd be nice if there were more motivation for me to rack up score or soemthing. There doesn't seem to be a functional difference between the cars, and they all cost one coin to unlock (you get a coin by finding three parts in a level.) So after you've found one coin you'll unlock the car you like and after that there's no incentive to unlock more. The graphics are pretty rudimentary, and in places you'll think you're playing a PS1 game.
Despite these issues, the game is still fun if you like exploring an area and collecting things in a vehicle. It brings back memories of playing Diddy Kong Racing and San Francisco Rush 2049's stunt mode, and is comparable to the drive-around-collect-stuff mode from Joyride Turbo on Xbox 360. I only wish this game's player investment system had gotten a bit more attention.

This feels like the alpha version of a game. Within the only 5 minutes of playing the game, I encountered the following:
- The game didn't start on the first attempt - after the intro screen the window stayed black. Had to kill the process and restart.
- When starting out, there's only one game mode, one car, and one "track" available. You have to collect items on some sort of open-world island to unlock even other race modes. The open-world collect-things game mode was not fun to me, but of course that's completely subjective.
- The controls are laughably bad. A small change in slope may suddenly jerk the car around. You will do lots of flips and crashes for no reason. It's almost impossible to consistently go where you're aiming.
- The physics are hilarious or terrible, depending on your point of view. The car will do multiple flips in one jump all the time for no reason. At one point after my car exploded on impact, I respawned like 100 meters in mid-air. Instead of falling down, I "fell" up for probably 200 more meters before falling back down. I was in mid-air for at least 30 seconds total before hitting the ground and exploding again. This happened within the first and only 5 minutes of playing this.
- I gave up on the game after about 5 minutes. When quitting, the process crashed, got stuck and I had to kill it again via task manager.
I like small casual games, but this one is ridiculously unfinished. Avoid.

If you check out most of my reviews, they are just under 1000 words long. Usually, I feel the need to write a long review talking about what I feel is important. This is not such a case.
In short, it's a lot like Big Rigs, but better.
This game is... dreadful, but also kind of fun. The main reason its fun is because of how lighthearted it is, and how colourful everything is, along with the pleasent, if repetitive music.
But it's also completely broken is almost every possible way. The environments are glitchy, the car controls kind of crappily, the controls don't really work sometimes, and there isn't really much of a goal except to collect all the stuff in the level and go to the next...
It really just that simple. Here's a level, collect the stuff, move on. That's it. No racing. No real need to do stunts at all. It's just... here. Drive around and collect stuff.
Just to give an example of how broken this game is, I came across a bug after 4 mintues of playing where, if I jumped, and then held the backwards key ("s" for me), I instantly started flying up into the air, and as long as I kept the key pressed, I kept going. While this is actually kind of fun, and I would hate to see it removed, it does sort of highlight how broken this game is. Also, every time I died, I couldn't access the first person viewpoint any more. No idea why, it just didn't let me. You can also drive directly up vertical walls, and your car goes faster going backwards than it does forwards. Once again, this is actually kind of awesome, and does have some fun in it, but I doubt they intended it to be like this.
It's a lot like Big Rigs in that sense. Terrible glitches, but ones that serve to be entertaining. Without them, the game would ironically be a lot worse I feel.
At the same time, despite all of this, the game doesn't really lie about what it offers. You can do stunts, I guess, though there's no reason too. And you drive a small car. It's sort of enjoyable, so what the hey. A thumbs up for now. Maybe I'll change my mind later, but right now, it's 3:20am here in Australia, and I need to get some sleep.

Very uninspired, very standard platformer with a food/time mechanic that would be interesting if any thought was put into it.
As it is, you have to cross the levels left to right while your health drops down every few seconds because you're a caveman, so duh, you get hungry! You still lose health while getting damaged by enemies though, of course. On the other hand, you can replenishes that with the somewhat plentiful food items (which are set drops in every map, not random ones.)
While crossing the levels, you'll either have an easy time (because there's few enemies and/or lots of food) or a harder time (because there are lots of cheap shot enemies and/or little food.) This means that little to no thought was put into balancing the food/time mechanic/drops, rather it was something implemented as a pitch and gimmick to sell the game. You have very little choice in your approach to this game: your best option is to run as fast as you can and know beforehand when the hits (or pitfall deaths) are and keep trying until you get through.
In short,
.
It would be a good idea if there was any room to manouver around it, anything that could make the gamer feel empowered. Here's some ideas: standing still doesn't draw health; enemies can drop food sometimes; you can carry a food consumable on you. But no. This is any platformer ever, with time=health. You have 15 seconds, go.
This isn't all bad of course, as few things actually ever are. Decent effort is put into the art, the boss battles (which aren't bad; they're ok) and in the item/weapon carry-over which adds a little extra depth.
Unfortunately, this game offers no challenge other than how much time you're willing to waste on it.
I suggest you waste none, and move to another platformer or any other game whatsoever.

Dinocide is a retro styled platformer.
+ Charming graphics
+ Creative creatures
+ Relaxing game
+ Seems good for kids
- Controls are kind of stiff
- Weapon/Dinosaur store is pointless
- Must go through menus everytime when you die
In Dinocide you control a caveman that must rescue his girlfriend from the evil Dinosaur God. It is a retro styled platformer.
In each level you must cross the map before dying from hunger. There is a hunger meter at the top of the screen that is constantly decreasing but you can fill it up by eating food lying around. You don't have much time to think in game. There is a large variety of creative creatures trying to stop you like mexican skeletons, pooping birds, lazer firing bears, exploding bats and so on.
To help you out, there are weapons and dinosaurs. There are four weapons each with it's own damage, trajectory and recharge speed and five dinosaurs each with it's special ability. Dinosaurs also have their own life, so if you die when you're riding a dinosaur only the dinosaur dies. You can find weapons and dinosaurs lying around in each level or you can buy them in a store in some levels. When you finish a level you get to keep the weapon and dinosaur and choose which weapon and dinosaur to use in the next levels. However if you die while holding a weapon or riding a dinosaur you lose it and cannot chose it anymore.
There is some variety of maps like forests, deserts or under water maps. Sometimes you get to chose the path you want to go but not often. It's a nice little feature but doesn't really make much of a difference. The game is almost entirely linear. There are also bosses at the end of each section. The bosses are funny but also very easy to defeat.
The graphics style and feel in general is simillar to Alex Kid. Very simple pleasant graphics. The game isn't hard at all and it is in fact relaxing. You can beat the game easily without the dinosaurs or more powerful weapons. The only real difficulty is that the controls are kind of stiff and you don't know what's next. It is a trial and error kind of game so you will die but you can easily avoid the obstacles in your next attempt. One annoying aspect is that when you retry you must go through the weapon and dinosaur choice everytime. I don't see the point of getting to chose the weapons/dinosaurs. Such a feature just makes the levels you want easier in an already easy game. Perhaps it would have been better if these weapons/dinosaurs only belonged to some levels or if it was a permanent upgrade system.
So this is an easy, relaxing and short game. It's not a bad game but not an amazing game either. Could be a good game for your kids.

The opening words
Dark Souls was a terrible port. We all remember how terrible the graphics were, how optimization was borked and framerate suffered, and how butchered the controls for the keyboard/mouse were. We all loved the game for gameplay, but we all hated the game for the PC port. From Software promised that this would not be the case with Dark Souls II. That the platform will be treated with the respect it deserves. Did they manage it?
As with every Souls game, Dark Souls II is an action/adventure game, similar in a way to the Zelda series. You travel the more or less open world, fight off enemies, deal with some simple puzzles, beat bosses, and aquire new cool abilities for your character. What's possibly the most iconic thing about a Souls game is the fact that it's HARD. You will die a lot in this game, but usually if you are calm you can avoid dying in the same place multiple times, and if you do fall you are sent back to the last bonfire. There are quite many of those and I never felt like the game punished me too much in this regard. The thing is if you die, you lose all unspent souls, which are currency in this game. You use souls to level up your character and to buy weapons/spells/armor. After dying you can still get your souls back, if you get to the same spot without dying again. So this game basically punishes you for screwing up on the same part multiple times, which is fine by me, but it takes some getting used to.
I won't say much about the story, because for a non-fan it would be too complicated to understand, and fans already know it. What I will say is this: you play as an undead. You once had a wife, a child, a purpose... but the undead curse took that from you. And as every undead, you slowly start to forget your past. Now the only thing that drives you is the lust for souls, and the possibility of learning more about the undead curse. But will you manage to succeed before you lose your mind and become hollow? Will you find a cure for your condition, or are you destined to die and be reborn over, and over again?
The good
If you own a gamepad and you loved the first Dark Souls, stop reading this and go buy DS II. That's it. The gameplay, although little different, still delivers the same Souls experience we've come to expect from a Souls game. The action is satisfying, the environments great by design, and the stories interesting, if you are willing to dive in. The graphics on PC are better than on the consoles, so at least the devs were truthful to their word, but more on that later. The game should run correctly on a PC that meets the requirements.
The combat, which is the most important part of the game takes some getting used to at first. But once you get the controls down, you will enjoy this part the most. The enemies can behave unpredictably, and the game will be a challange even for the fans of the first Dark Souls. There are a lot of items, weapons and armor that you can get from enemies/buy from merchants. Every piece of equipment has it's own model, so for all of you looks-first kind of players this is a treat.
There are some gameplay changes (since the original Dark Souls) that I liked, particularly the splitting of Endurance into 2 stats. Now you have a stat that increases your stamina, another that lets you wear heavier stuff, and one more that offers you higher speed of moves like dodges or drinking health potions. This let's you tweak your character more, which is good. Oh, and the online features are FUN as hell. That's good too.
The bad
I know what you want to know: can I play with mouse and keyboard? Answer: Yes. Sort of. Kinda... maybe. It is possible, and I tried it for myself, but you will have so much easier time just by picking up a 360 gamepad. The fact that the game shows you only controller button prompts doesn't help eighter. If you are set on playing with keys I'd suggest tweaking the controls first, and then during the gameplay, to find what is the most comfortable for you.
Graphics could look better. We've seen the beta/demo builds and the lighting looked awesome, so why is it, that the finished game looks nothing like this? There's barely any use for a torch, aside from few areas in the game and even there you can still see more clearly than you should be without the light. That also would have been a great gameplay change: will you sacrifice a weapon, or a shield and carry a torch in one hand? Or will you sacrifice visibility for better offence/defence? Nope. Scrapped, probably because consoles couldn't handle it. Tsk, tsk. Don't do that again, From Software. I'm watching you. If you pull a switch like that again, I'll stop buying your stuff. This time I'll overlook it, even though it's bad...
The ugly
There are two things I really hate about this game. First is a change from the original. In Dark Souls 1 it didn't really matter if you lost all your souls. You could always farm some more, because monster would respawn every time you rested at the bonfire. Not the case anymore. Monsters respawn only 14 times, or so I'm told (haven't really counted myself). If you kill a monster 15th time, it stops spawning and you can't farm it anymore. This has some good effects: you can clear the way to a boss, and just focus on trying to beat him, rather than dealing with the hardships on the way. But to me this seeems like a mechanic to punish players who struggle with the difficulty. A good player won't need to farm souls, so he won't care about kill limits. But a bad player may want to level up and level the playing field a little before going to the boss battle. This is quite frankly unnecessary. There is a way of respawning the monsters in an area but that involves increasing the difficulty, which is the last thing you want if you are already struggling. Mind you, you can still obtain more souls by going online and helping other players with bosses - you use an item called White Sign Soapstone, which you get quite early, and then other players can summon you in that spot in their own world. You are then tasked with helping that player and protecting him from dangers. Reward? A share in souls he gets and an item if you manage to help him beat a boss. You could also leave one area and go farm another, but again, it will deplete as well at some point and I don't like that.
The second ugly thing is major. The servers for the game are ♥♥♥♥ED. I've had the game for little over a week and I've been unable to connect multiple times. And even if I did connect and got pulled into the game by other players, the lag was sometimes just impossible. I think the devs said that the online games will take place on a server, but that's clearly not the case. The lag depends solely on your connection, and the host's connection. If his provider suck, then you'll lag a lot, which is annoying for any kind of PvP. You can still play offline, but the game is just much less fun.
Also I've found some graphical glitches. For example, after beating two dragon riders in the castle and resting at the next bofire, turn back and look at the floor near the walls. Doesn't really influence the gameplay, but is still ugly.
The lowdown
Overall, I'd say the game is worth buying. The gameplay itself is fantastic, and that's what matters the most in the end, right? And if the server problems are dealt with, the game will be near perfect. Well if not for the controls that are still bad on keyboar/mouse. So all in all I'd say you will HATE this game at first. But if you make yourself go through the first rage, and get little good at it and start succeeding you will LOVE every single minute of it. Try it out for yourself and see if you have what it takes.

Call of Duty has been coasting for a long time, but Advanced Warfare is a big step in the right direction. The EXO abilities change up the flow of multiplayer in a big way, making for the fastest and most fun CoD multiplayer experience yet. The customization is extensive, and includes creating a custom character of either gender. You can't make your own face, but there are a number of pre-made options to choose from and there are quite a few armor choices, some of which can be unlocked in the campaign.
Speaking of the campaign, it's reasonably lengthy for CoD (6-8 hours). It has an upgrade system and a solid story. The ending throws in a disappointing "There's totally going to be a sequel" line for no good reason. Kevin Spacey and Troy Baker deliver fantastic performances, and the facial animation looks incredible. It's not revolutionary, but it's a lot of fun and that's what matters.
The game also has a coop mode, but it's not a super in-depth mode. It's good for a few laughs, but it's not the mainstay that Zombies could be... though apparently they'll be kind enough to add that through paid DLC.
Finally, as far as a port goes, Advanced Warfare is pretty good. It runs fairly well, and I've experienced very few glitches. Unfortunately, the online suffers from non-dedicated servers and some lag. It's far from the worst lag I've seen, but it's just noticeable enough to be frustrating and detract from the experience. It's not enough to keep me from recommending the game overall, but if lag is a sticking point, Advanced Warfare will not make you particularly happy.

A genuinely gorgeous little Visual Novel, Voices from the Sea really captures what it's aiming for; a relaxing, charming tale about a girl by the sea.
While the two main leads are walking tropes, they are done in a very cute, heartfelt way to make seem a bit more than the sum of its parts. Cantus, the main character, is your average "I never smile" character, and Maris, the mysterious girl by the ocean, wants to make him. She talks in the third person, and it's a bit tropish and annoying at first, but the artistic direction and masterful use of colors in every shot really overcomes the standard plot. Even though it barely clocks in at an hour, the tale really is quite incapsulating, and while the ending is predictable, a part of me finds that to be a good thing. It accomplishes what the ultimate goal was. It made me smile.
For a free game, the quality is ridiculous, so don't be afraid to support the developers. There is DLC that asks for a measley 5 bucks and adds voice overs and a few new scenarios. One of these days I might pick it up, because I really respect what they've done here. They hope you pay for it out of love for the game; pure good will. That's something we do not see enough of these days, so for that, I definitely thank them, and I'll be looking forward to whatever else they do next.

From the start, i will say i experienced performance issue, as mentioned in many reviews before me. I won't talk about them, as i have a beefy system, and the performance issue impact was not as significant.
Get past the performance issues, however, and you will find a very good game.
Gameplay wise, it's just as tight, fun and varied as the first one, with missions having multiple ways of aproaching them. The game wants you to play it multiple times, everytime finding new ways of moving forward. However, the story, IMO, is not as good as the first game. The characters are dull, and the narative line is quite cliché... Without spoiling anything, you can figure out the plotline from the start...
And it's a shame, for a game that wants you to invest your time in attempting multiple ways, figuring out different methods of completing your objectives (and all the extra mini-quests and moments that fill up the world) the story doesn't provide a good reason to play the game as the other character...
It's clear the producers fine-tuned the gameplay to perfection, and had the multiple aproach idea from the start, working around it. And it shows. I can't praise the "fun" and the ingenuity of the game, and the many ways you can have fun with it's mechanics, it's multiple pathed maps. But for a single player-story driven game, i found the story lacking...
Still would recomend the game. I had a lot of fun with it, and i think this is what Arkane wanted players to do. Have fun, more than be invested in a story...

Got this from the Yogscast jingle jam bundle.
All in all it feels somewhat lacking.
Now, don't get me wrong, it can be fun. But only sometimes.
Controls
First of all, I found the controls a bit wonky even while using my gamepad.
I have no such issues with other games so I have to assume that the fault lies on this game.
Gameplay
The biggest flaw concerning gameplay is that winning never felt rewarding.
There's no rush of victory. Merely chugging along going to the next level.
The main levels are merely a rush to the end due to the time constraint.
And boss fights felt severely lacking. In fact, they were not challenging at all.
That's because the challenge in this game comes solely from the time limit.
Some of the enemies are pretty badly designed to boot,
serving only to eat away your health/timer with no way of avoiding it.
Some of the vulture enemies, for example, are unavoidable.
Audio
While I enjoyed the music, the sound effects are glitchy and don't always play properly.
In fact, at times they refused to play at all.
Conclusion
Barring nostalgia for something similar but not quite like
Wonder Boy and/or Adventure Island, there is no real reason to get this.
Especially not at that price.

While it's not quite as good as the other two Souls games, this is still one of the best games I've ever played. They've added a new mechanic where lots of enemy strikes will "home in" a bit instead of staying in a proper Street Fighter-esq fixed animation, which adds a certain organic quality, but also takes away from the "purity" of mastering the enemies and combat. Otherwise, it's good old business as usual: gorgeous, sometimes unsettling art direction, audio, and a sense of exploration and accomplishment that other modern games don't come even remotely close to. It's a combination of new technology and the "good old days" where games required some thought and experimentation for full understanding, being proper interactive experiences instead of interactive movies. It also gladly takes advantage of the interwebs to create really cool asynchronous multiplayer elements, like ghostly visages of other players wandering through your game, leaving marks where they've died (and how), as well as little messages that can be helpful or purposely trolling. Aside from the other Soul games, there's nothing quite like it. You are missing out on the "next big thing" if you sit these games out, though since this one doesn't really add much to the formula, you may as well play the first Dark Souls first since it's cheaper and bit better.

First off there's two things I want to address, then my review.
1. To those who complain about PVP, there are PVE servers where players can't hurt each other.
2. This game is free to play so stop your whining.
With that out of the way, here's my honest opinion of this game.
I played the original game that came before this, ISS or as it was known at the beginning War Z.
This game is by most rights a direct upgrade to that game, in every way possible.
It's looks better, performs better, doens't have the same level of "pay to win" and has improved on it general.
What this game is not:
- An in depth simulator of survival in a zombie apacolypse.
- A story driven world rich with NPC's and lore to get lost in.
- A crazy open world free for all with explosions and mayham like some other shooters.
What this gmae is:
- Free to play.
- A simple looting based shooter with lots of grind.
- Something you can pick up and play without needing to know a books worth of lore.
- Simple battle mechanics and little to no penalty on death other than lost loot.
- Offers the option to play against or with other players in PVP and PVE respectavly.
- Is fun to play around in with friends, no hard thinking required.
- Offers exceptable level of character customization after creation.
- Alows building of bases and claiming of land.
- Is no where near as buggy, laggy, or all together broken as the game that came before it.
- Is still being updated and patched.
- And once again, FREE TO PLAY.
In short, I enjoy this game.
Yes, that's my opinion and yours may vary.
No, this isn't for everyone obviously.
I recommend this game.

There's something so wonderfull about ASTRONEER that you can only experience if you play it. On paper, the game is extremely simple. Take [mining tool], click on [resources], get [resources], craft, repeat. However, the developers took this tired old survival gameplay loop that we're all too familiar with, and did something wonderfull with it. For example, the mining tool can be used to completely modify all terrain. You can add some, flatten it out, destroy it, whatever you want. They also added a modular base system that adds another level of complexity to the game, by making you really think about how you want to use your base.
The developers have also done something that I've seen very few space games accomplish: make adventure interesting. You really feel like you are adventuring in this game when you decide to explore, because you can come across all sorts of neat sights and wrecks. There are plains, mountains, hills and caves, crashed space stations and resource pods, massive solar panels, not to mention the sight of other planets on the horizon, and all sorts of stuff that make the experience beautiful. Another aspect of adventure that they get right is the risk vs. reward. There are a lot of things that can kill you. Deadly plants, crazy sandstorms, general lack of oxygen, falling into a massive hole, etc. But there is a lot to be gained from the exploration, like rare resources, research objects that could yield more resources or different blueprints, or parts for vehicles. Overall, the developers did a tremendous job at making exploration fun and worthwhile.
If you're interested in a somewhat casual space exploration survival experience, this is the game for you. Overall ASTRONEER is a great game, even though it is still in early access.

[Note: I brought up some of the topics below in the forums with the developers and eventually the conversation devolved into an unpleasant experience with one of the developers. It got to the point where he (I'm assuming it was a he) responded with flippant, sarcastic remarks to almost every one of my comments while I was trying to be respectful and serious. I wondered to myself the age and maturity of this developer. It was really disappointing to see that kind of poor attitude from a game developer and it put me off playing this for awhile. That experience doesn't reflect my opinion of this game but it makes me a whole lot less likely to support them in the future.]
NMRIH is a curious game. If you dissect and examine it by its individual flaws and merits, it should be a failure, as the negative aspects appear to outweigh the postives. But when put together I think the adage, “the whole is greater than the sum of its parts” seems to apply appropriately.
Let's look at what I mean. We'll start with the bad. First, the game has severe hit detection problems. Like basically broken. You can have your gun perfectly aimed at a zombie's head, fire, and still miss. Why? The developers have stated that the game lacks "NPC lag compensation". So a moving zombie might not be where they appear to be. They'll be a little off. Their heads also seem to have small hitboxes. Ok this sounds like a huge problem right? A badly coded first-person shooter where you can't hit the enemy consistently because the game is unable to display their correct location? Many people might stop right here and look for another game. And I wouldn't blame you. But yet this seemingly monumental flaw doesn't kill the game. Not really.
The vast majority of the zombies are the slow moving type right out of a Romero film. That makes up for the lag problem some. The few that are fast run straight at you so the aiming isn't too much of an issue. It's usually when the zombies are moving sideways that it's harder to hit them.
Your melee attacks are also affected by the lag and it will definitely be frustrating at first. You will miss A LOT and get grabbed and bitten a bunch but with practice you learn how to swing each weapon at the right moment to compensate for it (mostly).
Melee range is another issue with the game. Some of the ranges are inconsistent or just plain don't make sense. For instance, you would expect that holding a lengthy object in your hand would naturally extend your reach. But strangely your fists have the longest range of all. Their attack power may be weak but their range seems to be superior to all weapons. Using the flashlight as a weapon has the shortest reach even though it looks like it should give you an extra foot of melee range. Is this logical? No. Does it detract from the gameplay? Again, not really.
I think herein lies the irony. The game thrives on its difficulty. And make no mistake it is hard. You won't know where to go or what to do at first. Your guns never have enough ammo. You will most likely fail and die. But the difficulty of it makes it challenging and these broken features make it more difficult and challenging which adds to the experience. If you were going around chopping heads off like it was nothing, like you were in L4D2, the game wouldn't be as fun. I still want them to fix the broken features, but it kinda works in this game.
Another gameplay element introduced in NMRIH is proximity chat where players' mics and text have limited range and if you wander too far away other players can no longer hear your mic or see your text chat. There are walkie talkies you can pickup in the game that allow your mic to be used anywhere on the map (other players need the walkie talkies too in order to hear you) but nothing for text chat which is unfortunate because not everyone has mic (like me) so if you're too far away from everyone you are basically cut off from any communication. I'm not really a fan of this feature.
Also when you're dead you cannot communicate with people still playing. I really don't like this at all because many times you have players who don't know what they're doing and they just wander aimlessly all over the map for what seems like forever and there's nothing you can do to help them because you can't voice or text chat with them. Be prepared to spend a lot of time waiting to play in this game or leaving and joining other servers.
The game also has magically respawning zombies. Like teleporting right before your very eyes. Blah.
So, given all the negative stuff I mentioned I still think the game's ok. Because the challenging nature of it is addicting (and also prone to make you ragequit). The atmosphere is dark and spooky. The levels are well designed. The child zombies are a nice creepy touch. When you die and restart, the previous objectives you had routinely changes so it doesn't feel stale. It takes patience to play and truly feels rewarding when you manage to survive and get rescued. And best of all it's free.
Would I recommend this if it wasn't free? Based on the crude attitude of some of the devs and their inability to fix the broken gameplay, the answer is a resounding NO.
But since it is free you should give it a try and don't give up right away when you notice the game's flaws. Try to play through an objective-based game (There are two game modes, objective and wave. I recommend objective more.) See if you like it. And if you end up hating it, well, I totally understand that too.

Man, this game is a large and heavy chunk of nostalgia, and it is a nice quality game too, if only it had a larger community.
Say, you're playing Age of Empires. You create a villager, and that's it. That guy goes to collecting food, maybe farming, or maybe mines gold, but he's your average villager guy at his best.
But Cultures takes a way different approach. You want to create a villager? You don't create him, you have to be born him! And same way, as that guy is born, he grows up, and becomes a "Civilian", and then, you're free to do what your heart desires with him.
But of course, even that desire is limited. Say, you want him to be a potter? Now that's possible, assuming you had some clay extractor somewhere and he is skilled enough to be a potter. Or maybe you already have another potter. Then you can train him at a school, otherwise, you need to make him go through the dirty work too. Clay extracting, I mean.
As the game says, "every Viking is unique!". Every of them has different skills, and your Vikings will become even proficient in their, well, "proficiences", as they work or fight.
The game also has a nice combat system if you ask me, it is not bulk "spam soldiers and go fight", but you can also work wonders with a few soldiers fully equipped with longswords, plate armours and a few amulets on them.
Building a village is way fun tho, it might get a bit repetive, but that speed-up button serves that purpose quite well if you ask me.
If you like strategy games, but bored of usual way the things go, you should try Cultures. It is some different approach out here, and hell, it is very cheap here on Steam!
...I wish they had implemented the Steam client to the game tho, oh well! It is still some nice bargain here.

I am going to break this into 3 parts, singleplayer, multiplayer, and cooperative.
Singleplayer: 5.5 out of 10, fun to play, doesn't get too bogged down. Props to Kevin Spacey for acting the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it.
Multiplayer: 3.5 out of 10, suffers from the same flaws as previous editions, some enhancements and flaws thanks to the new abilities. Server ping is a joke.
Cooperative: 8 out of 10, something new, instead of survival and relying on team mates to revive you in the midst of a 400 goons+ attack, you can let your team mates die, instead of having to run into the middle of a pack of goons, and better yet, they keep their kit. I rate this.
Spoilers will follow;
Singleplayer:
1- I am F#$KING SICK OF "THE GOOD GUY IS REALLY THE BAD GUY". Please, Activision, nearly everything you've done since you focused on WW2 has had this same tired plot device. It's not inventive, hell, I could see it coming a mile away.
2- I am just as sick of having to do missions where I have no 'real' control. In the final mission, I have to stop a giant missile full of bio-weapons from firing, and am in an exosuit running down a fire filled launchway. This was stupid, because I was on fire in a fire filled environment and would have cooked to death. None of your future gadgets can stop me from realising the stupidity. Next, I could only fire at the missile once I got to the end of the corridor thanks to 'fake' control, aka, through the exhaust gasses, and only once I got almost directly UNDER the ♥♥♥♥ing rocket engine. Lastly, on this point, rockets don't take 5 minutes to take off from ignition. It's pretty bad for the fuel supply.
3- What's with our new main character? He looks like a nerd. IS this because you want to touch your audience on a subliminal level? He has mangy long hair, his facial hair is something similar to a 19 year old uni student... actually, ♥♥♥♥ it, I completely understand what you did there.
4- The campaign would have been mediocre if it wasn't for the inclusion of new abilities such as threat grenades and the exosuit, otherwise, it was the same campaign I have played over the last decade of COD.
5- Minor grumble, but when you have an 'action sequence' where I'm hanging off the side of a bus, or have to knife someone, don't give me exactly 1 second to see the prompt and act on it. I won't make it in time, and you'll reset to my last save, which was at the start of said scene, about 5 seconds prior. This annoys me, because there is no point to it. I get to replay the same situation, only I now know what button to mash because I did it earlier.
Remember 90's games? Weren't they hard? None of this 'respawn 5 seconds earlier' crap, it was 'continue from the start of the level?'.
Multiplayer:
Ok, real review. It's the last COD multiplayer with jumping and cloaking fields. The guns and upgrades are unlocked by player level and kill-rewards, so bad news if you're a casual looking to have fun, because you will be mercilessly gunned down the second you spawn, and some 12 year old will proceed to tea-bag your corpse and tell you he ♥♥♥♥ed your mum. Add to this, you are unfortunately in for LAG BY THE BUCKET. There are no dedicated servers at the time of writing, and the game suffers for it, with instinct being almost unplayable, even on my ASUS G75V. By searching for games to join of up to 800 ping, the server sets you up for failure.
Add to this, the fact that the way the weapons actually function in multiplayer is a joke. I'm not terrible at the game, (not great either), and I have got to level 49 on multiplayer before doing this review in order to build up a fair opinion. I often will shoot an AK-12 or Bal into a person, at least 5-6 shots center mass and they will turn around and 1-2 shot me. I often watch the kill-cam and confirm this, which makes me really wonder if they are just THAT GOOD or if there is something wrong with the programing.. Also, the laser weapon (not the attachment, the actual heavy weapon) is broken, and the term 'laser noob' is commonplace, as people wielding a couple of lasers can lock-down a hardpoint or domination game. The sniper rifles and side arms are all terrible, also, the melee option is a joke, with players able to slice you from several meters (a meter is about a yard) away at times. The submachine guns can sometimes pop you from about 100 meters away, and the assault rifle damage at times is a joke. Also, some players seem to have superhuman damage absorption abilities, as you can often watch a killcam with them on the red with blood all over their screen running at you and still knifing you to death, all whilst you are registering hits.
Cooperative:
The only genuinely enjoyable part of the game. No zombies now, they're gone, and I'm happy with that. Frankly, zombies was ruined when they made the last Zombies in COD Black Ops 2, where it was all hard, and no fun. I know, I regularly played Zombies with mates and we didn't laugh during the last Zombies like we did in original zombies or black ops. Also, an improvement over Modern Warfare 3's survival mode, as there are no juggernaughts, and enemies are not made of diamond and impervious to your bullets. This isn't to say it's not challenging, rather, the enemies are hard to kill because they are sneaky, and well armed, not because the developers are lazy and just dial up their health bar by 10% each round. Also, an improvement is no 'levels' to perk up on your character. Instead, weapons and abilities are unlocked during game as a reward for surviving. I like this, because it changes the challenge. In Modern Warfare 3, survival till level 25 because easy once I was level 40, because I just brought a machine gun with red dot, and mowed down enemies from a camping point with a sentry gun until the bots were too tough to hurt (that limit btw is about level 30, where you have 2 machine guns and a sentry gun, and so does your mate, and you don't kill anything with a full mag...).
All around, the game is fun. I say fun, not good. The gripes I have about the unoriginality with the single player and the broken multiplayer cause me to negatively view the game. I personally recommend survival, it's something you can enjoy with mates, and you don't need to have the levels and perks. As always, stay away from the multiplayer. I judged it not just because I knew what it was like in the past, but also because I actually have played through to level 49, and yes, I have the good guns with good upgrades, but I still get killed by those 12 year olds. That's ok, I can kick their♥♥♥♥♥at N64 Mario Kart or Sonic 2 on Megadrive.

I really couldn't figure out whether to recommend or not - it's just that Steam didn't put a 'meh' or 'in-the-middle' option. I recommend it to those patient enough to put up with the technical issues of this game, but don't recommend to those who want a perfect game right away or have a high standard.
Storyline: 7/10
I liked it for what it's worth. The campaign length was decent and I didn't have too much trouble apart from the penultimate missions. The idea was pretty good to me, but ending was disappointing and noticable plot holes to say the least, it has a Sequel Hook to it, so guess what? There's gonna be AW2. Not going to spoil for anybody.
Graphics: 8/10
They're pretty good for a title like this, I really like the whole photo-realism thing, I thought the campaign cutscenes were live-action because of how lifelike they were. For some reason, this game likes to take my PC to its limits and stutter, which is one of the technical issues marring the experience.
Gameplay: 8/10
Single-Player mechanics are well-implemented, most of the time. I found it annoying to fight the red-helmet guys 'cause these fellows take more than a clip or an exo-punch to defeat them. The game mechanics weren't too hard to remember or master. I feel that the new exo-suit mechanics are pretty gimmicky (Double-jumping and quicks sidestepping = so much dodging to delay the inevitable), but that's the point of Advanced Warfare.
Sound: 8/10
Sound design is good, but for some reason one patch broke the cutscene voice audio, making voices in them almost inaudible and totally breaks immersion within the campaign. You hear your usual gun-shots, explosion effects, war chatter, ambiance, etc. Nothing much to say here.
Exo Survival: 6/10
I found it to be the weakest link of the game, it's like a combination of MW3's Survival Mode (Buying guns and doing objectives) and CoD Ghosts' Extinction Mode (Classes). Enemies in this mode are quite relentless, even on the Regular difficulty. These guys are no pushover unlike the campaign grunts. Difficulty curve for me to be honest was somewhat high, I could only get to round 8 solo before being overwhelmed by the cloaked troops, so it's best to have three more buddies to help you out and plan out ways to defeat the waves. To be honest, this reminds me of CoD: BO - Declassified for PS VIta's Hostiles mode since the enemies encircle you and back you in a corner, which isn't a good thing for me, but at least I gotten farther into that than AW's Exo Survival!
Multiplayer: 8/10
Ahh, the meat and potatoes of Call of Duty. It's safe to say while it has potential, the multiplayer has issues of its own. Connection issues, lack of Dedicated servers, unbalanced weapons, and lag hurt the experience, but this is only the beginning, Sledgehammer's probably trying to figure out how to short these issues while we're trashing on the game. It's fun, has your usual modes like Team Deathmatch, Kill Confirmed, Capture the Flag, etc along with some new modes. This is where I do and don't recommend the game. If you're a picky person who wants their multiplayer to be optimal, this game isn't for you, if you're a person who wants to chill for a couple of games go for it, the choice is yours.
Overall: 7.2/10
CoD is oversaturated and being milked to death, but it couldn't hurt to give this a try if you've been a long-time CoD player and haven't played one of the newer ones for a long time or at all, there's at least a second chance, but other than that, it's a hard choice to pass or buy. I wouidn't recommend dropping $59.99 with or without taxes though, just wait for a sale, I'd say less than $30 would be worth it. Bought this game for $44 and despite feeling ripped off, I still enjoy the game.

Generally the only mode is arena fight with many varieties and rule sets, tournament, survival etc. All things you have to unlock though playing story mode. Overall, easy to learn and casual friendly fighting game but still satisfiying. +You don't have to spent weeks to learn any combos, because they are straightforward like in Musou games. Very good if you just want beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your opponent, without training a lot, basics are enough to play in comfortable level.
I wish there was more games like that, maybe from: JoJo, Fist of the North Star franchise, anyway looking forward to the Berserk game, next year.

Okay, this game has gotten some negative reviews, mostly (at the time of writing) about the hunger/life-bar. Going by them though you'd miss out on a very neat game, let me tell you why.
Essentially, this game is very similar to the Adventure Island series for the NES, which started as a retool of the Wonderboy game. You're on an epic quest to save your girlfriend from a continent-sized prehysteric monster. You chase after her through a series of levels with their own themes (swamp/forest/desert/cave/lavacave/etc.), collect power-ups, food and dino-eggs in order to make travelling and finding hidden things easier. You also have to face big bosses and be speedy about going through the levels due to the hunger/life bar.
So far, it sounds like you just need to shave your character to find Master Higgins, but the truth is that Dinocide has some of its own charms and flaws. Big point on the charm side is that each level has at least one hidden something, be that a crystal, a mecha or a group photo of the dev team. Each level has a fun design with surprisingly detailed bg's. Downsides are that the hunger bar depletes quickly and that you can't return to a previous level so exploring them takes multiple playthroughs. Bottom line is though that while most of the challenge comes from the hunger bar, it is a very fun game and definitely worth the price.

A major nostalgia trip. The Cultures series is one of my absolute favorites and I still hold out hope for another; a modern game. Nothing has really changed about the game except the resolutions supported, and maybe the music quality, but I'm not sure about that one. I've sought games similar to Cultures and have never found anything that I have felt quite the same about. It is a great series, pure and simple.
My only real disappointment is that FUNimation has STILL not publicly released the REAL scenario editor. The one that comes with the game is extremely limited in function and has always been that way. I really don't know the reason why some people are allowed to have it and the rest get the dumbed-down version. It's been over a decade since this game was released! Why don't we get to breathe new life into it?
Cultures will remain an important part of my gaming history; it is the series that piqued my interest in RTS/Strategy/Economic games. Managing my economy and trade were my favorite activities, and are important functions that I look for now.
This game is worth far more to me than $5, and I'm really grateful that 2 of the games landed here on Steam.

I still have my disc for the original Cultures game and seriously love the whole series. I'm so glad there's now a legitimate way to get Northland and 8th Wonder in Australia because they were never released here. I played 8th Wonder last night and got sucked into it again for 3+ hours. The games are sort of a mix between age of empires, the sims, banished and anno. There's production lines but everything is a little more personal as you have to sort of micromanage the Vikings, including telling them to get married, assigning them jobs and dwellings and telling them to have children etc. Unlike Anno there is a little bit of fighting with several types of 'soldiers' etc but I tend to play on Free Play and just focus on building big civilizations. I still like the graphics style now and the music/sounds aren't too bad either. Overall still love the games and look forward to playing more!

I loved this game as a kid and can happily say this release works perfectly. It supports modern HD resolutions (up to 1080) and I had no problem running the game. The fps is still low which is understandable for a 2D game but it means window scrolling is a little janky.
The game itself is a commodity based city builder that focuses on population and resource management over combat. It's unique from other games I've played like that because you control the lives of individual people, tell someone to become a farmer and they will, then promote them to a miller, then to baker, or send them to school so they can learn to be a tailor or a brewer. This is central to the games mechanics. It's The Sims crossed with Anno or Age of Empires and although it's not quite as strategic as AeO I can remember sinking 60+ hours into single levels just because it's so fun bulding and running your colony. It could have some more depth but I enjoy it a lot.
------BUG FIX------
If you're getting bugs while trying to play the game you can download a program called DXWnd found here:
As I said in my review, I haven't had any troubles so haven't done this personally but people who have told me this worked for them. I have used this method on other games so I trust it.
- After extracting the file run the 'dxwnd' .exe
- A little blank window will open, select the 'edit' menu and click 'add'
- A window with a bunch of options and tabs will open, fill them out as follows:
- "NAME:" = 8th Wonder(can be anything you like)
- "PATH:" = C:\Program Files\Steam\SteamApps\common\Cultures 8th Wonder\Game.exe
Note: you may have the game installed at a different location eg. "Program Files (x86)"
That's it, Hit OK and you should see '8th Wonder' appear as an option from the window that was blank before.
- Select it and go >edit>run and the game will run smoothly
You will have to launch the game using this program or have DXWnd open when launching it from steam every time.
DXWnd is a hook program that you can use to get a lot of old games running smoothly on new systems. I didn't create DXWnd.
is a trustworthy site for developers and you can get more support from the guy who made the program there if you need it.
As I said, I haven't had to use this fix myself so if you find any settings in dxwnd that improve performance even more let me know in a comment below and I'll add it.

I think based on what the Dev had to work with, they did an pretty ok job. The game feels very good in the sense that it possesses a creepy atmosphere, and the controls are very easy. While the voice acting is by no means fantastic, I have certainly heard worse. the music is minimal but it fits in fine. Figuring out the puzzles was not difficult, but that's subjective. If you're good at solving puzzles, this game may not be challenging for you. If you just looking for a bit of fun (an hour at most), then this may suit you. Unfortunatly, while there are two routes to reaching the end, the end is exactly the same no matter how you get there. There are no moral choices to be made, and how you solve the puzzels seems to not make a difference. The overarching mystery will remain unsolved no matter what you do, which I find disappointing. This game is more aimed at an escape rather than uncoving the mystery. That said, considering it is a free game, and the fact that it works fine (no crashing, only one point that caused a noticable FPS drop, and only one or two non-game-breaking visual bugs), I would say if you think you may enjoy it, there is no harm in giving it a try. The series begins with a monkey-tailed boy named Goku befriending a teenage girl named Bulma, whom he accompanies to find the seven Dragon Balls (ドラゴンボール Doragon Bōru?), which summon the dragon Shenlong to grant the user one wish. The journey leads them to the desert bandit Yamcha, who later becomes an ally; Chi-Chi, whom Goku unknowingly agrees to marry; and Pilaf, an impish man who seeks the Dragon Balls to fulfill his desire to rule the world. Goku then undergoes rigorous training regimes under the martial arts master Kame-Sen'nin in order to fight in the Tenkaichi Budōkai (天下一武道会?, "Strongest Under the Heavens Martial Arts Tournament"). A monk named Kuririn becomes his training partner and rival, but they soon become best friends. After the tournament, Goku searches for the Dragon Ball his Grandfather left him and almost single-handedly defeats the Red Ribbon Army and their hired assassin Taopaipai. Thereafter Goku reunites with his friends to defeat the fortuneteller Baba Uranai's fighters and have her locate the last Dragon Ball to revive a friend killed by Taopaipai.
At the Tenkaichi Budōkai three years later Goku and his allies oppose Kame-Sen'nin's rival and Taopaipai's brother, Tsuru-Sen'nin, and his students Tenshinhan and Chaozu. Kuririn is killed after the tournament and Goku tracks down and is defeated by his killer, Piccolo Daimao. The samurai Yajirobe takes Goku to the hermit Karin, where he receives healing and a power boost. Meanwhile Piccolo fights Kame-Sen'nin and Chaozu, leading to both their deaths, and uses the Dragon Balls to regain his youth before destroying Shenlong. Goku then kills Piccolo Daimao, who, just before dying, spawns his son/reincarnation Piccolo Jr.. Karin then directs Goku to Kami-sama, the original creator of the Dragon Balls, to restore Shenlong and revive his slain friends. Goku trains under Kami for the next three years, once again reuniting with his friends at the Tenkaichi Budōkai, where he narrowly wins against Piccolo Jr. before leaving with Chi-Chi to keep his promise to marry her.
Five years later, Goku is a young adult and father to his son Gohan, when Raditz arrives on Earth, identifies Goku as his younger brother 'Kakarrot' and reveals to him that they are members of a nearly extinct extraterrestrial race called the Saiyans (サイヤ人 Saiya-jin?), who sent Goku to conquer Earth for them, until he suffered a severe head injury and lost all memory of his mission. Goku refuses to continue the mission, sides with Piccolo, and sacrifices his life to defeat Raditz. In the afterlife Goku trains under the North Kaiō until he is revived by the Dragon Balls to save the Earth from the invading Nappa and Vegeta. In the battle Yamcha, Chaozu, Tenshinhan, and Piccolo are killed, and the Dragon Balls cease to exist. Kuririn and the galactic tyrant Freeza learn of another set of Dragon Balls on planet Namek (ナメック星 Namekku-sei?), whereupon Bulma, Gohan, and Kuririn search for them to revive their friends and subsequently the Earth's Dragon Balls, leading to several battles with Freeza's minions and Vegeta, the latter standing alongside the heroes to fight the Ginyu Force, a team of mercenaries. The long battle with Freeza himself comes to a close when Goku transforms into a Super Saiyan (超サイヤ人 Sūpā Saiya-jin?) of legends and defeats him.
A group of Androids (人造人間 Jinzōningen?, "Artificial Humans") created by a member of the former Red Ribbon Army, Doctor Gero, appear three years later, seeking revenge against Goku. During this time, an evil life form called Cell also emerges and, after absorbing two of the Androids to achieve his "perfect form," holds his own fighting tournament to challenge the protagonists. After Goku sacrifices his own life to no avail, Gohan avenges his father by defeating Cell. Seven years later, Goku, briefly revived for one day, and his allies are drawn into a fight against Majin Boo. After numerous battles, including destruction and re-creation of the Earth, Goku destroys Boo with a Genki-Dama (a sphere of pure energy drawn from all intelligent beings on Earth) and wishes for him to be reincarnated as a "good person." Ten years later, at another Tenkaichi Budōkai, Goku meets Boo's human reincarnation, Oob. Leaving their match unfinished, Goku departs with Oob to train him to be Earth's new guardian.

Anyways, here's my review. At frst glance the whole interface seems very confusing, but believe me... After a few hours you begin to realise the great potential this game has. Over the years, shooting zombies became mainstream. I mean really? You pick up a gun and fight through the horde on your own. This game manages to achieve something different. It's extremely unsettling and disturbing in a strange and unique way. I've been lanning this with my brother lately, and halfway through the missions you start getting a very strange feeling. It draws you in so well that you end up feeling like it really is a situation of life or death. Also, the maps are extremely difficult to clear, and once you get through one objective map, it feels GREAT! The sense of achievement is absolutely overwhelming and the joy of escaping with someone you know is brilliant! Beating a map will not only require practice and skill, but cooperation too. This is probably what stands out the most in NMRIH. You can go on and about grabbing all the weapons etc but believe me, you won't make it out alive on your own. It's about time we stop mindlessly gunning through hordes and use tactics as well as teamwork to progress through a game.
Thanks to the developers for creating a masterpiece.

As the Sequel to what most people intend to be one of the Best RPG's ever made, Dark Souls 2 had a lot to live up to. And guess what? It does, impressively. Just like the original, you are a hollowing undead, bent on breaking the curse. The gameplay is very similar to the first, however, the mechanics are different JUST ENOUGH where your Dark Souls 1 experience may not matter as much as you think it should. This, in turn, makes the game just as refreshingly difficult as picking up DS 1 for the first time. The enemies in Dark Souls 2 are, strictly in my opinion, minorly lacking in comparison to the first. While the first had incredibly intimidating fights, strong, immense challenge, the second falls a bit short. The Bosses in Dark Souls 2 are, at times, almost a pushover for the moderate player. During my first playthrough ( in which i never summoned assistance), I died a scarce amount of times... to bosses.
The mobs around the areas you explore in Dark Souls 2 are among the top tier of difficulty. Some have powerful moves you won't realize until your moaning on the ground and spot the infamous "You Died" screen. Something I really am fond of, they never let go. You will continuously attempt to get through the various areas (all of which are gorgeously designed and textured) and will very rarely find two enemies with the same move set. ( Assuming you're comparing two different areas.)

All in all, Dark Souls 2 is a massive, difficult, and mystical achievement of a video game. Should you have not played the first, Dark Souls 2 is a great place to start. A game like this should be played by any hardcore gamer who looks to overcome a variety of immense challenges. ( Minus a few of the bosses ;) ).
