Been a huge Castlevania fan for years and figured I'd finally give this one a go since I heard it has a pretty decent story, but although I tried hard to enjoy it, I simply couldn't. That said, I still finished the game because I wanted to experience said story, but this will be the first and last time I ever play this game.
Boss battles are way too gimmicky and often rely on you climbing around and sh*t rather than actually fighting.
The climbing itself is also kinda badly implemented, with the character just ignoring grapple commands every so often, ending up in me falling to my death.
Oh, and the developer seem to really enjoy the concept of having the player actively pull a crank only to be interrupted by enemies when you're 80% done so you have to beat them and then do everything over again. That's happened 10-or-so times.
The biggest issue by far though is the camera. Who in their right mind uses preset camera angles in a third person game nowadays rather than giving the players control of it? There's a reason most developers have moved on from that formula.
There are also some pretty annoying bugs in the game, and if you keep reading, I'll give you an example.
(minor spoilers ahead)
I was searching for the last fairy in chapter 3 for quite a while (managed to miss that I could use the crank on a second gate), found it and went back to the ground floor to open up the fairy door. As usual, the gates before it had closed, so I turned the crank, some werewolves ambushed me and destroyed it, and then after I beat them, all my fairies were gone and I had to collect them all again.
Unless you're a diehard Castlevania fan who wants to play this game for the story, don't waste your money and time on it.

This is a very impressive game overall. The most impressive part is that unlike most other puzzle games, not everything that you interact with can be used! In fact, you may spend a solid 5 minutes trying to get a certain item, just to realize that what you needed was simply laying on the floor in another room. And even though some of the puzzles may seem unintuitive at first, they actually turn out to be quite logical when you look back on them. Well, except for the fact that you could just climb the fence and get out of the house :). The only other problem are some glitches that may cause you to start over from your last checkpoint (such as dropping through the map, your flashlight becoming stationary, etc.) But this isn't a big inconvenience since once you figure out the puzzle, you can most certainly make it back to where you were within one minute. Plus it's a in depth game, for free! I highly recommend giving it a go! If you're stuck on a puzzle, consider checking out my video!

What if SCP: Containment Breach but asymmetrical multiplayer game?
SCP: Secret Laboratory is pretty close to that. It was released recently (29 Dec 2017) so that means everyone is still fairly new, but not so new that they don't know how to play basically. A good time to test it although for me personally it can crash fairly frequently. There's no overall progress as such, but hopefully they can cut down on the crashes soon, as it means waiting in a respawn queue after a crash.
Game itself:
Up to 20 people can join one game, once there are 20 or if the connecting circle fills up the game starts.
The controls are simple and explained mostly in a tutorial (at least for D-Class, there are guides that explain differences in others).
Basically WASD, Tab for inventory, shift for sprint, C for silent walk(nobody takes advantage of that yet), space to jump, RMB/LMB to aim/fire, E to interact.
Once the game starts, you start as a random class, generally at the start the players are divided into lots of D-Class, at least 1 scientist, at least 1 animate hostile SCP (usually 2) such as 106, 173 or 049 and usually a 2nd SCP which could be 079. Then the remainder could possibly spawn as a group of up to 3 or so MTF(evacs scientists) or ChaosI(evacs D-Class), which are antagonists to each other and everything else. When people die or escape they'll respawn as MTF, CI or an SCP that hasn't been activated yet (4 total).
There doesn't seem to be a game timer, the game usually ends when all D-Class/Scientists are escaped/rescued and all SCPs neutralized, or when the nuclear warhead is detonated. If the SCPs are killing everyone, then in general people will continue to respawn as MTF/CI in large groups until the SCPs are overwhelmed. It might be possible for 049 to win as he can turn everyone into a playable zombie but I haven't seen it happen yet. I've had up to around 4 zombies as 049 mainly because I didn't figure out how to zombify until I reached the surface.
Besides running around and killing, the game area is divided into different sections. Generally you start in Light Containment with SCP-173. The other SCPs are a bit farther away in Heavy Containment. If you get through Heavy you can reach the Entrance area which contains the intercom and connects to the surface. Doors have different levels of security and there are upgradeable keycards to get into places, you can either find or steal from someone who dies or dropped one. You also need to upgrade a keycard to deploy the nuke from the surface, although there is an on/off switch somewhere inside the facility.
Summary:
It's free, early community is sociable/friendly/funny. The intercom room is pretty popular for funny messages and is used frequently by MTF (I think CI don't start with a keycard with Intercom access, only MTF Commander).
I recommend in this early period despite the crashes. Balance seems okay so far, that might change later as everyone gets familiar with the meta.

If you enjoy classic point and click adventure games, especially if you enjoyed the incredible "The Raven" which came out recently, DEFINITELY take a look at this gem.
It takes a little bit (getting past the first half hour of gameplay) to really get into it and used to the gameplay, but once the story kicks in, you won't be able to stop playing until you beat the game. Which will take an average adventure game player 3-4 hours in total - longer if you stop to smell the roses.
I found a few things to be a bit clunky though. Mainly the click to move, which wasn't as fluid as I'm used to, after being spoiled by such masterpieces as the Sherlock Holmes series by Frogwares, and the aforementioned "The Raven: Legacy of a Master Thief". I'd guess the movement awkwardness is due to the game being originally made for touch control - as it was released first on the iPad app store, AFAIK. A few of the puzzles might not be as obvious either, especially at the very beginning, when you're first learning the game's puzzle logic style. Again, once you get past the first half hour, and access the basement, things will start clicking until the game is complete.
The graphics are very charming, with engaging cutscenes and gorgeous environments and characters. The voice acting is quite funny - though I'm not sure that's always intentional. I wish the accent/voice work could've been as exceptional as Broken Age's/TellTalle games/Sherlock Holmes: CP/Ethan Carter/etc, as that would've made this game much more solid. The accent kinda sounds like an American imitating a Swiss/British accent, which can be kinda jarring at times. Some voice work/actors do a better job than others though.
The story is the strongest feature of this game, and is quite original and glorious. Much philosophical musing, and deep plotting awaits, with a good amount of emotional gravitas.

All in all, this game is well worth the affordable $10 ticket it carries. It's one of the better adventure games to come out this year, though not quite the caliber of Telltalegames or Frogwares best fare.
4/5 - Strong Recommend, especially for adventure game enthusiasts.

Perils of Man is a point-and-click adventure game, and a rather good one, at that.  The science-fiction premise is interesting, the emotional attachment becomes stronger as the game moves on, and the invention that factors so prominently into the storyline is quite original.
Pros:
+ Most puzzles are fairly logical and can be determined by thinking through the clues and items you've already uncovered.  One of the most satisfying feelings in an adventure game is to work something out in your head and then see that you were right.  For the most part, the game gives you what you need to figure out the problem logically.
+ The art style is charming, and the voice work is strong and distinctive for the most part.  Many of the bit-part NPCs even have distinctive speech styles and voices.  All of the main characters come through as individuals.
+ The characters are memorable and well-conceived.  The game does a good job of using story-driven narrative and small, but impactful, backstory detail to give emotional depth and substance to its characters.  Given the game has a playtime between 3-5 hours, efficient characterization is important.
+ Despite the efficiency of the characterization, nothing feels trite.  Similarly, the themes are not overdone.
Cons:
- I said that most of the puzzles were logical, but there are 2 in particular that don't make a great deal of intuitive or clue-based sense, which caused me some frustration.
- There are also some puzzles that are dependent less on visually spotting something and more on moving your mouse pointer over every inch of the screen's surface.  Not a new problem for adventure games, but sometimes the point at which the cursor would indicate something was spatially off from where the item or spot physically was in the gameworld.
- The same issue manifests itself when you have multiple hotspots close together, but one or more is not visually distinct from the surrounding items.
- There are some bugs.  Clicking on room/area entrance/exit transitions can be weird/misaligned at times, inventory slots can sometimes be more/less than the actual number of items you have (normally the game adjusts to match), and of course the aforementioned hotspot issue.
Overall:
There are some minor technical annoyances, and a couple of puzzles whose solutions are illogical and not hinted at in the game's clues, which can be frustrating.  But there are also many simple puzzles, as well as more complicated ones that are well-thought out and solvable within the game world.  This keeps the game moving, and provides a sense of satisfaction to the player.  It isn't the hardest adventure game ever, but the story, characters and voice-acting are all well-done, and by the endgame the emotional emphasis has ramped up considerably.  Given that the game should only take 3-5 hours to complete, and given the low cost, it seems easy to recommend Perils of Man despite its minor shortcomings.

Now let's get this out of the way, Dark Souls 2 certainly is a hard game... but not as hard as everyone is making it out to be. It's not unfairly difficult, it doesn't slay you over and over again just to make you cry. Instead, like ye olden days, Dark Souls uses "game design" to make you learn their game. So instead of rushing through and killing hordes of enemies in the next Dynasty Warriors, you're expected to pay attention and change your tactics.
Whilst you hold your shield up, your stamina won't replenish as fast and you might be stunned by the final blow. Whilst in a narrow corridor, try not to use a huge swinging axe, it just won't fit... nor do you have much chance to dodge. Accidentally caught the attention of a crowd of enemies however makes that same corridor a god sent. And if this isn't common gaming knowledge for you guys, we'll remind you by actually adding some penalty to your deaths... I would imagine after that you don't need an in game guide telling you not to jump down a pit.
So don't just believe everyone telling you how hardcore this game is, when you find a message near a cliff suggesting you should consider a leap of faith I'd imagine you'd use that healthy brain of yours to actually think for once... which certainly is rare during gaming nowadays.

I consider this the pinnacle of twin-stick arcade shooters. I go on benders with this game so long that the brightly colored shapes burn into my brain and I see them behind closed eyelids. I've been a fan of the series since the first one (the mini-game) and watched it grow, and this iteration is leagues ahead of its predecessors as well as any similar titles you might find on Steam. The production values are top-notch and the gameplay is finely tuned and addictive & varied enough to keep you playing for hours and coming back for more. From the slick menus to the creative, psychedelic 3-dimensional level designs and variety of ways to approach them, it's clear the developers put a lot of love and effort into this. However, what impressed me most wasn't the polished presentation, but rather the variations on the basic types of gameplay modes and how they translate over to 3 dimensions. There are still flat-surfaced levels, but on the 3D stages, you (and your enemies, the types and behaviors of which are vast) have command of the entire surface which is sometimes covered with stragetically placed walls and other interactive objects. This opens up worlds of new possibilities, and the developers clearly explored a large amount of them. In fact, a recent free update (in which "Evolved" was added to the game's subtitle) introduced even more level designs. With the attention to detail and sheer amount of gameplay elements - some of which are continually being added - you really get the feeling that this is a labor of love for the folks at Sierra.
I'd like to address a very common complaint I've noticed: the difficulty. When I first started playing this, I agreed that it was insanely difficult and the learning curve too steep, but after spending a few hours with it, I felt increasingly comfortable and began to advance quite quickly through the adventure mode. In fact, a few days after getting this, I revisited those early stages I initially had so much trouble with and wound up getting the full 3 star score on all of them with relative ease. It's true that the amount of enemies on screen at one time and the frantic pace at which the game operates can be extremely overwhelming to people not used to it (as can the cheesy techno soundtrack), but it is not impossible. If you have at least decent hand-eye coordination and a twin-stick controller (and I cannot stress how important it is to use a modern, dual analog stick controller like the Xbox 360's with this game), rest assured, you'll get the hang of it. And this is one game most definitely worth getting the hang of.

After playing Lamment of Innocence on the PS2 back in the say, this game has really shaped that entire era to a whole new level of hack and slash of Castlevania. Judging by the trailer I given this game the benefit of a doubt to impress me and....it did! Just everything about this game was just spot on for both the graphics, characters, and the story altogether.
The narrator, Patrick Stewart, is simply one of the best to choose this role and being the character who helps Gabrielle Belmont on his question to conquor the Lords of Shadow to bring his wife back from the dead from Earth to Hell itself. Let's talk about this for a minute....
From what we know of the series, if you ever followed the past games, that Castlevania entirely means that you approach the castle to defeat the same boss as always name Count Dracula. But this time there is just "a castle" and the rest is land with one trail to go to (so thankfully no open world) from start to finish. Instead of defeating Count Dracula you have a new arch-enemy to defeat, the almighty skin of evil himself, Satan. Yes, Satan himself is who you have to defeat. Before that you must defeat the Lords of Shadow in order to get to him and retreive something to bring Gabrielle's love back to life.
Besides the story the gameplay and graphics really stand out in Konami standards making everything look far more realistic and blending in what the characters represent. Smooth controls for a hack and slash game, fun puzzles, and just seeing the beauty of the scenery is just simply to die for. From being more nature as it gradually becomes grimmer the more you lurk to the later stages  which is both nostalgia and new at the same time. And instead of equipping a whole bunch of equipment like you do in the previous Castlevania games you get enhancements that utilizes throughout the entire game for a better strategy. Just amazing!
I highly recommend getting this game, I love it while playing on the Xbox 360 and would give another go on Steam!

** This is the first review that I've ever written on steam ** Why? Becuse this game is DAMN GOOD. One of the best games I've ever played in recent years and I don't say that lightly. The gameplay is superb but it's not just about that. The game is very, how should I put this, alive. What Arkane has done here is nothing short of impressive.
The game has a believable world where you can see people live in. It also offers some background stories and lores around the characters you meet along the way, further enriching the story and make yourself even more immersed into the game. On top of that, the gameplay is great! It doesn't matter whether you want to go guns blazing or play stealthily, the game manages to cater to both type of players.
Story is interesting so far, graphic while not so great is counterbalanced by the great art direction. Level design is AMAZING!!! Last game that had level design as good as this is Deus Ex: Mankind Divided. Players are offered with many options on how to complete a specific objective, how to sneak up on enemies, which road the player can take to reach a destination, etc.
So..., why can't I recommend this game then? I mean, so far I've been gushing how good the game is, so what's the problem? One word, PERFORMANCE.
OH. MY. GOSH. the performance in this game is terrible!! I am running a GTX 1080 and i7 4790k and I have to drop down the graphical preset to "medium" (I'm playing on Ultrawide monitor 2560 X 1080) in order to get a playable framerate (50-60 FPS). The performance is SO bad and I just can't recommend the game to anyone EXCEPT those who has GTX 1080 / GTX 1070 / Titan X Pascal. Even then you will have to drop some settings to get playable frame rate.
It's extremely unfortunate because I know that underneath this (huge) performance problem, the game is ABSOLUTELY AMAZING! However, for now, I really can't recommend it to anyone except for those with high end GPUs/CPUs
TL;DR:
The game itself = 9/10 -- Freakin' AMAZING!
Optimisation = 4/10 -- Absolute TRASH!

BROFORCE!!! Just as epic as it sounds, guns, bombs, explosive tanks just lying around asking to be shot, tactical swine, this game has it all!

Silly, stupid, and totally OTT - Broforce is a great side-scrolling shooter, laced with direct references to many 80s and 90s action film characters.
Each member of the Broforce team you manage to free along the way, swaps your controlling character to that newly liberated player. Bruce Willis, Arnie, Mr.T, Stallone, Robocop, Wesley Snipes (as Blade) - are all here, amongst others. What's better - is that each character has their own unique weapon and special weapon too.
Where Broforce really shines however, is that the level and scenery itself plays a BIG part in your progression. Manage to detonate a few fuel tanks close to a group of enemies? Not only will the explosion take out the immediate foes, but if a suicide bomber is amongst them - he in turn will trigger a further explosion. Such well placed shots add further enjoyment to the game as it can end up where the enemies themselves take each other out.
For the price, I cannot recommend it highly enough. I just hope that there will be future DLCs or expansions for it. 9/10

I wish my verdict could be kinder than these two words: Wasted potential.
The fantastic premise could have offered so much more in terms of character development, storytelling and most importantly: MEANINGFUL CHOICES. At least in the end, multiple choices for multiple endings would have saved some grace.
Because you know: for a game with a story that dramatically emphasizes the worth of risk and the consquences of change, the whole plot, down to every little segment in this story is tightly on rails.
At least point'n'click games of the TellTale variety *try* to give players a somewhat individual way of navigating the broadly pre-defined story - in Perils, all important choices are entirely made by Ana, without any player involvement whatsoever.
The result is a game that utterly betrays the very lesson it is trying to sell story-wise.

I pray to Dark Souls every night before I go to bed. This game is not nearly as good.
While this game does have some strong points, it is ultimately plagued by gameplay that I feel is very uninspired, repetitive, and heavily scripted. That is ultimately why I do not recommend this game. I wanted to like this game as I am a fan of the old-school castlevania games myself (which are quite superior)
Pros:
- Graphics that look good even now. . . .6 years after it has been released. They are especially good if you install the helix mod and sweetfx mod.
- The game has some nice music, but the game needs to use it more often.
- Combat, overall, is quite nice. If you are a god of war or DMC fan, you will enjoy it. However, I didn't like it that much as I heavliy prefer Dark Souls styled combat to this game. Level Design and Camera also makes combat worse as I will explain in a moment.
- The game is prettly lengthy at 20+ hours.
- Story so far is. . . . .a mixed bag for me. It doesn't complement the other elements of the game as it is a little confusing and dis-jointed. It is interesting, but it isn't flushed out enough to really take a from that I can like.
Cons:
- Camera: This game is the perfect example of why giving players the ability to control the camera is so important. Even if the camera is always positioned perfectly in platforming and combat (which it isn't all of the time as I am often fighting enemies off-screen) the game encourages the player to explore the level and find secrets. However, it is hard to do and painful with a camera that can't be controlled.
- The level design of this game is uninspired and repetitive. First, there's a flat area where you fight monsters. Then, there's a platforming section that feels heavily scripted with the ledge-jumping and gripping mechanics that the game has. Then, more fighting in flat areas where the environment doesn't change how the fighting happens. To be fair, the game introduces a little bit of variety through giving the player new abilities, weapons, and creatures to fight a lot of the time, but that doesn't change the fact that the environments do not add any depth to the gameplay. Castlevania 4, on the other hand, had many areas where the environment greatly affected how you fought enemies, and platforming was fun and not scripted in that game. Combat and Platforming complemented each other and made the game extremely fun and varied. However, Castlevania: Lord of Shadows has bland combat and bland platforming sprinkled throughout the game. If it weren't for the good combat mechanics, I'd feel like this game would be terrible.
- A lot of boss battles are just glorified Quick-Time events. I HATE quick-time events in a game. There are also times when I fight bosses where I have no idea what I'm suppose to do because the game doesn't properly communicate anything to me, and these boss fights aren't like the "Legend of Zelda" bosses where you have fun figuring out how to fight the bosses. You might be hanging on the side of a boss when the boss just knocks you off of him without the game giving any clear indication of how to prevent that form happening. Remember that these fights feel heavily scripted, and creativity just doesn't help when you are restricted in the scripted-style climbing that the game requires of you. To be fair, though, the bosses in the game look awesome, and it's cool climbing up their gigantic form.
- The game plays terribly with keyboard and mouse. A controller is REQUIRED.
Overall, I do not recommend this game. The game doesn't really have anything redeeming quality that makes it stand out and worth purchasing, and the combat and story are only decent. There isn't really anything that really "carries" this game and makes it better than others. It would be an good game if it didn't have the major issues that turned me off. Even if the 6 year-old graphics are impressive, visuals do NOT make a game.
But even if the game is only mediocre, I'll still finish the game. I'm interseted to see where the game goes from here, and I want to make this review "complete."

I've been playing Smite for a couple of years and out of all mobas i've tried this one is the least annoying and aggravating... mostly due to the fact that there aren't as many kids playing or the fact that you can't talk to enemy team or voice chat in game.
Yes there can be quite a lot of rage from your own team and after the match but overall losing is not as punishing and enraging here as in the most moba's.
You could say that Smite is more "casual" than other moba's. This is due to the fact that there are different game modes on different maps, some of which are easier and faster than classic 3 lanes mode. Third person view and actual targeting make this game even easier on most characters. Ability to surrender at 10 minutes also hastens the process.
There are however some issues and oversights which unfortunately make this game inferior to Dota 2:
1) Matchmaking. Its downright horrible here. The game apparently tries to put experienced played with less experienced players and often ends up grouping really new players against several good players. In fact you often get a 5 stack clan or team versus 5 solo que players which is quite bad for a competitive game. Quite a lot of times i've ended up with someone who apparently just started playing on my team and someone who's been playing for years on the other team and had a much higher rating than anyone on my team and vice-versa. Grouping up with lower level players also allows to get some easy wins.
Basically - the matchmaking is nearly completely random in here.
2) Bugs and reconnecting issues. Servers are prone to crashing in Smite and disconnects are quite common as well. The worst part is often being unable to reconnect or when it happens after you already won and it doesn't count as a win. You often get "deserter" status as well which will prevent you from queuing again for some time and lose your goodwill which adds a bonus amount of points each game. Its impossible to get a single day without at least several games where someone would crash or dc.
3) Disconnecting players. They are VERY common. Unless you are playing with your clan - get ready for 1 or 2 people dc'ing and often not coming back. Especially in Arena and Assault modes. Either due to bugs or their pc's or whatever. The worst part is - there is no handicap. You can't get more gold, you can't control or swap to other gods. You will get slightly more XP but more often than not it won't help you much. Unfortunately the game will still count towards your won/lost count and you can't leave it early. In fact - you can't safely leave games at all here, unless you surrender after 10 minutes.
4) Bots. Basically there is no point in playing versus them. You don't get any rewards (besides miserable amount of points, no xp, no gems) and they are almost completely passive and absolutely dumb. The bots in Dota 2 at least know how to gank up on someone and can pose some challenge while in Smite you can destroy them alone with your main attack. As a result there is no way to practice at all before playing versus people. The bots haven't been updated and no new bots were ever added.
5) Complete imbalance of some gods. Unfortunately there appears to be only two way new characters are released - either they are so weak they require 3-4 patches or even an overhaul to become viable, or they are so overpowered you just roll your eyes and hold on until you can surrender. This appears to be a result of clashing between a couple of devs, one of which keeps pushing for OP characters and the other one keeps adding weird "special needs and situations" characters. Recently they've released Khepri which is the only one god that can resurrect people and counters quite a lot of other gods in most situations and they released Ravana which is mostly useless despite receiving 5 or 6 buffs already. Before that we had Nox which received an overhaul... but it took almost a year for devs to admit she was useless. Unfortunately it takes weeks before devs fix broken overpowered characters and even more to buff underpowered characters. To this day they haven't done anything to Bellona which quite often becomes indestructible or to Ah Puch which basically guarantees you can win in an assault mode.
6) The store. There is no way to refund your purchases, no way to sell your skins, no way to get some skins if you just started playing and missed beta or special events. Personally i feel like they overprice their skins as well. While the top tier skins often look nice they come no where near the quality you get from Arcana or even simpler items in Dota 2. The different voice lines are nice though. 8000 gems (80 euros or 90$) would get you about 10-20 different tier skins and a few voice packs, provided you buy chests and during sales. In Dota 2 i've made some money just by playing and getting items or investing in some items and reselling them. In Smite it feels like im just throwing the money away and not getting enough in return. Not to mention that you don't get all gods for free and either have to buy a god pack for 20 bucks/euros or play free rotation gods.
7) Graphics. No way around it - they are quite dated. On the other hand - game is not as demanding resource wise as Heroes of the Storm for example. You do get a feeling that you playing an older game though. Hopefully they'll update the graphics someday and add DirectX11 support.
I would recommend not spending your money on it unless you played for at least half a year. I would also recommend waiting for special events (like upcoming Odyssey this winter) or tickets with multiple rewards or 50% sales on chests. I would also not recommend going into Conquest (classic) mode right away and trying Arena or Assault first as they are faster, easier and more enjoyable for new players. The perfect starting gods are Ares and Neith, which are available for free and probably two most versatile characters in the game, Ares being able to support (meaning tanking in Smite) and deal damage, and Neith being able to deal a lot of damage, disable and escape.
Overall the game can be fun and can provide you with an easy, less challenging experience than most moba's. You can easily learn some of the gods and if you can master some of the harder ones you can become one of the Bellona's or Ao Kuang's that everyone hates.

So I'm going to just jump in, SMITE is a free-to-play MOBA (Multiplayer Online Battle Arena) but unlike other MOBAs where it's a traditional Top-Down View, where you have to click everywhere to move and activate spells. SMITE does it differently with instead it is a third-person camera and you have to aim almost all of your moves to your oppenents. Now that might sound a little bit difficult, but after some practice you will get the hang of it, infact the aiming system is realitively simple. Now the third-person camera makes get put into the action, so if you find other MOBAs to slow pased or too boring, try out SMITE its free and you won't regret it.
Now for Characters: There are 60+ at the moment, and they each have there own stats,abilities,passives,personalites,voice acting, skins,etc. And are fairly balanced so that way no one is more broken or over powered most of the time...Unless it is a new god...I am talking to you Xing Tian
Now for Maps: At the moment there are 5, (Arena, Joust, Siege, Conquest, Assault) and they are there so that way if you don't like the main mode of the game "Conquest" you won't be stuck with nothing else to do, so they added 4 other extremely fun game modes to do instead! Arena is basically just a killing fest, it's a small arena with a 5v5 just go head to head trying to push their minions to the opposing teams base, Joust is one lane 3v3 with side jungles and you try to push up the opposing teams Titan (Which is the objective in SMITE, is too destroy their Titan), Siege is a 4v4 with 2 lanes, too push to the titan and a objective in the middle which is a monster which helps you push to their titan. Conquest is the main game mode with it being like other MOBAs with the traditional 3 lanes +Jungle + Neutral Monsters which drop buffs once defeated to help you win. Now Assault my personal favorite is ALL RANDOM GODS, ONE LANE NO JUNGLE, NO RETURNING BACK TO BASE OR STORE TIL DEATH. Sorry I just really love that game mode.
Now Items: This game comes with an Item Builder for your gods if you do not know what to buy, I recommend this for beginners because the items it builds are relatively decent and you should perform well with them, however I HIGHLY ENCOURAGE YOU LEARN WHAT TO BUILD, don't rely on Item Builder til your level 30 like I did xD. You will regret. The Items are easy to learn with you being either Physical or Magical the shop items will change to whichever ones you are, because unlike in other MOBAs, if your character is Magical or Physical your abilites will ONLY scale to that.
Now for quick questions:
Is SMITE Pay-to-Win?: NO, like no... if you think a god is too broken or too op it is more likey you just don't know how to play against them OR they are a new god which will be balanced in the next patch if they are broken. And the only thing you can buy in SMITE are gems which gives you things like Skins.Gods.Boosters for Favor,Ward Skins,etc. But just because you don't own a god and the other person bought him with gems does not make it pay to win.
Can I only buy gods with gems?: No smite has a built in currency system to where everytime after you finish a match you will be awarded A DECENT amount of favor, fluctuating on whether you win or lose of course and unlike in other
MOBAs it does not cost a ridiculous amount of money to buy them, instead its a fair 5500 for each and every god.
How is the community is it as toxic as (Insert MOBA here): The community is relatively nice in my opinion with their like every community some annoying people who think they are better but hey thats what the Mute Button is for and you can block them after the game to never play with them again. :^)
So finally yes I HIGHLY recommend this game, it may say I have been playing for a little while but trust me.. I have been playing since early open beta...I've been here for a while! Hope you enjoy!

Smite is the game that got me into MOBAs. I tried both League and Dota 2, both with friends, but I couldn't get into either. The isometric viewpoint and the huge amount of characters and items were offputting. When I tried Smite, I found out they had options for both auto-leveling and auto-buying, so I could try the game out without having to worry about either of those things. In addition, the characters in Smite being mythological gods was much easier to get into as well since you can have a feel for what a character will do before you even play them. The final factor that made me get into Smite is the behind-the-character viewpoint, which makes the controls much more like a third-person-shooter, which was much more fun than clicking around.
Once I got into Smite, I was hooked, and I've put in over 1000 hours. The god pack is a great deal in free-to-play games, and I highly recommend it to anyone who gets into the game. The variety of game modes gives so many options to casual players, and the classic conquest mode is great competitive fun. The community is generally pretty good, in my experience you only experience ragers every couple of games, and the easiest way of dealing with them is the mute button. Hirez support of the game is awesome, with regular patches and balance changes every other week or so, and at least one new god a month. The game is in a fairly balanced state, and all characters are totally viable for casual play.
Ultimately, there isn't anything I would change about this game, I would recommend it to anyone to try out, and I am glad it is on Steam so it can get some more exposure.

Chapter 1 review only, some suggestions:
Visuals-
Character models and sprites appear very nice, and areas remind me of some RPGs I enjoyed on the SNES. The character pictures accompanying the dialog do not match the mood for the situation, specifically when Sophie opens the gate initially, as the picture is of what appers to be extreme joy for a situation that would generally call for concern. The second time this was noticed was when Mark approached Sophie from behind, and Sophie seemed to be pleased with this encounter instead of shocked or startled.
Dialog-
There are three spelling errors in the first chapter:
wounder - wonder
enery - energy
what they doing - they're or they are
Sophie's discussion with her dad, Mark, is lacking depth. It seems like she's not too worried about the situation. The line "Dad..." when she is told to just go home doesn't evoke much from Sophie's character, and makes it appear that her brother will just have to deal. This makes the opening feel a little washed out as I too did not care what happened to her brother.
Audio-
The Demonic growl when showing the controls is unsettling and a bit loud. Maybe a more gentle sound or no sound effect here would benefit.
Opening song is repetitive and does not strike me as audio I would like to hear with an opening game or sequence. Granted, this is only title screen music, and I'll give credit for that.
The second room past the guard with the enemies that give chase has some extremely loud sounds to accompany being found. Recommend lowering the volume for these.
Card game music is super intense. Would be better suited for actual fighting. Card game music should be something slightly softer and moody, but light.
Controls:
Arrow keys fit the style, and are intuitive. Controls screen does not give a thorough idea of the controls, including the A button requirement for the first guard to activate for a game of cards.
In-game option for audio settings would be nice, but manageable with Windows mixer, albeit all game sounds are lowered at this point.
Gameplay:
Card game is a nice touch. It's different than the standard expectations most card games have had, giving a puzzle like feel to the game itself.
The opening of the card packs is cumbersome, having to open the menu each time a new pack is to be opened. I suggest modifying this to remain in the menu until exited with the Cancel button.
Combat:
I did play through a few minutes of the second chapter, and the combat felt intuitive, like most turn based RPGs.
Overall:
I want to like this game, but the story and characters lack depth. I found myself not wanting to care about the characters or their plight to save themselves, or the world, or whatever was happening. Maybe spend a little more time on story and chacter development. I also do not like the idea of this opening sequence and first card game considered as a chapter, as the game's content has barely even been hashed out. I definitely do not like the idea that the second chapter would be considered a DLC. To play through in a handful of minutes would not be worth the possible dollar the single chapter might launch for. If you are seeking an option for DLC, maybe implement a separate story arc for Sophie's friends, or her father, or maybe a skin swap or something.
I understand the game lacks polish as this is an alpha freeware game. Clean up the base mistakes and add some content to the opening. Really give something that will hook the player. This would warrant a chapter based DLC, like most games that employ this strategy (see anything from TellTale Games). Fix the audio levels and clean up the controls screen, and this may become something completely different. For now, I'm gonna have to go with a NO recommendation. Not because of game breaking bugs, but simple mistakes and a total loss of interest.

Pretty much everything thing we do has an element of risk attached to it, there are clichéd risks like crossing the road, once you’ve set foot upon the tarmac, there’s a chance you won’t make it across to the other side, it happens to people every day.
There are the obvious risks like, “I’m going to go sky diving” good luck with that!
Then there are the more subtle risks like... making yourself a coffee.
How could that be risky?
Well... you grab your favourite mug, flick the switch on the kettle and... ZAP!
There was an electrical fault that had gone unnoticed, an unhealthy voltage surges through your body, within moments your mug is smashed on the kitchen floor, your smouldering corpse lying next to it, and all you wanted was a coffee!
It’s unlikely, but that doesn’t make it impossible.
If only there was some way to see the risks around you more clearly, some sort of magical goggles you could put on that could highlight the dangers, maybe something could have flagged that broken appliance as deadly before you flicked the switch, you might have gone without your coffee but at least you wouldn’t be dead!
There are risks involved in gaming too, from the ever present threat of getting RSI from a ten hour session of Call of Duty to the financial risk of buying a game that might turn out to be awful and remain unplayed forever; I’ve seen plenty of “I want my money back” threads on the Steam forums, we’ve all wasted money before.
Thankfully the risks involved in The Perils of Man aren’t the “Should I buy it?” variety
(hopefully this review will help a little in that respect).
You see, Perils of Man is a game themed around risk and if you liked the idea of the magical “risk assessment goggles” mentioned earlier then when you get about a third of the way through the game you’re going to be in for a treat!
You play the role of Ana Eberling, a Swiss girl whose family is shrouded in mystery.
Her father and his father before him shared more than just their bloodline, they were both scientists and more than that, they both disappear under mysterious circumstances, never to be heard from again.
You join Ana on her  birthday, it’s been several years since her father vanished but she hasn’t given up hope of uncovering the mystery surrounding his disappearance.
A mystery added to by the strange object she has just received as a birthday present, a recently discovered item that used to belong to her missing father.
Unlocking the secret of  this strange item will be your first step on a journey to discover the truth about your family, a journey which is going to include some whacky clockwork inventions, some touching moments and...... Time Travel!
You’ll find yourself jumping around in time “trying to put right what once went wrong”.
You’ll even have a side kick with you on these “Quantum Leaps” to keep you company and offer up a tip or two should you get stuck.
You’re unlikely to get stuck too often though, the puzzles here, whilst fun, are a little on the easy side (or maybe I’m finally getting better at point and click adventures!).
On the whole, the puzzles are logical, they make sense, at least I haven’t encountered any frustrating “Combine the chicken with the pulley” moments that Lucas Arts were so fond of!
The graphics are crisp and stylised in a Tim Burton kind of way, they’re not stellar but the cute and quirky visuals do fit well with the narrative, and a good story is the back bone to a point and click adventure.
The story here is a pretty good one, you'll quickly become absorbed in the mystery of the Eberlings family and their research, unfortunately you'll also quickly reach the end of the game, The Perils of Man is fairly short, you'll get a few hours of game play from it, but then its price point reflects this, and it will be a fun few hours.
The characters themselves are a mixed bag, Ana herself is well developed and superbly voiced, in fact the voice work across the piece is of a fairly high quality, sure it's a little cheesy but that just adds to the quirky charm.
Unfortunately the other characters you'll meet along the way tend to be a little two dimensional , not distractingly so, but a little more depth would have been appreciated.
The Perils of Man is an enjoyable game, but it can't shake off its IoS roots, almost all aspects feel  a little simplified, which isn't  surprising as it was designed for the handheld market.
The locations could be larger and they could use a little more  detail, the story is interesting but short, the puzzles whilst fun aren't that challenging, this is the fast food equivalent of a point and click adventure.
As an IoS title,  the Perils of Man is an impressive point and click title, as a PC game release, it feels a little shallow.
Having said that, it does tell an interesting tale experienced through a charming main character, all for the price of a couple of drinks at a coffee shop.  (sure you could make your own but why take the risk!)
This is the fast food of point and click gaming, it's enjoyable, it's cheap, its quick to consume and it once it's over its quickly forgotten, is this a bad thing, no, I love fast food!

The Perils of Man is a fantastic point and click.
The art style, animation, music, and voice acting are all fantastic. Helping set atmosphere and help guide you.
Ana, the main character certainly does a lot of talking. Although it adds to the experience as you know what's going through her mind while she narrates the story.
The puzzles aren't too difficult so far, but as someone that's never been very good at puzzle games they can take me longer to figure out than someone more proficient. Even so I've really been enjoying the game, and it's story so far, which is a rare thing when it comes to point and clicks for me.
I'd easily recommend it to veteran point and click fans, and people that simply want to play a really good mystery.

Perils of Man
Point-and-click adventure
IF Games, Vertigo Games
Vertigo Games
is the port of an iOS point-and-click adventure game developed by IF Games and designed by Bill Tiller and Gene Mocsy, who previously worked on LucasArts games that I love like
and
.
After ten years since the disappearance of the scientist Max Eberling, his daughter Ana starts looking for clues of his whereabouts. The investigation leads her to discovering a family secret which involves time travel and the possibility to detect perils in the environment.
The story is probably the strongest point of the game: while most of the characters aren't well developed and many inconsistencies are present, exploring the different places, interacting with the robot companion Darwin and discovering all of the family's secrets put this story above your average adventure game.
The game doesn't look all that great, and it shows its nature as an iOS game: the character animations are really wooden, the lip syncing is really bad, the environments are small and lack detail and you can't interact with many objects. When moving from one room to the other there is a transition that usually results in weird clipping with the environment. And the pre-rendered cutscenes run at 40FPS rather than the 60FPS of the gameplay.
The game is a simple point-and-click adventure in which you can pick up objects, use them and combine them. After a certain part of the game, you acquire some goggles which let you see the dangers in the environment. Unfortunately, they act more like a gimmick than anything game-changing. There are some puzzles which are either really easy to understand or require some incredibly unintuitive thinking, making you feel more frustrated than smart.
The only real challenge comes from the puzzles and your ability to beat them: because of the small amount of exploration and items that you find, you will most-likely try every combination possible until you figure them out. There is also a Hint system which either spits out the solution to you or stays really cryptic.
Nothing special here: the voice acting is bearable, the sound effects are clear and the soundtrack suits the tone of the game, even though it's really forgettable.
Skilled players will beat the game in more or less two hours, while others will require more time to figure out some of the hardest puzzles. There are no bonuses by completing the game, and all the 14 achievements are unlocked by playing the game, so there is no reason to come back rather than thoroughly exploring the environments.
Overall, adventure game fans of modern titles like A Vampire Story, Ankh and Ghost Pirates of Vooju Island will love this game, while hardcore fans will be put off by the simplistic puzzles and small environment interaction.

+ The gameplay is loads of fun and deeper than I ever would have thought. In a basic sense you are a Slime rancher who goes out and catches a variety of slimes. You then feed them fruits, vegetables, or meat (chicken) which makes the slime create "Plorts" which you can sell and use that currency to build up your farm.
+ I found this game to be very charming and surprisingly relaxing. It is very casual, so you don't have to worry too much about getting killed, and even if something does goes wrong you can easily rebuild in a short amount of time.
+ Visually the game is super cute with adorable slimes with faces, and a very pleasing art style that is colorful and just a joy to explore.
+ "Plorts' are gems that every slime creates. If you feed a slime a plort from a different type of slime it turns into a brand new cross-breed slime. It is so much fun to experiment with different slimes and can be very rewarding too!
+ There is a large variety of things you can purchase at the shops. Upgrades for your character, upgrades for your pens, new pens, farming fields for food, and you can even purchase the ability to unlock brand new areas to explore.
+ The game kinda just throws you in, and allow you to learn and play at your own pace. Normally this would be a downside from my perspective, but Slime Rancher is incredibly intuitive and very easy to learn. You sorta just learn as you go without needing any help or tutorials.
+ Nice relaxing soundtrack
- There doesn't seem to be any story or character development. I feel like there really should be a main objective or some sort of plotline to keep you invested. At the moment there doesn't seem to be any goals or reasons to advance besides getting to new areas and finding new slimes.
- Currently lacks content. From my expeirence, you can do just about everything there is to do in under 3 hours. There needs to be more variety of slimes, and more things to do overall which I hope will find its way into the final release.

Tight Platforming
Methodical Combat
Familiarity-based Exploration
Sense of Character Progression
Everything you love about the Igarashi-era Castlevania series...
... none of which can be found here.
Instead, what you get is a God-of-War-like, Quicktime Event riddled, "Western Take" on a truly beloved franchise.  Everything down to the feel of the "whip" weapon and "kill all enemies to proceed" gameplay elements from God of War (read: Devil May Cry) is here, and gone are the things that made Castlevania so magical.  The story takes itself seriously (a huge no-no for a great Castlevania game: "WHAT IS A MAN!?") and feels SO serious that there's hardly any levity or fun to be had in the narrative, let alone the gameplay.
If you want to play a better version of this game, go play Darksiders, or Devil May Cry, or God of War... if you want Castlevania... well, you're just going to have to wait for Bloodstained.

Note: This game is in a pre alpha state and may change blah, blah, blah.
Astroneer is an intresting game which includes blueprints, multiplayer, vehichles, exploration of a randomly generated open word solar system, mining which can lead to rinse and repeat, weather, an intresting power and oxygen system with tethers, and base building.
The game consists of four characters to start off as including 2 skinny white space suits looking slightly diffrent, a larger whit space suit, and a larger orange space suit. Upon choosing your character you will launchoff what seems to be a space station onto an empty planet with only remanents of satelites and dead astroneers who came here before you. After being shown the controls quickly you will most like come across compound or resin (resin is used for base expansion while compound is used for crafting most of the in game objects.) after coming across these ores you will probably expand your base and begin improving. After so much time you will most likely have a research station which can get materials and blueprints when given unkown objects. There are many thing to research such as a winch, oxygen tank, drill, shuttle, seats, rover, battery, generators, filter, dynamite, etc. You can either make these objects at a printer or a vehichle bay which you have made. To make objects such as these you must collect copper alluminum which have been given diffrfrent names in their raw and materials like that to smelt. you can encounter storms which hurl rocks around and are one of the four current ways to die (the other three are falling, poison gas, and spikes.) You can create walls, go inside a cavern, or enter a vehichle/ habitat to survive, but these storms do not last long. You can also obtain energy for yourself and modules you have made by catching wind or the sun by using the appropriate machine. The current goal in this game is to survive and expand. In caverns you might come across plants which spit poison gas, spike you, or just sit there luckely the plants are easy to identify from each other giving you a warning. thanks for reading my current review and sorry for putting things out the second they pop in my head.

THIS IS A FANTASTIC GAME
The story is amazing, and although not all of the characters from the first game make an appearance *cough, cough Samuel* they do in some way come up again in the world, one way or another. I don't want to spoil anything for anyone, so I'll just give my brief opinions on a couple important parts to the game. The gameplay itself is graceful, once you have the graphics on your system figured out that is. The plot itself is deeply rooted in similar concepts from the last game and it's DLC content (though you really don't have to have played it to fully understand the story).
Decisions seem to play an equally powerful role in this game, with the people and environment in some way reacting to your decisions as you progress. The game length seemed about as long as the first one was, it took me about a day to replay that game and a day to beat this game with just one of the two character choices (though both can be easily done in one day if someone really wants to spend hours playing, or wants to decrease the difficulty). The levels themselves are impressively well thought out and quite lengthy (there are 9 levels in this game) , and in each one there is so much lore to be discovered between Jessamine's heart (which will tell you something about the environment and it's inhabitants), books, conversations, and even songs ( THERE ARE ACTUAL SONGS AND POEMS MADE SPECIFICALLY FOR KARNACA IN THIS GAME ). The ending seemed a little dull compared to Dishonored's endings, but still the game itself makes up for a lot of that just through feeling so alive. It keeps you wanting to come back to it over and over again.
I've finished the game now twice ( low chaos as Corvo and high chaos as Emily on legendary and hard difficulty respectively ) and I'm not sure if it was just because of how I was playing or the way the game was designed, but it was so much more satisfying to play as Corvo, especially while meeting the Outsider again. It was a little weird this time that his voice actor had changed ( and also that echo in his voice + his high pitched voice was a little annoying at times) but really his dialogue with Corvo made me forget all that. However, playing as Emily I just thought his character sucked. It didn't really seem all that thought out and he really didn't leave a lasting impression. Again, it could just be because of how I was playing the game. I haven't played low chaos for Emily yet, so keep that in mind. This is just my first impressions.

Call of Duty Advanced Warfare is a large subject to tackle, since the multiplayer is the main appeal of the series, I will be focusing on that.
Right away when you start playing the game you notice some huge changes in the formerly stagnant CoD formula, they added boost jumping and dodging.
This adds a ton of dynamic gameplay, using the battlefield to your advantage like never before, and almost makes you mind your surroundings like arena shooters do.
The game feels a lot quicker than predecessors, bar MW1, this certainly works to its' advantage in most maps, adding a lot of verticality to the mix, which is what CoD needs, since it's a fast-paced, arcade shooter.
What really pulls the game down overall is the gunplay, the characteristic gunplay of CoD is quick and deadly, however I feel like in this game all the weapons are peashooters.
Sledgehammer did a bang up job for their first title, but they're simply not skilled enough to handle a game like CoD.
The main appeal of each CoD game that really makes or breaks the title is the gunplay, in this game the weapons simply don't feel satisfying to use imo, the models stay relatively static and the sounds the weapons make aren't that characteristic, I just had a 5 hour play session, and if you asked me to recall a single gun sound, I wouldn't be able to recall it, the sound design is severely lacking.
I can still remember the Garands' sound effect from CoD2 clear as day, the characteristic pmf pmmf pmmf of the silenced UMP in MW2 still stays with me to this very day.
The gunplay just feels very weak, and I feel like this would be my favourite CoD if the guns didn't feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to use, it's simply not enjoyable.
The PC version has a few issues, to name a few:
-TERRIBLE, I mean TERRIBLE ♥♥♥♥ing lag in multiplayer lobbies, I have a decent internet connection, yet I'm lagging every game
-You still can't alt+tab out of multiplayer games.
-FOV switching bugs up the game a bit, the FOV also resets sometimes while mid-game
-Some levels lag for the first few minutes, simply because it's loading in the textures, every GPU has this same issue
The PC support has  been decent, but a dedicated server browser REALLY needs to be added,
the graphics look alright on ultra quality, but the bleak stark colour palette they used really isn't my thing, but artstyle is just personal preference anyways.
Would I recommend buying it?
Simple answer:
Complete answer: I'd like you to buy it, but I can't justify it for more than 30 euros.(luckily there're CD-keysites)
I absolutely love the CoD franchise, I grew up playing CoD 1 and CoD 2, and I spent my teens playing MW1 and MW2, and I feel like CoD is finally moving in the right direction: fast-paced movement, innovation with each yearly release.
Will we likely see the boost jumps and the dodging in a new CoD title? No.
Will we show Activision that they shouldn't be afraid of changes being made? Yes, well, maybe.
Activision won't see innovation as successful unless they make more profit than they did with the last title, currently, this is Ghosts, which is why this game will hopefully be such a tide-turner for the series, if the game turns a decent profit, we might just see some high quality, more fleshed out CoD titles in the future.
Activision leads, most other publishers will follow in their wake, do we want more risky moves, like the gaming industry did in the past?
Remember: We're the ones who can choose, using our wallets.

First off, I'm a huge fan of the Castlevania series.   So that foundation may color my opinion of this game and it's ensuing interquel and sequel (which I'm currently in the midst of).  Something about medieval through Enlightment era Europe with a heavy gothic/baroque aesthetic, corrupted through dark forces that threaten the world?  Awesome.  Tons of monsters pulling on a multitude of inspiration from the myth cycles of antiquity through the modern Universal monsters?  Yes, please.
Konami struck gold initially by creating these dark adventures that took a quite serious tone for the early Nintendo systems, offering a beefy challenge of vintage Nintendo difficulty through several increasingly impressive platformer games.  They then evolved into the famed Metroidvanias with the release of Symphony of the Night on the Playstation - trading a bit of the reflex-intensive difficulty for massive sprawling environments that took forever to explore and fully unlock - and followed this formula with several excellent installments on Nintendo's handhelds where they found their most sustainable home and success through the late 2000's.  Then Konami, sensing the increasingly stagnant nature of the series as it became mired in repeated iterations of SotN's sprawling platformer/RPG hybrid, started searching for a way to revitalize the series again, just as SotN ignited a sort of Golden Age for the series.
As the winds throughout the greater video game market were blowing increasingly towards epic, story-based RPGs, Spanish-based developer MercurySteam was contracted to take the series in a new direction (probably due to Konami's increasing focus upon more purely profitable directions, such as the Japanese gambling market).  MercurySteam, for their part, took a pretty bold new direction though this was not without its share of controversy.  The good came from a heavy focus upon story and aesthetic.  Gabriel Belmont, who apparently becomes the progenitor of the famed vampire-slaying family in this continuity, is dispatched by the human agency, the Brotherhood of Light to confront and destroy the eponymous Lords of Shadow who have become a blight over the world of humanity, separating the Earth from the Heavens and unleashing demonic horrors upon the hapless human kingdoms and villages.  Interestingly, this game devotes a lot of exposition to the powers of good as well.  Traditionally, Castlevania always had an air of horror and darkness, though maybe not a sense of supreme evil.  LoS heavily invokes God, Satan, and, to a lesser extent, Christ and the church.  The old games had less direct references though they were still there with Judeo-Christian enemies as well as religiously themed environments (though due to the setting, Baroque Europe, this is hardly surprising).  LoS made the series simultaneously more and less personal.  Gabriel is on this quest in the hopes of reviving his dead wife, Marie and we spend a great deal of time getting to know him through his terse interactions with the allies and enemies he encounters in his quest.  On the other hand, the game focuses much more of the scale of humanity as a whole.  The powers of Heaven and Hell are very real in the LoS universe and they are actively vying for the souls of men.  Say what you will about the old 'vanias, they were great but while Dracula might wreak havoc on the world, he generally wasn't portrayed as damning his victims souls to an eternity in hell.  That however is the stakes for LoS.  MercurySteam went all out, bringing back narrative cutscenes, securing an A-list voiceover cast, and threw in a few Shadows of the Colossus style battles for variety.
The gameplay itself is a departure from the old series as it is a third person 3D platformer/adventure game.  Combat draws heavy influence from God of War leading some detractors to label the continuity God-of-Vania.  Given the Belmonts are famed whip users throughout the series (even non-Belmonts like John Morris and Nathan Graves got in on the whip action!), I'm fine with that decision.  The only annoying aspect of it is the volume of endurance heavy enemies.  I get it, I'm using a whip which isn't the most devastating of medieval weaponry (even if it is made out of holy-blessed metal) against creatures with inhuman carapace, hide and endurance.  It just gets a bit tedious at times is all I'm saying.  The whip combat is fun and creative though it could stand to be a bit more visceral.  Hits just don't feel like they have a ton of impact which makes bashing endurance-heavy enemies feel like a chore instead of exciting.  The game does offer an array of other options though to keep things fresh with the ability to infuse the Vampire Killer with Light and Shadow magic as well as several subweapons including classic staples like throwing knives and holy water.  The environments are big, winding, and varied and have a lot of detail invested in them, even if they aren't overwhelmingly interactive (though there are a number of destructible props placed about to makes combat a bit more tangible).  Being sort of a platformer, there's loads of obstacle courses and climbing sections to navigate that will break up your time between fights and give you a chance to cool down.  This generally works in that when you start to tire of combat, the game gives you a navigation section.  When you get tired of climbing around enormous walls and platforms, the game will throw a dozen monsters at you to slay.  In short, things in this world are huge, in terms of scale.
The shortcomings of the game tend to focus around repeating enemies (enemy variety has always been a staple of the series), the heavy God of War influence (though any departure from Koji Igarashi's metroidvania genre would have received a similar outcry), and the almost minimal touchstones of being a Castlevania.  By this last one, I'm referring to limited focus on the Belmont family, settings outside Dracula's castle, and chief antagonists other than Dracula.  These are complaints of taste in my opinion and while Lords of Shadow doesn't scratch those particular itches very well, it wouldn't be the first to break any of these commandments.  Bloodlines, Circle of the Moon, Aria and Dawn of Sorrow, and Order of Ecclesia all had non-Belmont protagonists and didn't really ever bring the Belmonts into the plot in a major way.  Gabriel, being the first to take the surname, simply doesn't really have a family history to call upon like the later Belmonts do in their increasingly storied feud with Dracula, never mind that Dracula doesn't exist in LoS1 as the Lords of Shadow are the antagonists.  Bloodlines had you gallavanting all around World War I era Europe with only the first level in Dracula's castle.  Aria of Sorrow and Dawn of Sorrow - some of the highest regarded games of the metroidvania era - feature a focus on non-Belmont Soma Cruz and feature primary antagonists who aren't Dracula.
Don't get me wrong, I understand the complaints and can empathize why longtime fans might feel alienated by the new direction and perceive the genre shift as pandering to younger markets (particularly the God of War style combat).  But I think the things it does well; story, atmosphere, music, symbolism, intensity, and variety make up for the departures.  It's an alternative continuity that freshened the series up and gives gamers of other genres and option to get interested in the series and the lore.  For that, I think it's a good thing.  Or it would be if Konami ever developed its IP franchises.  But alas, "Mobile is where the future of gaming lies." according to Konami's current CEO.  For shame, Konami!

I don't normally recommend Early Release titles. Ususally, they're a relatively incomplete experience, or at least not worth the price of entry. And while I won't call Broforce a complete title by any means, it certainly seems to be well on its way, far better than many of its early release brethren. It is a simplistic, yet surprisingly interesting 2D shooter that can be equal parts blind run-n'-gun or clever pseudo-stealth platformer (don't let that title fool you though, there's still plenty of bloodshed.) You assume the role of numerous non-copyrighted action movie bros as you seek to liberate the world of evil. With guns, bombs, lasers, and anything else within arm's reach. But, that's enough summary, here's the key information.
First, some caveats. The only (for practical purposes) complete portion is the solo campaign. But, that can seem misleading. There are other facets, custom maps, test maps (if you're one to delve into such content), a fair amount of community maps, and even the new (at the time of reviewing) campaign map work better than the touted features of some "officially released" titles. However, there are issues. The networking, in particular, can be nightmarish. In my testing instances, my buddy and I requently lagged out, before eventually disconnecting, despite being quite literally 6 ft. away from each other. If you want co-op, I highly recommend doing it locally, on the same system. Using one player on a gamepad and one on the keyboard can work, or two gamepads, et cetera, whatever's comfortable.
Now, the stuff that works. And, there's actually a surprising amount of it. As mentioned earlier, most of the single-player content's pretty playable. As for control, both keyboard & mouse and gamepads are supported (I used a wired Xbox 360 Controller to test gamepad fuctionality), and both are workable. Some may prefer a gamepad, but once you get the hang of the controls, keyboard and mouse can be just as precise and enjoyable. Lastly, the characters/updates. There's a pretty large cast of characters considering this game's in beta, and even more are slated for release. From the simple Rambro to the "aghluaghla" -spouting Bronan, it's pretty interesting watching these various heroes tearing through terrorists. One minor dent, however, is the random nature you get these bros. Outside of the one time you initially unlock them, the bro you play as is always randomly selected. This can lead to difficulty, as some of the bros are simply either more useful in certain areas, or more useful as a whole. Being able to select a pre-set squad of five-or-so bros to always cycle through in a stage, or even the option to play as one bro only, would be nice, at least in single-player games.
To finally wrap this thing up, the real question: should you buy beta Broforce? As much as a cop out as it may sound: it's really a matter of personal taste. If you're a thrifty shopper, or only have a passing interest in run-n'-gun/retro-simplistic style games (think Hotline Miami), you may want to wait until this game goes on sale, likely at the time of full release. But, if you've seen the gameplay, seen the trailers, and like what this game is going for, then supporting the devs and getting your hands on this title early may make a bro of you yet.

Played this game since June 2012, and still play it to this day.
One of the most popular Mobas in the world. And unique in so many ways. Uses a third person camera angle that give you immersion that you can't find in other Mobas. Usable Characters are all based on Mythology, with different Pantheons being present. As of right now, there are Egyptian, Greek, Chinese, Hindu, Mayan and Norse gods in the game. All the gods have lore-friendly abilities.
Another thing that I enjoy quite a lot about this game is the lack of purchaseables that give you a competitive advantage. Take League of legends as an example. You can buy Runes with the currency, which give you an advantage against an opponent that lacks Runes. In Smite, the only thing you can buy with the free currency are gods (characters) and some skins, that are mainly re-colors of the base skin of the god. This to say that if anyone dumps a lot of cash into the game, he/she gets no advantage over someone who doesn't spend a single penny.
You get daily login rewards, and the 6th and 7th day login rewards are 15 and 35 gems, respectively. This means you can buy a regular skin if you login for 8 weeks in a row, even if you don't play a game, you can just login and collect the reward. You also get Favor (free currency) with the daily rewards, that refresh after a week. Pretty cool too.
You can also buy a pack with all the gods in the game, be it available now and in the future, with one single purchase. When I bought it, it was something like 24€, for all the characters in the game, forever. It's a pretty awesome deal, if you ask me, since whenever a new god is released, you automatically get it without spending currency.
Definetely recommend

A great contender in the growing pools of the MOBA genre, SMITE is a very fun, action-oriented multiplayer game. The camera view is over the shoulder, 3rd-person, and there are no auto attacks on right clicks like DOTA 2, every single ability excluding some abilities and ultimates have to be aimed and fired, making player skill affect gameplay much more than other MOBAs. A very easy to pick up, hard to master game that is a blast to play with friends.
It is Free to play, sustained from micro-transactions coming from buying cosmetic skins like in League of Legends, but unlike League of Legends, you can get all 70 gods, PLUS all future gods, for $30 USD, which is an amazing deal if you enjoy the game. If you don't want to invest money into the game, you can purchase gods with the in-game currency, as well as having 5 free gods, plus 5 free rotation gods every few weeks. From my experience with League of Legends, SMITE has a much more fair and valuable deal with getting gods/champions to play than the former, but that is just my opinion.
I have sunk over 1600 hours into the game since March 2013 (
)when it was in Beta, and I plan to keep playing until Hirez shuts it down, hopefully not in the immediate future. It's a MOBA that is unlike the top MOBAs at the moment, and it has a bright future. It's worth AT LEAST trying. 8.5/10

When it comes to twin stick shooters, it doesn't get any better than Geometry Wars. As a past player of all three games, Geometry Wars 3: Dimensions hits the mark and goes a mile beyond offering a very solid game on all planes. Gameplay, visuals, music and all, it has risen to my top pick of the Geometry Wars series.
The gameplay is snappy, responsive and most importantly: intense. The contents is the same as per Geometry Wars -- shoot varius geometric shaped enemies with defined characteristics in a given plane. The number and diversity of enemies increases as you fend yourself off, which will have you clenching your input device as you weave yourself around the plane. As well as an array of classic modes found in past games, Dimensions has also included a story mode.
The nature of story mode might seem a bit head scratching at first, but its execution makes it feel like a natural extension of the game's experience. Each mission tweaks the contraints of the level and offers a unique twist to the game's original gameplay. What kind of plane you play on, the enemies you may see/how they spawn, and other quirks vary from level to level, which offers some good variety. Also seen is a feature called drones which is little bot that assists you in story mode missions. This feature is a neat addition as it allows the player to change its behaviour and upgrade its abilities using points accumulated through playing missions.
Leaderboard support is also well implemented. Every mode in classic has a leaderboard as well as every single mission in story mode has its own leaderboard -- both global and friends. For anyone who loves to score attack and compete with friends or others around the globe, this game has you covered.
All in all, Geometry Wars 3: Dimensions is absolutely amazing. It takes the elements of what makes Geometry Wars immensely enjoyable then builds upon it and gives it a refreshing polish.
Notable features:
-Addictively intense gameplay
-Responsive controls
-Loads of leaderboards
-Great visual polish
-Music that fits the mood
-Online Multiplayer and Local 4 Player
Shortcomings:
-Many story mode gameplay mechanics and enemies are exclusive to that mode
-Leaderboards are not available through Steam Community web interface
Rating: pineapple/10 (aka RTFR: Read the fine review)

It was a pineapple.
A FREAKING PINEAPPLE.

I quit the game.

If the game didn't crash for looking at it wrong and I was able to connect to servers consistently, then I would recommend the game.
Until then It's a gamble to even play the game.
Don't get me wrong the game is fun, but here's some of the issues:
1) Connecting to a server
It's a ♥♥♥♥♥. You try to connect to a server and 99/100 times it will say that the server is full. You try to connect 10 times and game breaks itself and will keep saying that it's connecting. Then you have to exit out of the game, relaunch it, and keep trying until you get into a game. Best part is that there is no way to tell how full the server is and there is no Autojoin.
This needs to be fixed and there certainly needs to be more servers.
2) The Crashing
It just happens. Hold down the mic key too much? Crash. Try to use the elevator? Crash. Survived the round and loading into the next round? Crash. It's just Crash, Crash, and more Crashing. Pair this with trying to connect to a server and you have a hell deemed fit for you.
3) The elevators
This happens every round. You are trying to get into an elevator so you can escape/enter the facility. Now imagine on both ends of the elevator are people spamming the buttons and SCP-079 Controlling the door. It literally just breaks the elevator so the doors can no longer be opened. So congrats, everyone in the elevator is stuck, everyone who wants in/out have to sit there until they die or the undefined round timer runs out, and the game just comes to a complete halt.
4) There is no way to add people in this game.
With games like CS:GO if you and some other guy enjoy each other's company, you can just head to recent/current players on the steam overlay and add each other. Not in this game. There were so many enjoyable people that I wanted to add but there was no possible way to.
5) SCP-079 is NOT FUN.
The only thing you can do is occasionally lock doors and move from camera to camera awkwardly. This is the worse experience in the game.
So yeah, avoid this game until some of the major problems like crashing are fixed.

This game combines combat, very nice puzzles and even some good ol' '3rd person platform' gaming.
I do say it's not only recommended to play it with a controller. You are obligated to do so, the UI system having been made for console gaming, rendering a keyboard clumsy and actually quite useless.
The only -downside- for me to this game, are the fixed camera angles. Sure, some love that, never getting lost in their own movements, but I sometimes like to peek around a corner, and sometimes it can make some 'have-to-follow-paths' or 'have-to-perform-actions' a bit elusive. But that didn't stop me from greatly enjoying the game.
All in all, I give this game a big thumbs up and would recommend it to anyone who likes the genre.
