Its a great game all in all. It has its fair amount of issues so first I'll be talking about those so I can end on a high note.
First of all, the game is easy as all hell compared to the earlier two souls games. It offers some items that make it all very easy and summoning phantoms on bosses is rarely required, but if you end up doing it, the fights will be over in less than a minute. So I strongly recommend first going into the bosses on your own, trying it out a few times and if you get frustrated, then just go for the phantom summons. No one forces you to use those OP items and such, so TRY to keep yourself from those if possible, incase you feel that it needs to be a bit more challenging.
A mixture of "easy-mode" and extremely poor game design are the new grey phantoms. Basically there are few covenants that allow you to force another player into your world, where you can kill them without any risks whatsoever (unless you are incredibly bad at this game, then it might be somewhat risky). You spawn into a clusterf*ck of enemies that attack YOU and you also have that other player to worry about. They get rewarded for taking you down and even if they die, fetching souls is risk free for them. Just this idea alone drops the overall rating of the game by one point. It is THAT bad of a thing. Granted, the areas are optional, but first time playing through, you might not know that. You just explore around like an idiot and get pulled out every 2 seconds, eventually get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off and flip the bird to the game.
Few other more minor issues are the badly designed bossfights. I talked about them a bit earlier, but theres a lack of inspiration, they rarely make you afraid when you enter and are over too fast. They often have cheap skills to compensate for the lack of actually good, fun, challenging moves and tricks. Sure there has been cheap moves on every boss in every souls games, there have been really easy ones too, but they should be over this by now.
The same goes for some enemies. While I LOVE killing humanoid type enemies in games, there were few too many of those in this one. The lack of inspiration and innovation is present with the enemies aswell and its kind of a bummer.
The story and setting is.. so and so. I never felt truly invested in anything and sometimes the lore part too fell kind of flat on its butt. But that stuff too has its highs. Some places also feel really out of place, but I wont spoil any of that.
Theres few other annoying things here and there, but mostly just me nitpicking. I wish that there were more armor sets and such, the character making thing should have been able to make other than potato people and shrek clones (you can create a decent looking character if you put in a lot of time, but not worth it). The removal of the kick attack also annoyed me a bit. it was fun to kick the poop out of the vases and other destroyable stuff. But like I said before, just me nitpicking.
Luckily the game for the most part is great! amazing new places, great scenery, great atmosphere, sometimes suprisingly challenging parts and bosses, some of the bosses are GREAT and there are few enemies that really send the chills down my spine. It feels like a souls game through and through eventhough those issues I mentioned earlier are strongly present for the most part.
I had a blast exploring the places, kicking baddies and had many moments where I yelled "YES! I did it!". part of the reason why most of it felt so easy was probably because I have played the two earlier games quite a lot so I knew to be extremely careful, when to back it up and expect some sneaky enemy. I also had a pretty good idea how most different types of bosses would eventually play out even if some bosses really kicked my♥♥♥♥♥a few times and beating them after that felt real nice.
Atleast this didnt take me nearly a year (real gametime maybe 90-100hours) like Demons Souls, that game was balls hard and the last "real" boss made me so angry that I both screamed out of anger, but once I beat it, I screamed out of joy and got drunk as a bee. This took a fairly low amount of time to beat because I really blasted through some of the zones and the bosses often required just that one try. There was much less of that "hmm, I wonder what I was doing wrong, I really gotta plan this out better."
That said, Dark Souls 2 was MUCH less frustrating too. Sure I said quite a few cursewords while playing this, but only once or twice it was REALLY because I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off like an ant that you pee'd on.
Its a great new title for both vets and new players alike. It offers many ways to make it harder if you really wish that, but I'd save that for the new game+. Most of the annoyances from the older games have been ironed out and theres more room for different kinds of playstyles. Overall I'd say that this game was a great success and well worth the full price. The keyboard+mouse controls are still poop, so just use a ps3 controller or something similar.
8/10, bretty gud, wuld recommend, no need to git gud.
EDIT: Forgot to mention that yes, theres a craaazy amount of replay value, the pvp side if you like that and lots of optional bosses ect. I'll be continuing to play this for quite some time so dont be hesitating to buy this because of my game hours.

Geometry Wars 3 is simplicity in its best way and proves that we Humans can be amazed by bright lights, flashing colors, and techno music. You basically control a little ship flying along  a 3-dimensional map while shooting brightly neon colored enemies and collecting small little gems(that the game calls "geoms") that increase your highscore and give you multipliers. Along the way you can defeat bosses(that are pretty interesting in their own right, and serve to break up the 'shoot this and get this score' pretty well), play other game modes(pacifism is my favorite) and play online.
Geometry Wars 3 is a fun arcade style shooter with a colorful retro artstyle, great gameplay, and a pretty dope techno soundtrack, for 15$ it's a steal and would make a great gift for any gamer or steam user(if you've avoided getting your holiday shopping done until the last moment.)
PROS:
-Artstyle, the game just looks good
-Soundtrack
-Some of the best feeling arcade style controls I ever got from a keyboard and mouse.
-Gameplay is immensely enjoyable, you don't even have to like video games to enjoy it since it's basically an arcade game(and everyone loves arcade games) My father and mother(who are both well into their 50's) were able to play this with ease and enjoy it because of how simple it is
-Great use of 3D maps, the cylinder one is especially trippy and the first one most people run into that breaks up the gameplay so well
CONS:
The game doesn't have much in ways of direct faults, but however things that should be noted and things I felt that could have been improved that aren't necessarily bad.
-This game is very much a 'quckie game' this is not something you buy and expect to have a full varied expierence with or be able to play for a couple of hours. Geometry Wars 3 is something you boot up in windowed mode and play when you want to kill 30 minutes before closing it, and for 15$, that's ok.
-After a week of playing and going through classic mode and all of the other game modes, the game becomes pretty boring. There's achievements and highscores, but that's it. Expect this game to start gathering dust in your Steam Library under your games that have much more meat to them after a month or so.
-Whenever I played, no one was ever playing the online mode(up to you if this is a con or not, depending if you even care about online modes in games or not)
Overall, I would give it a solid 8.5/10.

Slime Rancher is a surprisingly well rounded early release.  You play the role of a wanna-be slime rancher, stationed at the outer reaches of the galaxy.  Simply put, you round up slime, feed them, and sell their poo, called plorts.  Its a pretty simple game, kind of like Viva Pinata.  Its not hard to find and round them up, but some of the challenge lies in the idea of feeding them.  Feeding them their favorite food maximises their output, which in turn earns you more money.  More money earns you more farming space, better upgrades for your collector...you get the point.  Money is the key element.
So whats big issue?  Its simple.  Literally, its simple.  Which in turn gets reptitive, quick.  I haven't looked at the road map from the developement team yet, but it also lacks a multiplayer setting.  This could actually be a really fun multiplayer experience, but according to some of the posters, it's not going to get one.
Whats good?  Almost everything (except above issues).  The gameplay is smooth, and controller response is as it should be.  The sound is good, but a little too quirky for my taste.  Graphics are actually pretty good.  Bright colors, goofy design, decent shading.  At 7 hours, i havent experienced any game breaking bugs, or graphical twitches.  Its important to note, if it had not been for this months HB, i probably wouldn't have given this a second look.
7/10, great for littler players.
6/10, value.  At its store price, you might feel jilted, on sale, its a bargain

If you are asking yourself "Should I buy Broforce?" then you need to consider the following:
- Do I like classic action movies?
- Do I like references to classic action movies?
- Do I like 2D action platformers?
- Do I enjoy slightly dumb 'Merica! type humour?
- Do I like amusing action co-op?
If the answer to 2 or more of these is yes then Broforce may well be the game for you. Of course this comes with the caveat that it is in early access, but it's incredibly playable and fun as is. The main campaign can be blazed through solo fairly quickly, but there is more of it to come as with the games ever growing selection of characters and modes people who enjoy the formula will find that Broforce just keeps on giving.
Some players may find the game a little simple at first, but the later stages become elaborate combat puzzles as you work out how to handle the enemies with what you have at the time. Broforce pits you against staggering odds just like the Bros (and lady-Bros) to whom it pays tribute.
So ultimate the question is, are you a bad enough dude to fight the good fight?
If so, get Broforce!
Seriously though, it's damn awesome!

Worst COD made to date. Absolute horrific connection to lobbies, unbalanced guns, annoying bunnies jumping around the map constantly, impossible to win 1 on 1 gun fights. The game is a huge waste of time and money.

Well... another new Call of Duty game released! This time, it is a new "universe" as it is unrelated to previous COD stories. I can truly see the big inspiration taken from the "EDGE OF TOMORROW" movie, with the exosuit mechanic minus the invading aliens!
This CoD: Advanced Warfare, is like a mixed-up Black Ops 2 and Modern Warfare 3. It gives you some sci-fi elements, items, weapons and the new addition, the exosuit.
The biggest pro of this game comes with Kevin Spacey. His performance in the game is stellar and saves the campaign mode greatly. The other characters weren't as thoroughly developed but are believeable nonetheless.
Did I liked this game? When it worked properly, it is fun but lots of times, the game lags a lot, hence truly poor optimization. Aside of performance isssues, my biggest irritant is you just cannot choose your loadout before the beginning of a new mission. Same goes with the Exosuit modes. The Exosuit is way too restricted. Advanced Warfare tries to be "CRYSIS" with cool suit modes but you are handled some specific modes for each missions while other modes are disabled. So basically, I felt like a crippled 'NANOSUIT'.
PROS:
+Kevin Spacey performance! Honorable mention for the other actors as they did a really good job there!
+Visuals... graphics were thoroughly tuned up in this COD game and it shows!
+Story is quite decent, even if it is quite predictable!
+Multiplayer has many modes but fun when it works and doesn't crash!
CONS:
-Poorly optimized mess of a game. Even after a game update and Nvidia drivers update, the game still stutters like hell on many areas, both in the campaign and the multiplayer.
-Gamebreaking bug at the end of the game, where you have to sprint around and chase "SOMEONE" then once you try to sprint+slide, the controls doesn't respond and I had to use XBONE gamepad to get past that part. Also, couldn't skip the credits as the "PRESS SPACE TO SKIP" doesn't work at all.
-Way too linear... even for a COD game, this one was way too restricting.
-EXOSUIT Restrictions.
-Lacks mission variety.
-Still no dedicated servers for the multiplayer and the matchmaking system is left to be desired, as usual!
OVERALL:
Poorly optimized game, that lags and stutters not only on the campaign but worse on the multiplayer. The game is ultra linear, tons of invisible walls akin to COD games but in this game, not only you are forced to pick certain corridors but on some missions, you can't even go backwards, let alone turn around and look back! Another big irritant that I've experienced was on the last mission, when I had to chase a certain individual, I had to sprint and slide at the same time under a closing glass door. Thing is, the mechanic never got to work as the Keyboard key was unbounded and even bounded afterwards, it still didn't work. I had to plug my XBONE gamepad to go through that lame a$$ gamebreaking bug.
RECOMMENDATION:
If you're a diehard COD fan, you will love the game, no matter what! If you like to play military shooters every now and then, you should enjoy this game too. If you're a newcomer to COD (well, it can happen no?), you may want to play the better ones, namely:  COD1 (game that started it all), COD United Offensive, COD2, COD Modern Warfare 1 and COD World at War; at first.
As for Advanced Warfare, I'd recommend getting it once it is on a good deal, like around 30$!

Hey everybody! I work for Grab The Games website and I have done a first look of what this game is all about. So come check it out and let me know what you guys think about the game and my review.

I really got sucked into the enthusiasm that this indie dev team generates, but there are several basic problems with this game that prevent it from being fully realized. The long and short of it - I believe it's spread too thin.
By that I mean the devs have spread it too thin. The scope is far too wide, to where the basic problems with the foundation have not been repaired. There's still much work to be done on the core gamemode (Harvest) before branching out and "reaching for the stars" by introducing new content such as the Dogfight gamemode and dozens of new maps. Basic gameplay features (like missing enemy hit noises, unplayably laggy servers, grindy leveling mechanics, and cluttered menus, for example) are unfinished and these cracks in the foundation should be filled in before the devs continue to build outward.
Additionally, the devs have discussed how they couldn't continue development and considered the game (in its very unfinished state) "complete", as they could no longer continue work on it. I don't blame them, money is money, but if they remained hyper-focused on their core game, they could have had a strong, sellable base game instead of building outward for a project that they would simply need to abandon. While the team has appeared to resume work on the project, it's shaken the community's faith. We know that development of the game could stop at any moment.
All of this is not to say that great work hasn't already been put into this game. You still have to give credit where credit is due - beautiful aesthetics and great marketing campaign. Unfortunately, I believe that this wears off quickly and is eventually dwarfed by the larger, more basic problems at the game's core.
At present, I can't recommend this game, but I look forward to changing this review in the future as the game develops.

This is literally the best twin stick shooter I have ever played in my entire life and I have spent a good portion of my life searching for decent twin stick shooters.

Fun, very difficult twin stick shooter. Its flaw is that it comes across as unfair. The special stages it has, where you play on funny shapes such as a cube, look nice but it limits your field of view and you get easily blindsided if you stay close to an edge. That or you run the high risk of dying immediately after switching sides due to running into an enemy you could have easily avoided if you could have seen him. The signal you get that an enemy is about to spawn is pretty short too, so more than a couple times I died just because an enemy spawned on top of me. There are also special abilities such as having a minion that collects geoms (the green diamonds that increase your multiplier) or placing mines on the battlefield. This sounds cool too, but it just makes the screen too busy. In Geometry Wars 1 &2, it was easy to make snap judgments on where it was safe and where it wasn't; the green geoms are safe to grab, nothing else. But now you have your geome-collecting minion flying around on his own, and your mines place around the battlefield, and in the heat of battle it is too difficult to make out what 3 things on the battlefield are okay to run into out of the 20 things on screen.
Frustrating is part of the genre, but feeling like your death was unfair and out of your hands is not fun.
Honestly, I don't like the 3Dish effect they've added, but it's the closest I'm getting to Geometry Wars 2 on PC so I have to recommend this.

Geometry Wars 2 is one of the greatest pure arcade games out there, and this game includes it whole. Almost whole - the devs seem to have taken out local co-op from it, for some reason, and you should absolutely hold it against them*.
If you haven't played it and don't have access to a console, and a score-attack twin-stick shooter set on small arenas sounds like something that you may even marginally enjoy, you should consider it essential. The feel of the game is perfect, and the mechanical flourishes for the different modes are absolutely brilliant.
That's classic mode. As for this new sequel: The new modes are ok; some bits are good fun- otheres, not so much. The main change was to map the arenas to a 3D shape, a couple of new modes, a (non-story-based) campaign linking short levels, upgradeable companion drones from a Wii-only version of the game, and... boss battles.
I have a theory on how boss battles were introduced. There's this high-profile consultant - let's call him Pat - who's brought in whenever a game studio doesn't know what to do with a beloved franchise.
"So, Pat," they'll say, "we're terrified of screwing this up what's essentially a perfect arcade experience. How should we go about this?"
Pat tuts paternally, and responds "What you need to do is to make the game yours."
The developers nod enthusiasthically; "We've actually got a few ideas we can introduce organically-"
"Hold it." Pat says, and it stops them cold. "Don't be timid. How do you mark something as yours?"
Silence.
"You♥♥♥♥♥♥on it!" Pat screams. "You spray it with your urine until it's soaked through!"
"Well," the devs say, "I don't know if we want to..."
Pat's adamant. "How can you♥♥♥♥♥♥on this game? How can you get it good and wet and yellow and pungent with the sweet, sweet aroma of ammonia?"
"Hmm, we did talk about putting in boss battles..."
"Excelent!" screams Pat. "Make them multi-stage, long, and really annoying!"
"Annoying?"
"Sure - frustration creates attachment! Our studies show that that's the reason people like Dark Souls."
"OK!" The devs are on-board now, and excited. "What about gating progress behind star ratings, so that players need to replay levels to be able to progress?"
Pat takes a drag from his cigar, and almost purrs. "That's some grade-A weewee, son."
*: Unless I'm being thick and I missed it. If so, ignore that line and get this game and three extra controllers (with their corresponding players) NOW.

Yes, this is way better than Ghosts and offers a lot of updated/new features different from previous Call of Duties. The Exo suit changes gun fights in that the person who shoots first will not always win. Essentially it adds a new layer of skill and helps make the game even faster. Maps are pretty diverse and offer a lot of vertical play room, but does not rely on a "King of the Hill" style. Customization has also gone up a few steps. You can change gloves, helmets, knee pads, exo suits, boots, shirts, and pants. The guns are pretty different from previous games of the series. We now have lasers, guns whose accuracies get better the longer you shoot, and an akimbo LMG. Also the new player cards are quit unique and definitely add some art to the game. Spawns are a lot better than before most of the time, so less of people spawning in front or behind of you. You now get supply drops periodically that give you a chance of double xp, clothes, or special weapons. You can also sell the items for XP if you so wish.
One of the laser guns (EMR) is quite over powered and you will rage constantly when dying because of it. A lot of emblems have been taken away from the emblem creator, which is kind of disappointing if you are an "artist". The time limited loot items are awarded when doing well in a previous game. This is annoying when you consistently get a 5 kill streak every game but the items expire after 30 minutes. We should be able to keep these items if we achieve stated challenge.
First of all if you have an AMD card, good luck running this game on your usual settings. I suffer from horrendous lag with a 7950 with 3gb vRAM, 8gb RAM, and an FX 6300. Pretty annoying when you spend over $300 on a dedicated graphics card and get poor results even on lower settings. The first 10 or so seconds of every game I get about 5 fps, then roughly 25 for the next 20 seconds. Eventually it figures itself out and I get up to 91 fps, but as soon as I look outside on maps like: Greenband, Defender, Horizon, Recovery, and Retreat I get drops in the 30-40 fps range.  There have been some fixes out there, but I have yet to get solid performance like I do with other titles. This game suffers seriously from connection lag. Its pretty annoying when a game developer promises dedicated servers then continues to release the game with P2P hosting. I can unload a clip into someone before they run away then when they come back around a corner and shoot me a few times I die. Basically the game suffers from usual Call of Duty occurrences that have been around forever.
The game is very fun, when it wants to cooperate. Most maps are playable, but the few that aren't suffer. If you have an NVIDIA card with decent specs go ahead, but you won't forget that the connection lag is still there. This has been the most innovative game in the series for years, but the developers need to listen to their players if they want them to have an enjoyable time, but that probably won’t happen. If the devs decide to listen to their fan base, this will turn into a great game no doubt that offers hours of play time.
It seems the update released a few days ago has gotten rid of some game and connection lag. Still no dedicated servers though, but camos are now a lot easier to unlock! Pretty terrible how a developer can lie about selling you something that they promise to deliver. I am having fun playing, but still suffer from lag on certain maps, but not nearly as bad as earlier this week.
I still can't recommend something when a developer lies, but its definitely not a bad game and certainly a lot better than previous games in the series.

I'll start this review off by giving my honest thoughts right off the bat for those who just want to see if it's worth it or not.
TL;DR Yes, it's worth it. It has some small minor issues here and there, but that's it. It's worth what they're selling it for.
Now, onto the meat of the review.
Riff Racer is a game in a similar vein to rythm games, except in this one you can get in front of the song as well as fall behind it.
The goal is to stay with the beat (and get in front of it as much as possible for a x10 bonus) with the bonus you can do tricks like drifting, jumps and flips. The higher the bonus the more points you get, hence why staying up to the beat as well as getting in front of it is essential to a good score.
For things to stop you getting a flawless score there are barricades as well as the edge of the map, hitting barricades can slow you down and push you back by a few beats, putting you behind the songs, well, beat. And falling off the map can reset your car.
Riff Racer is very fun to play if you want to do something whilst listening to music (besides play another game). Not to mention since it's able to run on low end PC's it is very useful for people like myself. It's very smooth and plays pretty solid like, drifting is responsive and easy to do but hard to properly master. Knowing when to boost is also very essential as well.
Sometimes it can take a few runs on a single song to get the proper feel for the entire track as well as to get the score you want, but that's part of the game I feel. Learning and adapting to how the track goes.
Since there's no digitial based currencies or anything you have to earn everything the good ol' fashioned way, hard work and patience. You can earn the ingame currency by leveling up or just driving over it in the track, in an age where it seems every game gets in game purchases, it's nice to see one without it.
When it comes to negatives I feel all I can find are nitpicks, such as sometimes the roadblocks being hard to see with all the flashing colours, sometimes flying off the edge of a map because of where a jump is positioned, roadblocks being undodgable when you go off some jumps as well as some cars feeling like they handle differently or the larger rears making it harder. But I feel that last one is more in my head since I usually use the Comet, the other ones can simply be justified by randomised tracks, so take that with what you will. I don't think it detracts from the game at all really.
The only real issue I have found is sometimes I'll have a track I'm racing on, as an example Carpenter Brut's Roller Mobster, my friend however raced on one made himself. Which I found slightly odd, even when we changed the album, artist and name to all what I had he wasn't able to race on that one. That's the only proper issue I've come across, but there again. It doesn't exactly impact the game all that much in the end.
Overall I really think this is a good game, and worth the purchace.
Buy it if you want to race to your music and do many durifto.

Literally the best game for its price.
Considering that this game is still under development, some bugs will be present. For all the reviews stating that the game is glitchy, this is mostly a performance issue, as very few computers I've encountered can run the game at full ultra-maxed out settings. And yet... even on my 4-year old Toshiba, with the lowest possible graphics settings, the game still looks amazing and runs fairly well (However, this is map specific, as one or two of the maps with many assets or visual effects start to lag the game).
As for community, this game is a jewel. There are numerous guides tohelp with any game issues, and on the servers, many players are fairly cordial and even the people within the top 30 are ok playing with players in 1034th place (I know this from experience with those masters of the game). As for the developers, they are dedicated to this game, but aren't going to valve it by feeding a dead game. As part of the community, you actually get a feel of your influence, and the devs are highly responsive to Q&A.
With the storyline, the irony is that the players dissing this game for "not having a story like Orion: Prelude" (the predecessor to this game) probably don't know that they are part of the same universe. Some of the videos (The devs put them out with almost every post) give the complete storyline, which also boots up each time you start the game. To say this game is story-rich is an understatement. much of the game is built upon the lore. Of course, the gameply takes a parrellel to the history- you are a part of it, but not experiencing it- but the developers at Trek have stated future plans for expanding on this experience.
Gameplay:
Where to begin? As you can see if you scroll up and watch the videos and screenshots, the main part of this game is shooting dinos. Why? Mostly because they want to eat/gore/trample you and destroy your team's wonderful mining machine that is illicitly mining an uber-powerful superfuel. That's why the robots are trying to kill you, too. You may be asking, "How's this different from every FPS game I've looked at so far?" Well, besides all of the above, Guardians of Orion just seems to scratch that itch, that game that you pick up and mess with or spend hours doing, that's complex but amazingly simple. most shooter games don't give you that level of a midpoint between calm and control.
Of course, this game is coming out with more and more features constantly. The PvP module is currently FFA (Free-for-All), but is expected to get an overhaul with the next update. There is also space /planetary dogfighting, and quite possibly this game will become open-world. There's been talke of building and survival "modules," along with racing, mech battles, and a flurry of other ideas the devs have planned for the future.
Oh, and did I mention that you can change your perspective in real time? Topdown-->Thirdperson-->firstperson (Granted, this hasn't come to PvP yet...)
Timeline:
Yes, this game is under development. Yes. at least 50% of the negative reviews you have or will read complain about "not enough updates" or "I lost X, Y, and Z..." However, if you look at the dates of these, you'll see they are not incredibly recent. in fact, major steps towards increased development rate (Hey, Trek is a SUPER SMALL dev team) have surfaced over the past two weeks (before the time of this review, 7/17/17) and the whole issue of cleared inventories has been fixed- Trek no longer has to do this! Those who lost inventories lost them after a major update, not to mention they were refunder over the next 2-3 updates...  In other words, the inventory loss jibe stems from a one-time occurrence... Unless you were one of the massive cheaters Trek penalized during the first year of development. This is further proof of devs interested in their game who are willing to commit to their community.
Price:
Firstly, did you read that section above? Secondly, $1. It's one Fraggin' dollar to get this amazing game- WAY more affordable than some $50 Activision game! If you really ARE crazy enough to spend that dough, you CAN- you unlock more guardians (characters) early instead of just playing to get coins to buy them in game with virtual currency! The point is, the only sort of difference is that everyone gets the same basic things starting out, and everyone has access to everything, either instant or delayed.
VERDICT:
Just buy the darned thing. If you are a casual player, get the $1 starter edition. If you're a massive gamer who wants to delve into this experience, feel free to indulge yourself with the elite edition. The end point is this: if you want the one game that looks amazing but is super cheap, come here. If you're a

bargain hunter like me, buy a higher edition at one of the game's sales (fairly frequent but not every day like Sanctum 2). Hope to see you in game!

I feel like in their little office they were just coming up with ideas for marketing ploys and said "hey why don't we take geometry wars make a sequel and make it totally way over digitalized for the younger generation." By this, I mean they went out of their way to make some different songs all that have the standard bass beat line you would hear in any normal techno song. For some it might not be bad, but compared to the music they have put into this game to the original Geometry wars (they remixed that too, btw they should have just kept that one alone I can't even get into the remix version) music it just gets irritating. I don't like how in arcade mode even though you have just the flat 2d square they have to make the camera all warped. Really, I played this for thirty minutes, then bought Geometry Wars retro evolved for $4 (But please, read more)
Going on to positive side now.
Once you get to levels 10 and up in adventure mode, the get actually gets pretty hard. Which I am sure will entertain old veteran Geometry Wars fans. It takes some getting used to but it is great fun. I admit I had my doubts, I did buy retro evolved shortly after purchasing this game out of dissapointment. But then I gave this game more of a chance, I got to the first boss battle, then the second, and then things got interesting. I won't spoil much of it but I will say if you are an old old geometry wars veteran then you should consider buying both this game and the retro evolved version as you will find yourself wanting to play both version. This game has a good amount of replayability but I still think people will crave the old retro evolved version time to time, as at times you will get frustrating with the difficulty of having to unlock stars for further stages.
All in all, it is a good game and I don't regret my purchase. You should consider it if you have always been a Geometry Wars fan. 8/10 for a casual shooter.

I have been a big fan of the geometry wars games since retro evolved on the arcade.  The games are kinda difficult to understand but if you like twinstick shooters you can get hooked.  There is no other game where I get competitive about being on the highscore list.
The music is great, the gameplay is great, the screen will blind you,  but you'll love every minute of it.  If you compare this game to retro evolved, evolved mode is a lot harder as there are new enemies, black holes are much harder to take out as they make it impossible to see while shooting them, and chargers that spawn earlier than I remember in old retro evolved.  The guys that go in a straight line also kinda throw a wrench in my old strategy of just going in large circlur motion across stages where it was possible.  This makes for interesting gameplay imo since it lets you strategize per stage.  The scoreboards per stage also adds a bit of competitive fun for me.
If your a fan of the previous games this won't let you down and if your new to the series this is probably a good time to start.

Slime Rancher is a very casual game, encouraging exploration and adventure. Shut off the wiki because all you need is the ingame database.
You own a ranch, starting off with virtually nothing but an empty corral. Your most obvious goal is to build and upgrade your jolly little ranch. But you have no monies. How would one get fat dosh? By venturing into the wilderness with your trusty multi-purpose vac gun and jetpack (upgrade required
) to discover various wildlife, resources, secrets, and
. There's no invisible walls of sort. Exploration is truly free as long as your energy reserves hold up. With many different kind of slimes, it's not difficult figuring out their nature thanks to the slimepedia, providing every little thing you need to know about the world you interact with.
Simply put, learn about your environment and make your cutesy, killer, little slimes happy to make money. Use that money to improve efficiency to get more money. Capitalism, ho!
It's an early access game. It's difficult to judge an unfinished game that potentially could be in development hell. One thing I know for sure, once you get your hours out of Slime Rancher, you won't have much more to do. After achieving everything you can and banking on all the money you could possibly want, you'll have no contents left for you. Your experience will be left short. It'll take months for contents to come out and it won't be enough to satisfy your instant needs. By then, how invested are you still?
Now listen 'ere. I don't buy a lot of games. I'm a cheap, dirty pirate, and I also despise early access games. I pirated Slime Rancher out of curiousity one day and thought it was the best thing ever. I was overwhelmed with bliss. I couldn't get over how adorable everything was and I thought the concept was perfect. Months later, I bought it, despite my hatred for early access. The developer deserved all da monies. I've had a rare experience.

Okay, don't get scared by the title of this!
...
Wait, if you are already here, I guess that warning comes too late, sorry :D
So, what do I want to say?
Basically, that I got this as part of the Humble monthly bundle and damn. I would have really regretted not playing this game. This month's bundle seemed like a huge disappointment to me, considering all the games. Considering that a game named "Slime Rancher" was the second most interesting thing I saw should tell you quite much.
However, let me get back to my first statement:
Don't get confused by this weird name.
So, what makes this game so great?
1. Yep, it is early access. No, you don't get that feeling ingame. Most things feel very polished, the world itself has an air of intrigue and happy chaos about it and as soon as you are starting to get a bit bored by repeating the same things, new pathes open and lo and behold, the entire theme turns darker, toxic, still beautiful, but different. Or you choose another way and find yourself in a lush emerald jungle, with astonishinginly graphical accents (looking at you, weird pink lamps).
Also, what really flabbergasted me was how well the ecosystems works.
We have a natural habitat of Slime A and B. One Slime A gets born. Slime A feeds on stuff. Due to the feeding, Slime A "spawns" food for other slimes. Slime B (a different race of slimes) feeds on A's leftovers. Slime B growth, getting characteristics of Slime A and B. Slime population growth and growth.
Come Nightfall. Slimerace C appears, only in the dark. Same things happening, they feed, they leave leftovers. Now slime B comes along again, bigger and already has the characteristics of A. Feeds on leftovers of C.
Mutates to "The Tarr", a slime (and player) munching monster, kills most slimes in the area. Rinse and repeat. Beautiful.
So, hey. You sticked with me so long, thanks for reading it. As someone with over 250 played games in his library, let me tell you these two things: if you like simulations, good mechanics and awesome exploration, get aboard. You won't regret it (:
Just take a few minutes to get acustom to it, sleep at night (ingame), and enjoy the travel to a very foreign, but intricate world in which you can spend some quality hours, enjoying the happy, funny flow of the world.
Well done, developers, really, really well done.
Finnaly an early access game with an interesting premise and an active development group!!! Good on you guys, keep at it!

If you're wondering whether or not you'll like Dishonored 2, you really just have to ask yourself if you liked Dishonored 1, because they're basically the same in terms of gameplay. If you were hoping the AI would be less erratic, or there would be more weapons for a lethal approach, or the guards would stop repeating themselves, none of that has changed in any significant amount. If you've never played the first game and don't know if you liked it or not then you should probably do that first, because the plot of 2 doesn't coddle players who think it's acceptable to start a series with the second entry, so if you haven't played the first game and its DLC storyline (which is especially important) you might not appreciate most of the characters as much. If you liked Dishonored 1 and want another game's worth of it, go right ahead, if you have the hardware to run it. The optimization isn't unplayable, but it seems to be very picky in which computers it will run on and which computers it will barely start on, and while my 970 and i5 3570k @4.4 GHz was able to run it at mostly max settings at around 60 fps, others with similar hardware have barely managed to reach that on low settings. I'm submitting my recommendation as positive because the game itself is great, but I hope Bethesda learns a lesson from the rest of the recommendations burning them at the stake to not try to release your game a day early if you aren't going to properly optimize it. The "preorder and get the game a day early" scheme is the worst preorder idea I've ever seen and should've died with Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare, and maybe now it really will.

You run around with an axe, chop zombies, and die a bunch of times. At least, that's DayZ Standalone right now.
To sum up Dark Souls 2: You run around with any weapon from a wide variety, from whips to big greatswords, to katanas, kill zombies, giants, and big bosses. You don't die because you're already dead BEFORE the game starts. You just lose your souls.
Welcome to the twisted world of Dark Souls 2, where death is taken in stride and every corner you turn is cruel and unforgiving. There is no hand holding in this game, no quest log or markers, you're on your own.
Action and adventure put together in the best form, along with a unique type of multiplayer, creates a game you'll remember.
Remember 'Remember Me'? No? Me neither, but I can definitely remember the many times I've run through a doorway to suddenly be trapped between two groups of nasties trying to rip me to shreds!
Beautiful, atmospheric, challenging and addictive. Bought it twice so I can enjoy the game to it's fullest with all my friends.

The 3D levels aren't the greatest or revolutionary, but there's some fun concepts.
Worth the $15.

I AM TIRED OF THESE MOTHER♥♥♥♥ING SHAPES ON THIS MOTHER♥♥♥♥ING (geometric) PLANE.  Would cleanse the universe of geometry again, 8.5/10
Ok sorry I had to try my hand at troll reviewing.  In all seriousness its more Geo Wars that you love with a whole new adventure mode thats basically 50 smaller game modes in one with their own leaderboards PLUS all the Geo Wars 2 game modes (dubbed "Classic" modes).  The adventure mode also allows you to have one of 5 types of drones that can be paired with any one of 5 "special" abilities, its pretty cool.  The dollar spent per hour ratio should be pretty low with this one if its your type of game (twin-stick shooter).  A gamepad is necessary to play to maximize your scores.  My only three minor complaints are:
1) that the graphics are not as nice or updated as I would have hoped,  In general the graphic style is more understated and less colorful and flashy, like pastel colors or something.  This does generally create better contrast when stuff gets crazy but it still just doesnt look as cool and trippy as you would have hoped waiting 6 years for a sequel to Geo Wars 2.
2): Theres an enemy type they brought back from Geo Wars 1 (the little purple triangular shaped things that swarm you by the thousands from the 4 corners of the screen), except now they are orangey yellow color and can be hard to distinguish from geoms, thus you can be collecting geoms and BAM a single little triangle thingy is in the mass of geoms and you dont see it and die.
3) On the 3-d levels I found the camera to be kind of stiff (especially on cubes) and something off about it since you can see a background behind the plane or shape you are fighting on and thus the camera isnt as locked to your ship as before and somehow at first I found the game to be almost nauseating looking at stuff, took me an hour or two to get used to it.  Im sorry Im having a hard time describing it.  In general though, I also feel Stardust HD on the ps3 did a better job with 3d battlegrounds.  But realistically, what else could they try to add to the geo wars experience?
In the end, this is the best and most fully featured version of what is in my mind, the best twin-stick arcade game series ever made, and it isn't particularly close.

Summary: Mild, don't buy it if you are expecting something extraordinary.
Guardians of Orion tries a to do bit too much at once. It has level progression like prelude but this time it works similar to the level progression in Borderlands 2. Example: three skill trees, each skill requiring multiple points to max. However these skills have little effect on your character and the primary reason to level up being the ability to use higher level equipment. The equipment is dropped throughout playing the various game modes (although I personally can only remember getting drops in harvist).
The three game modes outside of the unnecessary hub world are:
Harvest, were you defend a moving tracker/robot against waves of dinos and robots, this is the only game mode played by the established community.
Mayhem, where you fight in a free for all and instead of kills the main objective is crates, this mode is uncommon to see played.
WarGames, where you fight other players in a space dogfight, but actually sit in a spaceship for 30 minutes doing nothing do to the fact that nobody wants to play wargames because wargames ♥♥♥♥ing sucks.
Also what is up with the ridiculous load times? It takes 10 minutes to get into the game and on to a server.
The visuals of the game are actually really nice if you stand still, but if you move around all of the reflective surfaces make the game just look bad. The maps look really pretty, but are uninspiring and boring. Also why does nearly everything look like plastic?
The soundtrack is great, I really liked it. and it might just be the best part of the game.
The backstory is too complicated for its own good, even though it is summarized in a 15 minute intro cutscene at the beginning of the game. Plus you nor I care about their loose justification for shooting dinos.
Currently I can not recommend this game even for .99 USD. For every good point this game has there seems to be at least 2 bad points. There are so many unnecessary features (microtransactions, really?), none of the game modes are very fun and
it is so much better for a USD.
It could take you 1-2 hours to 100% the steam achievements (no I don't care about the in game achievements),
and I rate it a 4/10.

So!  Half-Life: Source.  Valve's attempt at porting the original Half-Life from the old GoldSrc engine to the newer Source engine.  A lot of the reviews I had read said it was basically the same old Half-Life with some slightly new physics, ragdolls spawned on an NPC's death, and better lighting and water.  I was expecting almost the
same as Half-Life, but there were a few differences here and there.  Also, there's almost no mod support, unlike Half-Life.  Still being an older game, I was able to crank up graphical settings to get maximum enjoyment.
This is what I was most pleased by.  The original Half-Life had static lighting.  It was just a bubble of light placed in the map, and it changed the brightness of that area.  In Half-Life: Source, however, the lighting is much improved.
First of all, the flashlight was akin to that of Half-Life 2's flashlight, not a magical spot of light that pastes itself to a wall.
The ambient lighting is actually coming from a light source in this game!  Some rooms look very different with this new lighting.  Most of the time, these rooms were a lot darker than they were in Half-Life.  But this gives a pleasant ambient effect to the game that isn't in the original.  Plus, NPCs have real shadows.
Unfortunately, due to Valve not wanting to completely redo Half-Life, there's nothing you can pick up and throw.  The boxes still function the same way: You walk into them to push them, and hold "E" to pull them.  But they don't spaz out and fly against a wall when pulling them (which I somewhat missed).
Player physics are literally almost the same as the original.  I can still bunny-hop the way I used to, and I can do Schrodinger's Crouch.  But one thing I found odd is that the jump height is increased.  When in Half-Life, I could jump and zip straight into a pipe, in Half-Life: Source, I smacked my head on the top of the pipe, ruining my perfectly executed move.  While this might not affect average players, those who have a routine for the entire game will likely get screwed up by this.
Ragdolls are also a thing now.  Instead of playing an animation when dying, NPCs drop as ragdolls instead.  I will say that it is pretty satisfying to see a HECU Marine fall dead in his tracks with a right-click of my shotgun.
Source's new water effects have greatly improved sight into the water, but given the rest of the outdated graphics, the better water feels out of place.
The levels are almost the exact same as those in Half-Life...
.  Valve actually did change a few things.  I noticed that tubes at least in the beginning weren't octogons, and had a higher amount of polygons.  Some terrain was made slighly more realistic, instead of a ramp of sand, there was more of a "bumpy" or "hilly" look to it.  (after 80 hours of trying to speedrun Half-Life, you notice little details like this).  And of course, the canyon scene is very much fixed.  The pipes no longer end spontaneously in an abyss, and the skybox is much improved.  A clear bottom to the canyon can be seen, and you can watch the water ripple.  Other than aesthetic improvements, not much was made to the actual maps.
Enemies, however, I believe have been changed.  Vortigaunts seem to lightning you faster, as if the difficulty was set on "Hard".  I also feel like the HECU Marines do more damage, but maybe they're just a little bit more accurate (or because they actually turn around before you double blast them with the shotgun).  Some HECU vehicles take more hits than they did in Half-Life.  One example would be the HECU chopper that comes in after getting the RPG on the cliffside.  In Half-Life, it usually took one rocket, and it was done.  Now, I used all my rockets (granted I missed half of my shots) and all the Tau Cannon ammo, and it still didn't go down.  The tank after the cliffs also either doesn't take damage from satchel charges beneath it, or takes more than two (satchel charges is how I always dispose of the tank in that level).  Rockets did the trick, though.
Valve fixed some of my favorite glitches from Half-Life in this game.  The infinite health door is what really hit me hard.  I could no longer beat the game with over 9000 health.  Other fixes include not being able to push buttons through walls (which I missed greatly from my playthrough), and the ability to push friendly NPCs around, so I could skip those talk sequences in the beginning or skip almost the entirety of Office Complex by pushing Barney through a door, or riding the elevator from the outside.
Unfortunately, new bugs have found their way into the game.  Elevators make no sound when you ride them (which isn't terrible, it just ruins the atmosphere).  When I tried to turn on the HD textures pack, few of the weapons would make any sound.  Not my own weapons, not the HECU's weapons, no weapons made any sound.  I switched back and tried to load the save, but it froze and had to restart my Mac.  Started a new game from that chapter (Yes!  You can select a chapter now!) with the HD pack disabled, and it worked fine.  Speaking of textures, the conveyor belt rides in
had a serious problem.  I don't know how to explain it, but be wary of a graphical glitch in that chapter (might be my Mac.  I have no idea).
Half-Life: Source is an attempt at porting a GoldSrc game to the Source engine.  Granted it wasn't a very worthy attempt, but at least it's a start.  If this had been better, I don't think Black Mesa would have existed, and Valve would be raking in all the cash.  But I think the Black Mesa team did a swell job at completely recreating Half-Life, perhaps even better than Valve could've done.  Definitely better than what Valve has actually done.  Sure, I'd recommend it, but only if you need to complete your Half-Life collection.  If you want Half-Life, buy the original.  If you want Half-Life in the Source engine, go for Black Mesa.  Half-Life: Source isn't worth your time.

I have sunk months of my life into the multiplayer in Call of Duty, on all the various formats, and the peer-to-peer technology is solid. From a business perspective, its a no brainer. In my experience, it plays just fine, and with the advent of ultra fast broadband, and every day computers gettings more and more powerful, its only getting better. I have NEVER understood the gaming scene's constant criticism of this methodology. If you have an issue with lag spikes or other common online glitches, don't blame the way the game is hosted, blame the infrastructure of the internet. That, essentially, is what has to improve for these kind of glitches to become a thing of the past.
COD is (or was) as big as it is because of its PvP multiplayer, if it ain't broke, don't fix it.

I do not recommend this game. It is yet another call of duty game without any substantial steps forward within the actual gameplay. I am only reviewing the multiplayer (Who buys a Cod game for Singleplayer?).
The bad:
* Big Hit box which does not follow the shape of player (People blame rubberbanding, but It isn't always this. I have played plenty of strong connection servers, the hit box is massive, you can hit a player standing still by shooting off target haha it's terrible)
* No Leaning
* Sprinting has no aim penalty (Because your wearing an exo suit I hear you say)
* No 3D scope perspective (e.g. Cod Ghosts had it, RO2 players know what I am talking about) Instead you get a big black crappy edge.
* Weapon recoil is minimal meaning no downside to constant automatic fire
* Weapon cone of fire is incredibly tight, this allows easy firing from the hip without needing laser sight, ect..
* Maps are incredibly small, this makes for incredibly frustrating gameplay. You often spawn right next to enemies. Sniper rifles are a pointless weapon unless you have iron sites or acog as a long shot in this game must be considered 50 yards..
* Weapon atatchments make very little sense (e.g. Sniper rifle, take off a big scope, use an acog and you lose some weapon handling. (A lower powered scope, smaller sized optic, would allow faster target aquisition and less weight yet it takes -2 from wep handling) really strange..
The good:
* Incredibly fast paced action (If you like it)
* The exo suit adds a few more capabilities in the way of movement/dodging.
On the whole, I do not like the game. I enjoyed it for the first few hours but it is now just a very frustrating game. It has far too many negatives. It was 'not' a step forward in anyway. It really is the same trash recycled.

You can't have players feeling lonely and desperate, and at the same time answer the call of the community that demands that they can play with their friends. The idea of Riff Racer is wonderful, and the game-track sincronization works efficiently. The game is very fun, and I recommend it to anyone who is into music and beating records in cars.

Some tracks have many flaws, and a in-game editor would be nice to fix these mistakes. This editor would create levels for your friends and Steam community to try on too, where they could try to beat your created levels (like Hotline Miami 2 or Hitman Absolution editors, for example). Also, it would be cool if you could play an entire album of a band, like a mini-campaign for players to beat, with a bigger reward at the end (like PAYDAY 2 Crime Spree, for example). Moreover, the tracks are very similar on every music, and we would love to be able to customize it more.
Despite these suggestions, Riff Racer is very cool and brilliant. I hope you can add these stuff in the base game through new updates and patches, but if not, I really hope for a sequel, bigger and better.

As a big fan of the series, I'm tepidly recommending this simply because the single player campaign is such a drag.  The classic play types are still there, and the rest of the game is fun, but you'll spend hours grinding the same levels for just a few more points so you can get enought starts to continue the game.  Besides the 3D twist, and some modes like infection (I think that's what it's called), the mecanics aren't really as solid as the previous versions because they still rely on assumptions that were true when the playfield was 2D.  Have fun dying 10,000 times because some enemy you couldn't have possibly seen comes flying around the corner of the cube and the camera angle is fixed overhead.
I respect that the creators had a tough task to expand the series, but there are a lot of places where the older games (esp. 2) were a lot more *fun.*  I found myself saying "this isn't fun" too many times while trying to play the single player campaign.  There are some creative and fun modes, but having to play the same level 10 or 15 additional times to squeeze out 10,000 extra points or whatever to advance puts a huge damper on it.
Despite this, it is still geometry wars, and it still touches on a lot of the right notes, but do yourself a favor and have your kid brother/cousin whatever play through all the single player levels so you can go back and pick and play just the ones that are fun.
One last gripe: the PC port is lacking.  If you're playing with the keyboard, why can't you set space bar to bomb?  Why does the game show you what buttons to hit as if you're playing with an XBOX One controller?  Good luck figuring out what keys are left and right trigger & bumper.  Also, resolution is fixed, etc., rabble rabble rabble...
If you're a fan of the series like I am, go buy this because you have to and you were going to anyway.  If not, play it first to see if it's worth your investment.  I'm still on the "recommend" side despite this game's warts.

Still full of bright neon colors and lots of particles on enemy death.
The campaign mode is something I'm not super excited about, since I much prefer playing the game arcade-style, but I'll be damned if I'm not getting three stars on every single stage.  So, I guess it works in that regard.
The one thing I am a little disappointed by is that the soundtrack this time around isn't quite as good as GW2, and the original Evolved theme is conspicuously absent from this game.  That's not to say that the music isn't really good, because it is, but I thought the original Evolved theme suited the game mode so well.
Overall, I'm very happy that this game exists, and I'm definitely going to put an irresponsible amount of time into it after exams.

Rust is one of my all time favourite games. Look at my library and compare it to the amount of hours spent on other games. Rust tops every game I own almost 3 times over. That makes it in my opinion, a good game. There are, however, negatives to account for. First of all. The game has been in early access for a long period of time (4 years, edging on 5), but it is receiving constant weekly updates showing progress that the team at facepunch are attempting to create to enhance gameplay for us, the consumer.
There have been many changes in the "system" in rust. When I say system I mean how the game plays. The first "system" was the blueprint system, and was within the game for around 2-3 years. This system was loved by many players for its simplicity yet challenging nature. It challenged the player to find scraps of the blueprint to obtain items within the game that are increasingly rarer. This went from lower tier items like roadsign armour and pickaxes, to items such as AK's and Metal Armour. This system required the player to spend larger amounts of time within the game to grind for better items (Note: rust is a game where time has to be available. One cannot simply join a server and expect to find AK's and higher tier items. This takes time and gathering).
The second system was the XP system which was liked and disliked by many players. It took the aspect of grinding to another level. I remember when the system first came out, my group and I despised it as it was simply, farm, kill, harvest repeat until the golden level of 31 was reached for the ultimate item, the rocket launcher. This change to the system was upsetting to not only myself and my group, but hundreds and thousands of players who were thrilled by the raiding aspect of Rust. It was acclaimed as the system where farming and free time were key. After a wipe, sinking 30 hours into a base and gaining level was a common sight for many Rust players. This system had its pros and cons like all the others, but was generally the most disliked.
The third and final system is the current system, Components/Blueprints. This system was a comforting relief. I did not have to sink an initial 30+ hours to simply be up the XP level for an item I wanted, but simply had to find the resources, components and build away. I at first was unsure of this system, but came to like its simplistic nature and accessability to the more average rust player who has to balance his/her life with work, school or other activities and can only manage to scramble 5-10 hours a week. It gave the player a chance to have PvP guns and armour without sinking their life into what some would say a pointless video game. After a while, the system seemed too good to be true. In true facepunch style (sorry for the hate, but most players will agree), they f*****d it up again. This was when the component system was merged with a new and improved blueprint style system. This implemented an item called scrap. Scrap is an item which is used for most activities in rust such as researching an item to craft and use it later on, making a workbench and recycling components. Now, when this first came out I wasn't too fussed and played along, not seeing what the problem was. This wasn't until our group started to thin out to around 2-3 active players a week. Gathering scrap was, to say the least difficult. Items such as AK's require 750 scrap to research, and not to mention the cost of a Tier 1, 2 and 3 Workbench accumulating to 2000+ scrap. This is to simply craft items. Not to mention, rust has an enourmous quantity of items in the game. Tier 3 items are the most sought after and usually cost 750 scrap each. Let's jsut say it is quite a lot of scrap for lets say a solo player.
This system, although good and bad in its own way, is detering newer players from even buying the game. They look up rust solo for instance and see a player ranting about absurd scrap costs. This singular thing is stopping people from playing the game. It is hard enough to survive in rust and keep a base for longer than a few days, and facepunch decide to complicate it even more by increasing difficulty every patch.
I want people to like this game. I thoughroughly enjoyed it. It has been and experience going through new systems, testing out new base ideas, pvp'ing, making friends and more and more. Rust can be a good game, but facepunch, please listen to your audience. Make the game more user friendly. Right now it is a game which acts like more of a deterent rather than an enjoyable experience.
I want to recommend this game to all of the current people thinking of buying it, but warn you of the possible negative experiences and time you will need to play the game.
-Moose

I'll just make this a fast review from the first things that pop into my head.
Thoughts:
- Great Story (Predictable in some parts, but there were still surprises.)
- HUGE Game (takes several hours... which is a good thing and a bad thing. Good because it is entertaining. Bad because I didn't have the endurance for that length from this kind of game and just wanted to have the pay off of the game being over.) (80+ Hours on Pokemon is one thing, 20+ hours on this game was a little much for me.)
- A little glitchy (my game would freeze during some of the Baba Yaga cut scenes, and there were a few platforming glitches or lever issues)
- I hate the Titan fights, but there are only a few of them
- Easy game for a casual gamer to get into (I'm a very casual gamer.)
- QUALITY voice acting from the main cast
- Very different from your average Castlevania (You spend most of your time OUT of a castle, you don't have as many monsters, and the format of the game reminds me of Prince of Persia: Sands of Time for some reason)
- Fun puzzles (except for that dumb blood cup one)
- Interesting Character Design (Like, I LOVE the concept art in the game)
- Gabriel is a cutie.
- Graphics are pretty great too. Landscapes are gorgeous. People have a little of that uncanny valley going on. (Especially Marie. Those dead eyes...)
- Really great soundtrack.
- Fighting system is pretty easy to get a grip on. Combos aren't that hard to remember or figure out either.
- RELICS. (I really liked the Relics along with Gabriel's super fancy cross whip thing.)
Overall, I really liked this game. I would recommend it to plenty of people.

If you can survive the first, boring, slow, mind-numbing two chapters, you're in for an incredibly fun adventure. Amazing graphics, great enviroments, epic, yet unmemorable soundtrack, fun combat system, really good length (it took me 20 hours to barely finish it). Its only cons are, as I mentioned, the boring beginning, and the omnipresent "Uncharted" climbing sections. You might not enjoy it if you are a big fan of the old Vanias, but give it a shot, expecially when it's on sale.

I would have really loved to give this game a positive review, but unfortunately the Boss in chapter 2 cannot be defeated without a gamepad because you have to rotate your movement buttons impossibly fast (which would be simply rotating the stick on a gamepad). The fact that you have to use a macro or other weird tricks to defeat this boss by using PC hardware on a PC game is a no-go. The rest of the game was perfectly playable with KB+mouse, so I have no idea why this has not been adapted. I am a big castlevania fan and it hurts that this is what we get for buying the game on other platforms.
It's even stranger that i can play all castlevania titles availible for emulators on PC without problems like that, on KB+mouse.
Never happened to me before that the platform I play on actually became a plotstopper. The people responsible for this should be ashamed.

Borderlands 2 is a game for those looking to have fun in a world away from reality, with enough guns and explosions for the whole family.
I thoroughly regret not having bought this game sooner. I had always heard about it, but I wasn't really good at FPS games, so I didn't bother. In my opinion, that was a bad idea. I love this game. Here are some pros and cons.
Pros:
+Good humor
+Cool character abilities
+Pretty good music
+Intricate skill tree (It is pretty confusing at first)
+A lot of different kinds of enemies
+A wide variety of guns for any situation
+Very nice leveling system
+Many DLC's to extend your fun
+Very unique and cool art style
+Almost all of the quotes are awesome (Esoecially Tiny Tina, Krieg, and CL4P-TP)
Cons:
-Gets kind of boring after 500 hours
-Sniping gets extremely underpowered late game
-The grandma from the Thanksgiving DLC
Besides those minor cons, this game is truly one of my favorite games, and will probably stay like that. Well, time to wait for Borderlands 3!

I had never played geometry wars before, just a clone that had been available on Linux many many years ago. That clone isn't available any more, so I am extremely happy to buy and play the official Game, third installment.
I read through various reviews, especially negative ones, and understand the criticism. But to me as a casual player who would be happy with only the classic mode and needs games that run on Linux, this is probably one of the best shooters I can get.
The gameplay is basically always the same, there is a limited number of enemies, but I don't care. For me, this game is about hand-eye coordination, being able to read complex and hectic situations, and getting in the "zone". I can't say I have reached that level yet, it will probably take many many hours to be able to make millions of points in a zen-like state, and maybe at that level I will also notice the supposedly sluggish controls and inaccurate hitboxes. So... if you're a pro gamer, or familiar with the geometry wars series, read the negative reviews I guess. If you're looking for some harmless action fun, get this game.
Cons:
What annoyed me at first was that I can't switch to keyboard + mouse mode, the game always uses the controller. I could probably fix that by removing the controller, but I like the controller gameplay quite a bit after a few hours.
Another minor annoyance is that even the "classic" mode has a 3d view of the playing area, and that due to camera movement you don't always see all the borders of the field. So a wave of enemies can spawn without you seeing them.

The game takes minutes to boot for me, onto the review...
A lot of potential here, but almost no players are on to start a game and expect a lot of grinding, especially with the starter edition limiting your inventory slots and classes.
Orion Prelude is a much simpler survival/horde mode game. The $1 I paid for the ultimate edition got me every single unlock. It's also buggy but got some laughs from it.
Guardians of Orion is "protecting the harvester" and grind for loot and crafting mats. It is very poorly optimized, even worse than Prelude, as it takes up 18GB and runs poorly. The UI is clumsy and confusing. The ships have literal "pew pew" sounds and while having the "dogfighting" mode is cool, it's very basic and feels unfinished.
There are also a lot of microtransactions in Guardians, and because of this, I would not recommend buying any edition of this game. Prelude is a cheap and fun game(at least for a few hours), while Guardians requires either grinding or a lot more money than the $1 starter edition.
The only positives I have are that it does have really good graphics and the developers appear to be sticking around. I will change my review if they begin making improvements to the game.
There are far better games that are free to play and this is not worth playing in its current state in my opinion.

Very enjoyable game.  The storyline was quite immersive, thanks largely in part to the incredible voice acting.  The gameplay was generally quite varied as you develop new skills and discover equipment upgrades.  It did get a little overwhelming with all the combat moves, and to be honest most of them see little use other than in solving some of the puzzles, but at least there are some options.  I haven't played any Castelvania games since Nintendo had the license but I will definitely pick up others from here on in.
I will add a note in regards to the DLC.  While the first of the two adds some intriguing gameplay with some more puzzles and an opportunity to play as an alternate character in some scenes, the second is just plain terrible.  It was nothing but movement based mechanics with little options for any of the combat challenges presented in the core game.  The last boss battle is incredibly frustrating and based entirely on angling your attacks rather than choosing the right attack for the job or timing your blocks (none of the attacks can be blocked) and counterstriking.  In addition, the substitution of 2d comic scenes rather than cutscenes felt incredibly lazy, though the voice acting was retained.  Having said all that it certainly wasn't enough to take away from the overall game enjoyment and with the Ultimate Edition you aren't really paying any extra for it.

"Cute and fun" about sums up this game. You suck slimes, fruit, veggies, chickens, etc. into your vac gun (vacuum) and shoot them back out wherever. You have a little ranch and can build things like slime pens, chicken coops, gardens for growing plants as food for your slimes, etc. You put slimes in pens, grow food, feed your slimes, and sell what is basically their poop to profit. Not having anything to spend said profits on would make the game a bit dull, so thankfully there are two pricey ranch expansion areas, and your various things you can build mostly have upgrades like taller pen walls, ceilings for your pens, auto-feeders, poop-suckers, etc. Not only that, but you can upgrade your rancher with your money, getting a mostly-hovering jetpack, more health, more energy for running and powering your jetpack, etc.
The slimes are positively adorable and the game is fun...until you run out of stuff you need to buy. Eventually, I had bought both ranch expansions, but had no need to buy anything else because I had every upgrade and my original ranch land was producing so much slime poop that I basically could just stand in my ranch and feed slimes forever and never leave again, while my money exponentially grew. There doesn't seem to be a goal except to make more money, and that gets old when you have nothing else worth buying.
I would have given further exploration a shot, but I have a horrible sense of direction and memory, and the game does not have an in-game map of any kind whatsoever. I found rad slimes (radioactive) through a key door that I unlocked using a rare key, but I could never find the door again because I forgot where it was. In closing, this game is simply delightful and adorable, and while you still have things to upgrade and strive to have enough money to afford, it's a lot of fun, but once you run out of new things to buy, the game seems to lack any other goals, and I couldn't see continuing without an in-game reason to do so other than "your character wants to make more money."

If you ever played any other Geometry Wars game, then not a whole lot in Dimensions will be too surprising. If you never played Geometry Wars, you should probably fix that right now.
Dimensions has a lot of different ways of playing. 5 out of 6 modes from GW2 are found in Classic mode, and Adventure mode is where the new 3-D playfields, support drones, and drone 'supers' are found. The first drone you get is a little ship that supplements your main ship with a bit of extra firepower. The first super drops mines all over the field for enemy shapes to run into. Every other drone and super all do something along those lines.
New fields are nice, but present some challenges that take a bit of getting used to. It can be hard to see around an edge of the playfields (like the cube), but luckily you can prefire around the edges and be at least a little safer.
I am finding the playfields harder for me to read than previous Geometry Wars games. It helps that you have a bit more time to see a spawning enemy before it actually spawns, but the way even 2-D fields tilt a little bit can be, well, tilting.
Geometry Wars is also the only game where I actually care about leaderboards. The game isn't predictable, so replaying a level over and over is not a chore. It helps that every GW game is a masterclass in escalation of challenge.
Not much else to say. I love Geometry Wars a lot, and I haven't been able to play it since being separated from my Xbox. If you enjoyed it in the past, this is an excellent way to fill 5 minutes or 5 hours. If you never played Geometry Wars, please do. Everyone should have more simple and infinitely challenging games in their life.

Not exactly Grand Theft Auto, but if it was, I wouldn't need to play to find out where it goes. The freedom to roam the streets as either Criminal or Enforcer is enticing, like playing Cops and Robbers except I actually get to riddle them full of holes.
Criminals can keep busy doing all kinds of things, breaking into store fronts and stealing merchandise, mugging people on the street, stealing vehicles and turning them into chop shops for a finders fee, making that money.
Enforcers on the other hand kind of get the short end of the stick. With few opportunities to make money outside of missions, progression obtaining better gear is a good bit longer, but without Enforcers, Criminals would have no one to fight. I think that Enforcers could use a bit more of a pick-me-up.
Guns. Honestly, outside of vehicular manslaughter, this is your only kill option, and frankly, I get bored with just guns. I would love to sneak up behind those Crims and put a blade between their ribs. So many opportunities would have been mine if there were a melee option.
Third person point of view kind of hurts the excitement a little bit, it's difficult to really pinpoint the reason behind it but I always feel a good bit more control in first person perspective.
Driving is a challenge, but I actually like it that way, learning all of the nuances to different vehicles, knowing when to start turning, take your foot off the gas, and put it back on to make that absurd u-turn, all the while laughing because everyone else is smacking into the walls, trying to catch up. Learning curves are sick...
Movement and running are okay, no real complaints, but interacting with the world? Doors, ladders, fences etc. is very primitive. You can Only climb from the bottom of the ladder to the top or vice versa, instead of being able to sit on the ladder from the perfect vantage point and open fire, or waiting for the perfect moment to climb that last rung. The only barriers you can climb over are predesignated chainlink and wooden fences so entries and escapes can only get so creative. Doors, you can only kick, you can't open slowly and maintain anonimity. The worst thing about it all I think, is that your name is brightly displayed over your character, even if only a hair on the top of your head is visible. No sneaking up in this game.
Story? There's supposed to be one, but personally I think it along with the missions and gameplay lack any real depth and character growth. It's basically glorified Team Deathmatch.
Temporary guns. To get anything permanent, takes tons of grinding. I'm not even going to get into this.
Customization? I think that Second Life could have done a lot better if they followed this games rules on customization, giving you basic shapes to work into your own design. This allows for great degrees of creativity, matched with a lack of graphic-produced lag, making for a comparitively fluid, yet personal experience. Just be sure to go into the customization with patience and a solid plan, and it'll come out great.
Pros
Customization
Driving challenge
Freedom to roam
Cons
Primitive movement
Glowing names
No melee
Lack of depth
I think I'll keep playing on and off because it is a fun game, but I am actively looking for a replacement on my list, so let me call this a tentative recommendation.

The dialogue is unintrusive and to the point, and the game focuses more on the environment and atmosphere to tell its story, much like games such as System Shock and Thief. All in all, if you still haven't played Half-Life, you owe it to yourself to give it a shot.
