Aside from Modern Warfare 2, I haven't bothered with any other version, as they are all the same.  This one is no exception - they even use the same sounds from MW2 in the menus!
Graphics are okay - nice, but nothing special.  They do tend to be blurry in the single player game though.  You have to go through the "born bind" intro every time you resume the campaign mode - and it can't be skipped!
The whole game is slow and laggy - from the laggy menu, to the excruitatingly slow loading of multiplayer or bot rounds (you literally have time to make a cup of tea before it has loaded - assuming the game syncronising doesn't fail) before you can play.
Movement is poor, with erratic mouse movements and inconistent collision detection.  Game matching is poor.  Most attempts at game joining fail - much like Modern Warfare 2 really.
The only good part is that you can fight against bots - but even that requires an online server.
It doesn't feel like the game has been in development for three years - it feels like something that was developed for a few months and then rushed out for Christmas.  There is little that can be recommended with the game unfortunately.  I'm hoping to be able to get a refund for the game, as its not worth hoping that the game will be patched soon.
The game doesn't respond to ALT+TAB or ALT+ENTER, so you cant do much else whilst its loading.
In conclusion, multiplayer is a frustrating and irritating lag-fest.  Single player campaign is burden by an intro sequence that you have to watch every time you play it - and it can't be skipped!
The latest updates haven't helped in any of the important areas.  The first update managed to mute all sound in the single player campaign - whether the second fixed it, I have no idea, but it certainly hasn't helped the multi-player mode.

"Cute and fun" about sums up this game. You suck slimes, fruit, veggies, chickens, etc. into your vac gun (vacuum) and shoot them back out wherever. You have a little ranch and can build things like slime pens, chicken coops, gardens for growing plants as food for your slimes, etc. You put slimes in pens, grow food, feed your slimes, and sell what is basically their poop to profit. Not having anything to spend said profits on would make the game a bit dull, so thankfully there are two pricey ranch expansion areas, and your various things you can build mostly have upgrades like taller pen walls, ceilings for your pens, auto-feeders, poop-suckers, etc. Not only that, but you can upgrade your rancher with your money, getting a mostly-hovering jetpack, more health, more energy for running and powering your jetpack, etc.
The slimes are positively adorable and the game is fun...until you run out of stuff you need to buy. Eventually, I had bought both ranch expansions, but had no need to buy anything else because I had every upgrade and my original ranch land was producing so much slime poop that I basically could just stand in my ranch and feed slimes forever and never leave again, while my money exponentially grew. There doesn't seem to be a goal except to make more money, and that gets old when you have nothing else worth buying.
I would have given further exploration a shot, but I have a horrible sense of direction and memory, and the game does not have an in-game map of any kind whatsoever. I found rad slimes (radioactive) through a key door that I unlocked using a rare key, but I could never find the door again because I forgot where it was. In closing, this game is simply delightful and adorable, and while you still have things to upgrade and strive to have enough money to afford, it's a lot of fun, but once you run out of new things to buy, the game seems to lack any other goals, and I couldn't see continuing without an in-game reason to do so other than "your character wants to make more money."

I only have 20 hours of playtime for the game so far, but, as a veteren coming from the Demon Souls's days I can assure anyone interested in this game that it is a must buy. First thing you will notice loading into the game is exactly that, the loading times between consoles pales in comparison to the PC (Depending on your PC, you can warp 2 and possibly 3 times before the console finishes loading the first warp!) This is imperative because A) when it comes to immersion as you don't have a 30 second wait time to slough through in between the few loading screens. and B) flow, since this is a game centered around dying and re-loading back to checkpoints.
The second important aspect which I believe is an overall improvement to the core of the game is combat; moreso, dual wielding. Before in Demon Souls's you could dual wield SOME weapons ( Katana x Katana pushlock bleh) but not all. Dark Souls offered even fewer than Demon Souls's (Some try to use the Quelag Fury Sword. Yet I will let you all know now that DragonSlayer spear in left+ Murakumo +15 in right, STR/Dex/faith build= far range poking, wide swipes, heavy damage, and greatsword poisebreaking is just too awesome to keep a secret.) Dark Souls 2 offers the ability to dual wield with many effective combos. Heck, you can even dual wield ultra greatswords if you wanted to and with practice, become a feared undead to come across (Just level adaption.)
Which brings me to a third point, new stats are introduced to the level scheme in this game. No longer is equipment load tied into endurance, and previous useless stats (Resistance) are revamped and now offer variables worth exploring. Ever wanted to swing your weapons faster in Dark Souls 1 and realized that was never a choice? It is now and damn does it add to the badassery of your lightning fast swordplay.
The fourth reason you should get this game is just freedom. The game drops you into the world at one starting point and soon you are given the option to branch off. While some areas are more difficult to traverse early on, they are possible, and often rewarded for your courage- don't be afraid to explore. You will die, and die again, and when you think you've got the boss with just a nick of health left to cleave away- you die. But the rewards are common and frequent and far greater if you venture past the beaten path.
The final reason? Coop...multiplayer. Sure, VERY RARELY have I experienced enemies walking up into the sky with me staring at them all slackjawed and bright eyed (then suddenly backstabbed.) But the experience to summon players when you find their sign to help you beat the boss you just died 20 times to is...enjoyable. No reward is diminished because of coop, everyone gets their slice of the pie. And beating that boss with a buddy gives a feeling in your gut to come back a seasoned veteran and own the boss solo. Also previous Dark Souls/ Demon Souls's fans note: EVEN IF YOU ARE UNDEAD YOU CAN STILL BE INVADED REGARDLESS. This takes away from the annoying grind of needing to waste precious humanity/effigy just to get a chance at dueling or being invaded. Lastly, compared to Dark Souls 1 on PC, Dark Souls 2 is x100 better port.

- Very challenging combat, rewards persistence and tactical thinking.
- Lots of content; game encourages character variation and allows for creative builds.
- Breathtakingly-beautiful levels that are interesting in design and encourage exploration.
- Much more solid port than its predecessor. Engine-wise the game runs very well. Some technical issues were reported by other players, I have not experienced this myself so I can't complain there.
Personally, however, I am disappointed with DS2. How disappointed, you ask? It doesn't come close to the masterpiece that is Dark Souls 1. Why, you ask? Soul Memory... 'nuff said.
Dark Souls 1 used a player's SL (soul level) to determine matchmaking with others online. To connect with a player, whether for co-op or PvP, you needed to be roughly within 15% of their SL. This system had its own flaws, but it worked fine. DS2 innovated by negating that SL requirement, and replacing it with a similar "roughly 15%" calculation of SM or 'soul memory', which is the total number of souls ever collected by a character (be it from enemies, PvP, consuming soul-items... you name it).
You can't stay in a given "strength level". Let's say you're like me, and you LOVE co-op. You just keep placing your summon sign and helping people along with a boss, again and again. You can't do that now, since after a while you gain enough souls as a phantom that you are now "outside the SM range" for most players in the area, so they stop seeing your sign. So you move to the next area, rinse and repeat. Eventually you have collected so many souls that you are not valid for matchmaking
.
1. That's how I roll, and it worked well with SL as the matchmaking mechanic.
2. It goes the same way with invading - you get souls by destroying your targets, and eventually won't get invasions anymore. Love making a character for specific-area invasion? Too bad, gonna have to re-make it from scratch every once in a while to keep playing the same style.
False. SM counts souls ever COLLECTED, not souls ever SPENT. You can also get screwed over the other way around: Remember the core death mechanic of the Souls series? When you die, you drop all your souls and you need to go retrieve them. If you die before retrieval is possible, “bye-bye souls”... only except in DS2 those lost souls still count toward your SM, since at some point you DID collect them, even though you never used them. So a player that is doing poorly is going to have an even harder time with the game: technically his SM count will be very high while his character is pretty much garbage-on-legs. Then, every invasion will be against stronger opponents, and fewer co-ops will be possible since players in that poor guy's area are all technically at a lower SM count than he is, and he won't see their signs.
This last part leads me to
Seems like it was implemented to deter twinking; that is, to stop players from using overpowered gear against people who are valid for matchmaking. But it doesn't work. A good, experienced player in DS2 has a much, MUCH easier time clearing areas and getting specific items than a new player. So it is still very possible to get superb gear at low SM counts, and use that gear to grief the f♥ck out of other players with low SM counts (since they are
behind you in terms of power).
Arguably, the twinking problem is even
now than it ever was.
There are certain
, but I don't think they are of similar importance as this issue. They are also VERY subjective and hence I don't give them much weight. Some of those are:
- Limited number of respawns per enemy. GG, people who actually like to farm. Say 'bonfire ascetic' one more time. I dare you. I double dare you, m♥therf♥cker.
- New menu system is very much meh. Why fix that which is not broken? [edit: I got over it, really]
- Poise is now complete b♥llsh♥t. A crippled hedgehog can stunlock an enemy in DS2. Why, why, why?
- Leveling up actually requires talking to an NPC, who can only be found in one area.
- Controls are... "tighter"? What the hell? Let me pull off a guard-break or a leap-attack without feeling like it deserves a Steam achievement.
- "You require additional
durability!"
- Want to use a new weapon and need more titanite? Too bad you ran out materials at the blacksmith, eh buddy? Yes, you can get more later. But again, what if you're trying to enjoy the early areas? That's poor design.
... I would generally recommend the game for players
to the Souls series, since they would have an easier time accepting the new mechanics. And yes, I
torn about the final "not recommended" verdict that I give DS2, since it still is a very fun game (only it also gives a huge middle-finger to my favorite styles of play: co-op, invading with a build, and farming).
My recommendation is to see if a friend can lend you their copy of the game and spend a few hours playing. See how you like the new mechanics; see if the combat feels interesting and rewarding to you. Other than that, probably don't buy until SM is "fixed" in some way.
May 31th, 2014. It's been about a month since I posted the original review and I have played quite a bit since [from ~30 hours played to ~110 hours]. I still think SM is a broken mechanic, and my complaint about availability of upgrade materials is even more prominent now. However I still enjoy the game and I still encourage you to try and borrow it from a friend (Steam has sharing now, you know). Give it a try and see how you feel about it, then decide if it's worth your time.
I have also changed my final verdict to "Recommended Game" since I really do encourage you to try and pick this game up. Just keep what I mentioned earlier in mind.
That said, have fun playing. KTHXBYE~

As survival games go, Rust is pretty standard. Open-world exploration, base building, PvP and PvE, with other worldly dangers to worry about. There are some pretty neat features in Rust, however, that make the game stand out from some other entries in the genre.
First of all, I'm going to discuss how difficult Rust can be. Often, and especially on official servers, other people will be geared up, and most people practice a kill-on-sight attitude, regardless of your danger to them. In a game like this, where you spawn with absolutely nothing, getting shot at like that can be painful.
Second, I'm going to talk about the performance. It's difficult for me to run the game (Core2 Quad, GTX660) on low settings, but my friends (with a 970 and another with 970 SLI) have no trouble and hit 60+ FPS in all areas. It helps to turn down render distances, and turning down settings dependent on location (outdoors, indoors, etc.) can help, as there are multiple levels of quality for different areas of video settings.
Third will be some gameplay. I think, where Rust differs from other survival games, is a) the interesting character generation, b) the recipe discovery, and c) the atmosphere.
Ahh, character generation. If you've already played Rust, you've probably realized that you spawn completely naked. I believe it's censored by default, but what fun is that? ;) The character is generated in a way that you are given a gender, and based on that gender you are generated that gender's genitalia, and the sizes are pretty much randomized. So yes, you can compare virtual♥♥♥♥♥♥♥with your friends.
Recipe discovery is pretty interesting in Rust. If you've ever played H1Z1, you probably know that you discover recipes by throwing random junk into a discovery window and hope that you can make what you were hoping to discover. Rust, on the other hand, is a little bit different. You find fragments of blueprints on the map, and combine them into larger blueprints to in turn discover recipes.
The atmosphere of Rust is really unique. A lot of games have obvious backgrounds. Once again, using H1Z1, you can tell what happened: the H1Z1 virus came up and killed 99.99% of people and they became zombies. With Rust, however, it's confusing. It takes place in an apocalyptic stage, of course, but you can tell it's modern due to the presence of nuclear reactors and firearms. Speaking of firearms, they lend to the atmosphere. They're mostly makeshift, with parts from household items attached to build the body of the various guns in the game. It gives the game a vibe like Mad Max. Another thing: there are airdrops from big C-130-type planes and even map-wide attacks via Blackhawk helicopters. Why this occurs, nobody can say for sure, but it's eerie that these machines operate in the apocalypse like that.
Overall, Rust is a somewhat different experience from other survival games, expecially open-world ones. It's not particularly expensive, and it has a great developer working on it. There are updates almost every week, including updates inspired by community wants and needs. The game's unique atmosphere, endless playability, and this great community-developer connection make it a great buy.

If you like Geometry Wars 2 this is more where that came from (it uses the Gemetry Wars 2 ruleset). The big thing they added is a single player progression mode (different play areas/bosses/multiple mine & drone options you can level up) and co-op. Doesn't have a Geometry War 1 mode unfortunately.

Only somewhat disappointed at the lack of options, particularly control options. My first Geometry Wars was Galaxies and I was hoping to play with dpad/face buttons but there are only two controller configs.
After spending more time with it the controls seem more natural.
The difficulty curve seems pretty steep until you get the first drone compared to what I would expect.

If you're looking for a good arcade-style game to kill time and have tons of fun, look no further.
To start, 3Dimensions includes all of the classic modes from the previous games: Deadline, which is timed and gives you unlimited lives; Evolved, which has no time limit but limited lives and bomb attack; King, where you can only shoot in temporary safe zones; Pacifist, which doesn't allow you to shoot and requires you to fly through gates to destroy enemies; and Waves, where you try to fight off lines of fast-moving enemies coming from all directions.
All of the classic modes are good, though the movement of the player's ship feels a little loose compared to previous games.
The Adventure Mode is where things get a little more complex and, unfortunately, don't hold up as well. Each level has a certain classic mode attached to it; sometimes you'll be playing Deadline, sometimes Evolved, sometimes stuff like Titan where you have to break up large versions of shapes that break off into clusters of smaller versions of themselves. The levels also take on shapes other than a flat board, such as a sphere, a cylinder, a board with windows or walls that spin, and such.
The worst part of Adventure Mode are the bosses. The conditions for beating a boss are as follows; you have only one life and must survive and you must defeat the boss in a limited amount of time. You start with a certain amount of time (30-ish seconds) to drain the boss's lifebar. Once you do, it pulses a ring that will kill you if you are too close and the boss becomes invulnerable for a short time before going to its next phase. Enemies will spawn during this entire time. It's a little irritating and they're required if you want to unlock drones and supers and continue into the later stages.
Each stage also has 3 stars you must earn to continue beyond a certain point. You can only get these stars, however, if you upgrade your drones and supers so that you can score faster. Drones can shoot, lay mines, collect score multipliers, and do a few other things for you. This can be annoying, as sometimes you probably can't finish a level with 3 stars unless you spend time grinding geoms to upgrade your stuff (and you WILL have to do so unless you're highly skilled).
In the end, Adventure Mode is a cool bonus that will add a lot of replay time. I didn't get a chance to try multiplayer, however, as there were no games open when I tried.
If you've read this review and you're still on the fence, try out Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved. It's only $4, has all of the Classic modes featured in 3Dimensions, and will give you a cheaper intro to the new game.

Great game. I have enjoyed the reboot to the Castlevania series.  I am also a huge fan of old Castlevanias but the voice acting is wonderful and the story is very epic and worth the name of Castlevania

Does the franchise so much justice.  The controls are crisp and responsive (I used an Xbox 360 controller).  Weapon combos are easy to pull off and after taking months off from the game I could pull everything off within 5 minutes of gameplay.  Secondary weapons are actually extremely useful and powerful in the right context.  The puzzles range from easy as can be to wanting to pull your hair out difficulty.  Usually the answer was one of those "ah, it was right there the whole time".  Boss fights are intense and engaging but usually have a gimmic (full disclosure: I had to look up about 50% of them on a walkthrough).  That said, they are challenging but great fun.  The story is narrated by Patrick Stewart, which was a pleasant surprise, and adds a nice layer.  The main protagonist voice actor has a weird accent that's hard to place but overall, this game is fantastic and loooooong.  The game has outstanding visuals and each level has a unique atmosphere and visuals.  My only complaint is the camera, which takes some getting used to.  Highly recommend for anyone who loves action games and the Castlevania series.

I've played Geometry Wars since the original. I got the second one the minute it was put onto the Xbox Live arcade servers, and I am happy to report that I would recommend this game to any veterans of the series, or even newcomers.
Normally I'm not one to care about high scores and leader boards, but there is something about Geometry Wars that is insanely addicting. You find yourself constantly replaying levels going "I can do better." I love everything about it. Not only is the score-chasing a thrill, but the actual twin-stick shooting mechanics have always been the best in the genre. If twin-stick shooters were ecstacy, Geometry Wars would be molly. Pure bliss.
Both Geometry Wars 2 and 3 have added new things to the series. Geometry Wars 2 added several new modes, and they started to include Geoms to increase your multiplier. This was probably created to attempt to get players to not do the strategy that was pretty much required to do well in the first game, which was just flying in a circle and kiting the enemies behind you. It wasn't very dynamic, but adding Geoms into the mix makes it to where you can play riskier to increase your multiplier before they disappear. Now the third game comes along and adds this adventure mode where tons of new modes are added, AND all the previous modes from Geometry Wars 2 are available as well.
All in all, it's a great game, and I can't wait to sink even more hours into it. I can't recommend it it enough. Basically, Geometry Wars is bae.
PS: Obviously play with a game pad.

When you first enter the menu of ASTRONEER, you immediately feel the lightness and tranquility of this game. It all starts with a calming music and a beautiful world behind your mothership. After you select your favorite astronaut and land on a colorful planet, you then begin to explore the land for resorces to set up your small base, and use alien samples to research new facilities and tools, like vehicle bays and solar panels to maintain your power, all of which will help you in the exploration of the solar system and it's planets, be it alone, or with your friends.
ASTRONEER is an amazing game for the early access that it's in, it has a promising future, and it's one of those games to play when you just want to get away from all the action games or hassles from the life.

My rating for this game:
"LOOK AT ALL THIS COMPOUND" / 10

In general this game is simply amazing and gorgeous. Even though is still in early access it feels like almost a complete game, the developers are constantly working on it; and it's pretty amazing what nine people can do. The game has insane amounts of potential, and for me right now this is the best game I've ever played about Exploration/Survival. In depth analysis ahead:
|Gameplay|
The gameplay goes to the fundamentals of survivals, you explore and mine resourses so that you can advance and upgrade your equipment and base/s. With simple controls I believe Astroneer brought an innovative way of mining resourses, the Deform tool. Your basic tool throught the game, that you'll always have. I found very clever the ways in which you can use the tool, not just for mining but also creating new paths, like bridges, tunnels, etc. Simple gameplay but very well made and kinda addictive.
|Graphics|
In terms of graphics, Astroneer didn't went for a reaslistic aproach, instead it went for a cartoony/low-poly art style, which is insanely gorgeous! The lighting effects are really well made and the low-poly art looks really crisp and clean, doesn't even feel low-poly. The appeal for me is the simpleness of the graphics but the way which the devs made a very appeling and beautiful low-poly art style is oustanding.
|Mechanics and Exploration|
In Astroneer, the exploration is Open World, which means there are no loading screens, which is awsome. There's a limited amount of planets which you can explore, but I believe this is for the better because then the game feels like it has a purpose, explore all the planets, rather than having an enourmous universe you'll never get to explore fully. Even though the World is limited there is a lot to discover just in the first planet, that is smply outstanding. The vehicles for exploration are really versatile, just with the Rover and Truck you can do a lot of different combinations of vehicles, even combining between them. The same case with the Shuttle and Spaceship, you can't combine them both but you can do several amounts of combinatins for each of them; do you want a shuttle for exploration, with just seats for your friends or do you want to do a shuttle with a storage for resourses? Both are posible and even more types of combinations. There could be more vehicles in the future that can bring a lot of diversity but right now even though that it is limited to four it doesn't feel like little. In terms of space traveling your are rigged to go on type of railroad with just the control of point and click for where you want to go, but I believe this is for the best, because the appeal of the game is planet exploration, not space exploration; still just watching the shuttle/spaceship move around the planets and landing is awsome.
|Potential and Final Thoughts|
This game has just insane potential, the fact that this is still a pre-alpha that is really well made is incredible. I have for 17 hours worth off gameplay and I think I haven't even explore 5% off this amazing world, I know much people don't like to but early access games, because it is a risk, but for me this risk was really worthwhile. Finally, this game will keep growing and becoming one of the best Exploration games of all time.

Let's see here... SteamWorld Dig? The art style is charming, the controls feel really fluid, the characters... well... it has characters. The basic gameplay seems solid; go digging, collect money to buy upgrades so you can dig more and faster, find new abilities, yup, this seems like it should be a good way to waste a few hours. I started this game with more goodwill than I afford most games -- but it didn't last.
In the short time I was playing, I died twice.The first time I didn't understand what it was that killed me, but the second time I realized it was because I had dug under one of those rocks that fall when you dig under them. Now why would I have done that? I'd been using those rocks to squish bugs, I understood what they were and what they did. So why would I dig under them? Here's why: I was so goddamned bored that I started daydreaming about all the fun I could be having if I were playing something else! This game preys on your boredom. It is tedium incarnate, broken up only by occasional metroidvania sections in the numbered caves. These sections are too short and too far on the side of easy to engage. Maybe there are bosses, I dunno, 1.2 hours of this game were enough for me.
It's such a shame too; this game is really well produced. I wanted to like it, but ultimately couldn't.

But the thing that struck me most was the intro... It sucked. The "story" and the voice acting... the overall acting (animation wise). It was really really lame.
The first game built up this interesting world and then wow! WTF? But this game? You've seen it all in the commercials. And the build up is just "meh".
I'm hoping that the story gets better. I thought the original had a solid story, and I hope this one will as well. The gameplay is kind of just more of the same, which I like.
If I am to be really honest I think this game should have just been released as a quick follow up. It's not a massive improvement. It's just more of the same. Don't take this the wrong way though. I loved the first game, and I see few reasons why I shouldn't love this one as well. It's just that the difference between this and the original is like between L4D and L4D2. Not that big of a deal.
EDIT:
After playing for 21 hours I am very pleased. The intro did suck, but the game itself is just as good as the first one. I would'nt say that it's better, it is (as I said before) more of the same. So if you liked Dishonored I see no reason you wouldn't like Dishonored 2. The gameplay change isn't radical, it's subtle. The world (as I said before as well) looks just like the original. The new features don't really spice things up, they're just variations of the original gameplay. But so far I've gotten exactly what I wanted out of this game. It's kind of like the Batman: Arkham series. Great core gameplay, and consistent fun.

Borderlands 2 is a "role playing shooter" hybrid developed by Gearbox Software, published by 2K. Set in the world of Pandora, an diverse planet of different creatures and fauna the elusive Handsome Jack has taken credit for your discovery of the Vault, a magnificent prison of the beast known as The Destroyer who was defeated by the original discoverers.
The game works on a levelling up system that gives you experience points for doing quests, based on the NPC’s parameters; you may have to retrieve items, kill groups of enemies or fufill silly requests at the behest of the NPC. Co-op is recommended as enemies are usually in great numbers in the game.
Extremely repetitive grindfest for luck-based drops on a system that scales your levels to the enemies to create a challenging experience. Enemies encountered are varied and have different weaknesses to the elements of Pandora. Despite weighted gunplay, it remains repetitious and unfulfilling due to lack of tactility in the guns (which all function as projectiles) and the trope of bullet sponging which is pervasive in the series.
Wacky universe with a large open world setting that encompasses a large selection of Pandora's most beautiful to most vile, disturbing places possible. Large amount of content and the loot system is built upon on being limitless – which it achieves, albeit to the most mimimum degree.
Stale storyline progression. Cheaply designed combat system. More often than not, loot is dropped by random chance from than pseudo-random chance meaning you may gain Legendaries on even common enemies in UVHM which creates very imbalanced builds (different for UHVM)
Excessive DLC,
and outside of the main story. Case in point, references to pop culture, internet memeology and vidya memes (like arrow in the knee from Skyrim) to the point of making one livid. Who is responsible for this catastrophic lack of effort, who else other than Anthony Burch, the Cuck King? His trashy writing style (which consists of some NPCs shouting nonsense and references to age-old memes). His script quality is astonishingly unoriginal, trite and not immersive.
A combination of different genres from classical Western cowboy themes to techno. Peppy, upbeat and dynamic really helps push the pace of combat.
Cel-shaded graphics with a distinctive cartoon appearance. Animations are smooth, dynamic and full of lively motion. Environments are full of interesting design features from craggy outcrops of rock to cold ice tundras that scale greatly and give a sense of adventure, foreboding and scale sizes near epicness.
However, sleuthing has lead me to an interesting if concerning issue with the dynamic artstyle that game inspires itself from was plagiarized from an animation project which you can view here:
This is simply not acceptable for a company to do.
Five main damage types, Fire, Explosive, Corrosive, Slag and Shock. Fire is best on fleshy creatures and does more damage to the living, explosive is a non-resistant damage type that can't be defended against normally. Slag, the byproduct of Eridium processing increases non-elemental damage (i.e bullets with non-elemental types will do more damage, x3 damage on Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode) Gun variation is good from Sniper Rifles to Shotguns that when reloaded act like makeshift rocket launchers - feedback is also very satisfying and responsive, weighted and has great presentation in both kick and punch and works in different ways and functions based on the vendor you get a drop or buy from making you excited for the next loot-drop you may get from killing enemies.
Handsome Jack has taken the credit for the discovery of the Vault, a once fabled treasure trove proved out to be an interdimensional prison holding the interdimensional monster that costed the Eridians, a race of very advanced creatures known for the invention of Eridium, a highly coveted resource - their civilization, the "Destroyer".
After the Destroyer was coincidentally destroyed, the four original Vault Hunters (Roland, Lilith, Brick and Mordecai) departed. Four took their place searching for fame and glory as well as to assassinate Handsome Jack for his deceptive deeds for a heavy bounty...their names are Zero (as a number!), Maya as the Siren, Salavador the Gunzerker and Axton as the Commando!
Due to the overall poor nature of the quests including the main storyline and overall lack of actual endgame content, plagiarized artstyle and the surplus requirement to any form of actual replayability kills it. Also supporting Anthony "The Cuck King" Burch is the least likely I'd want to do.

If you came for an actual review here yeh go:
Great storyline:
everything you need to know is given to you, the people who are important and their relationships to eachother? explained by little quips after missions are turned in. If you are the type who wants to learn the full lore, everything that ever happened EVER, then get in line brother/sister cause half of this universe isn't explained and doesn't need to be.
I have started so many new characters both by myself and with others that I know the storyline by heart and can almost quote for quote the entire game, in fact much of my slang are Borderlands quotes, There are areas, yes, that get boring. places I wish I could skip because the story isn't actiony enough or I don't like how dark the building is, but if my main complaint about the game is I have played it so many times that I have developed opinions? then there aint much wrong with the game.
Graphics and performance:
Borderlands funky art style is a veriosn of Cel(l) shading, which highlights corners and edges in thick black lines and makes the scenery pop. If you are a fan of games with beautiful scenery or interesting art styles then buy the game already! There  is detail in every object you find, every randomly generated gun, NPC, Enemy, Friend, Flag and dirt mound has enough detail to fill 3 more games. Performance wise Borderlands is very versatile, almost every aspect can be lowered or raised, I play on a medium to low setting and The game keeps it's beauty, most of the higher options add small but touching details, such as blood, acid and slag pooling after an enemy is defeated, or being able to tear down flags if you jump into them, there is no downside playing on a supercomputer or a potato.
Customization / Will my second playthrough be different?
There are 4 given characters, each great, with 3 main skill trees, you only get 68 skill points to spend and that's just under 2 maxed trees, if you look at builds people have made, no two use the same skill tree combination, there is no "right way". Storylines will remain the same, but you have the main storyline which you can playthrough up to 3 times with the Vault hunter upgrade packs, 3 large DLC storylines, and (at least) 5 short dlc storylines all come with sidequests, new characters and new loot.
RNG-wise this game will never be the same, enemy spawns are semi random, and enemies have a chance to drop loot, which is sorted common through legendary up to pearlescent (stupid hard to get). Then, each type of weapon has different possible manufacturers which changes how it behaves, then a different name and prefix which changes small stats and the guns general behavior, added with RNG based gun PARTS, THAT'S RIGHT, you can have guns with THE EXACT SAME TITLE, and have them behave differently. hows that for replayability?
Difficulty?
This game can be hard, it can also be easy, you can be underleveled and one shot a boss and overleveled and get Dee-Stroyed by a varkid (small weak bug). A lobby can have up to 4 people in it, with each addition the enemies get slightly stronger and on some modes, will match the level of the highest player. Just because the enemies are weaker when solo does not mean the game is easier. You will have no one to have your back, if you go down you have to, literally, fight for your life in order to revive yourself, if you run out of time? down you go and any not killed enemies regain full health. If the main games is easy, and the new game plus is easy, and new game ultra plus excelsior is childs play, then you can try out the raid bosses and get rad loot, or test your hand at digistruct peak and be able to equip weapons 8 levels higher than yourself.

This is my first review, but not my first rodeo.
Synopsis: Gabriel Belmont of the famed Belmont family must defeat the Lords of Shadow to acquire their powers and heal the rift between heaven and earth which is allowing the forces of darkness to spread unopposed throughout the land.
Overall Impression: A beautiful, epic experience strongly influenced (in my opinion) by Dante's Inferno, both the literary work and the video game. However, for those of you who have played Dante's Inferno (which was only on console I believe), this game is superior in every way.
Graphics: Massive, haunting landscapes with excellent ambient effects such as rain and frost on the screen. I don't think the graphics could have been much better given the time and what the creators were aiming for.
Sound: Adrenaline-driving Gothic-style soundtrack that picks up at exactly the right moments. Useful sound cues when an offscreen enemy has been spawned. Also, Patrick Stewart as the voice of Sean Connery/Ramirez (from Highlander) man. The weapons sound effects are substantial and pair well with the force feedback on an Xbox 360 controller.
Controls/Gameplay: Flowing controls and somewhat simple combat/combo system which is conducive to button mashing. However, enemies usually dodge on the second or third strike so button-mashing is of limited utility.
Pros: This is truly a stellar game, with immersive graphics and sound with an engrossing storyline somewhat in the vein of Dante's Inferno (both the literary work and the console game). Significant replay value for completionists.
Cons: Not too many. If anything, the combo system could have used slightly more complexity to add more depth to the combat, but this may not have been feasible after everything was mapped out on the XBox controller (yes, you should definitely use one to play this game).
This game should be called "Where should i go next". You'll spend more time trying to figure that out than fighting.

Do not mistake your CHARACTER for being this games' protagonist - that role clearly belongs to your METAL CHAIN WHIP!
Remember that good ol' Castlevania feeling from WHIPPING (and Throwing Dagger'ing and Holy Water'ing) your way through werewolves and vampire monsters by pale moonlight? This game builds on that and you will chuckle many a time as you try out new combos and fun powers to experiment with.
I had a great time playing through the whole thing. Sure, it's a long game, maybe too long for some, but for me it was just about right.
Except for one annoying instance that took me many tries to beat, the game felt very balanced when shifting between medium (warrior) and easy (squire). And believe me when I say you should play it on either of those two difficulties, if you'd like to preserve your sanity. You may play for challenges if you wish, but they are not mandatory, so even the non-masochistic players can enjoy their METAL CHAIN WHIPPING game. QTE's are never great, but I didn't find them too annoying here. Cut scenes break up some of the game, but it's still very enjoyable.
Oh, and the art is mostly DROP DEAD GORGEOUS - I want these artists to decorate my house if they ever get tired of pouring their HEART and SOULS into games like this.
You can do some combat parts by button-mashing, but you should learn to counter, block and time your hits after some time. BUT FEAR NOT, because this is both fun and super-satisfying - the blood party starts for real when you pull something awesome off with your METAL CHAIN WHI...(okay, you got it), and the game goes into slow-motion as you smack your enemies around, consuming leftover dark and light energy orbs from their corpses, to fuel your powers for another round of METAL CHAIN WHIP (sorry, it's just the best weapon ever) carnage.
My playing it for all those hours should tell you one thing - to buy this game as soon as you get the chance.

Better late than never. I had this sitting in my Steam backlog for a long time, so I figured, "You know what? The sequel just came out to rave reviews. Let's give it a go."
I'm glad I did.
Lately, I've been more attracted to shorter games than lengthy, open world romps, and this didn't disappoint. It's very addictive, and it manages to merge your typical Metroidvania progression with a few roguelike elements to keep it fresh. Your objective is to keep digging and digging, and along the way you'll come across some enemies in the dirt and various minerals to collect. You trade these minerals in on the surface hub for money to spend on upgrades and items. The roguelike elements come into play whenever you die, and you have to go back to the spot you die to get your spoils back before you die again. However, the game is rarely difficult enough to make you pull your hair. Sure, I died a few times due to carelessness, but I was never frustrated.
What makes this game unique is the spots you dig stay dug up. Once you return from the surface, everything that you did previously remains the same. Enemies don't respawn, minerals don't randomly generate to new spots. The digging mechanic leads to some very strategic situations to where you have to think about what path you want to dig. I'm sure this heavily comes into play when considering speedruns. However, if you're just taking your time like I do, it shouldn't be too difficult, especially since there are items such as ladders to help you out if you need to. Hopefully in the sequel there is a little more strategy involved.
I was able to 100% it (collect all minerals, items, and beat the story) in about 6-7 hours, and obviously, if you're going for all of the achievements (which I didn't), the overall playtime will vary. All in all, if you're looking for a solid, simplistic 2D action game with a charming art style and setting, give this a shot.

First off, I played Dishonored 1 and all it's DLC and loved it. I pre-purchased this game literally within days of the option being available. Dishonored was an excellent game.
Now, this game has all the same feel as the original, but instead of focusing on the incredibly smooth, flawless gameplay the first one had and disregarding graphical fidelity, this game takes graphics into account. Honestly, Dishonored had fair enough graphics if you turned down the brightness enough. This game is in a whole different world. It looks gorgeous, even on the medium settings I'm playing at until the full on fixes are released. There's a high cost to playing on High settings. Frames still plummet at times and I've been doing my own investigation. I've noticed that even when I'm indoors in normally easy to run areas like inside a room with no windows, I still see my VRAM fly up and max out. Guess where almost 90% of the current frame drops come from... When the VRAM decides it wants to fatten up so much that it has to start handing off info to the slow system RAM. I believe the coding isn't very efficient for the garbage cleanup and it's just not optimized. If this gets fixed, fantastic. This game will easily be one of the best for the year once it's running correctly.
Now for the actual guts of the game. Having the option to play as either Corvo OR Emily is great. Corvo has all his powers you love, plus Doud's gift of Stop Time while aiming Blink, and Emily has a completely different set herself. Now, a few details would be nice, like how Corvo didn't tell Emily JACK about the outsider or his gifts, but... oh well. The most natural way to play this game would be to pick it up as Emily on a stealth playthrough, but do whatever since this is Dishonored. If you played the first Dishonored and loved that were secrets and stuff to discover, this game is on different level. You can lose hours on 1 mission uncovering everything. And trying to do the "No-Kill" playthrough is way tougher, especially because you have to actually investigate to uncover how to actually complete the mission without killing. The most time consuming playthrough is for-sure No-Killing on Stealth. Heck, there's even an option now to play the game WITHOUT supernatural powers! As I play, I'm beginning to realize when I do that playthrough it will be TOUGH. Using powers to climb the walls and rafters is the intended stealth route, so good luck. I've put in 11 hours and I still haven't finished 1 playthrough on stealth and I'm loving it, even though I'm forced to play on medium settings. It looks good, but I saw Ultra right away and holy cow I hope they fix the problems because it looks amazing! SLI support is really limited and doesn't really scale, so you don't get much of a difference. I have 2 980ti's in SLI and they run at about 60-70% and that's it. They don't ever go above it. I also have an Intel i7-4790K which never goes over 40%, so you can easily get away with a garbage cpu on this one. I get about 90fps on average but it does dip to 65fps sometimes. If you're running a 144Hz monitor like me, I'd change the Windows setting to 60Hz and turn on V-sync. Also play with a controller, because I don't think they've fully fixed the mouse input problems.
But, if you're a Dishonored fan, keep your eyes peeled for the major patches to be released and definitely buy this game. It's an improvement on the last game, which is still one of my personal favorites. I'm loving this one so far.

Playing Dark Souls II reminds me of old video games like Into The Eagles Nest and Ghosts and Goblins where the technology was so limited that enemies were ultimately fair, tutorials were non-existent, and I didn't mind playing the same level over and over memorizing and perfecting it.  Dark Souls isnt exactly fun all the time, but it is engaging and satisfying.  Its more like a challenge, keep that in mind as you calibrate your expectations and you can get over the initial steep learning curve.  I died at least 4 times before the tutorial section even started.  But the tutorial was actually effective if you pay attention and attempt to apply it as the game continues.  The story is very light and absorbed through infrequent NPC character dialogue so it is importatnt that you aren't expecting a strong story or character driven narrative.  The difficulty ramp has been even over time, with the exception of bosses which are very short and brutal until you get the hang of that particular boss.  As you progress, the enemies become more varied so to encourage varied tactics from encounter to encounter.  This is not a game with which you can check-out and just enjoy.  You have to focus on the enemies actions and responding appropriately.  There are no exclamation points to warn you of an incoming attack.  The game requires that you use all of the available mechanics, first order optimizations will only lead to frequent deaths and frustration.  The enemies have access to all of the same abilities as you, the player.  In this way, it is scrupulously fair.  Ambushes are always detectable if you are paying attention.  No monster closets or enemies popping into existence because you crossed a threshold. It is a game to focus on and feel satisfied when you succeed.  So far, I am really enjoying it.
Note: I didn't play Dark Souls or Demon Souls.  I havent engaged in any multiplayer, though it exists in a coop form where friends can help you with boss fights and a PVP form where presumably frustrating people do frustrating things.

3 years ago when Dark Souls came out I got the game not knowing anything about it, and I ended up dropping out of college due to my uncontrollable obsession with that game. Dark Souls 2? It's been 4 days, I've already been dumped and lost my job. I mean, how can you not marvel at this game? It takes all the issues of Dark Souls 1 and polishes it. Summoning? Such a simple task! Fast, easy, and simplified for trying to connect with specific people. More versatility with your character? Yes please. New spell school? Even more please! Easier bonfire transit? Absolutely.
But of course, that means nothing without the glorious battles. Of which there are plenty, I assure you. I tend to classify Dark Souls bosses into 2 categories: skill and gimmicky. If you liked Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved 2, you will probably like Geometry Wars 3: Dimensions. As for me, I regard Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved [1] as the gold standard of the franchise (and all twin-stick shooters). I ultimately did not like Geometry Wars 2 for its departures from GW:RE1, and I don't like GW3 for the same reasons and more. If you have never played Geometry Wars, you will probably like GW3, but I recommend Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved, instead. It is available here on Steam for just $4 full price. Unfortunately there are no online leaderboards, but the gameplay is far superior to GW3.
Here are the pros and cons of GW3:
Pros
Neutral:
Cons
The gameplay changes made from 1 to 2 apply to number 3 as well, so I will first list my gripes with GW:RE2 that also apply to GW3.
And here are my gripes that are new to GW3, in order of most to least egregrious. Some are patchable without a leaderboard wipe. I will update my review if these issues are addressed.
TL;DR Read the first paragraph. The gameplay changes made since GW:RE1 make Geometry Wars 3 unnecessarily frustrating and artificially difficult. Before you dismiss me as a noob complaining about difficulty, check my leaderboard scores in this or other GW games, or watch this video of me getting a Global #1:

Not the same kind of experience as the previous two.
All of the new modes are trapped within the adventure mode, and you need to grind through them in a specific order to unlock them. The other reviews will tell how difficult it is to progress through the first batch.
The progression system fosters more of a sense of "oh crap I didn't get a good enough score to move on" or "about time I got that score" rather than the "ooh I didn't beat my highscore, better try again" or "wow that's a great score!" that GW 1 and 2 had.
If you need progression systems to feel like you've accomplished something in a game, then GW 3 will do you just fine. But if you're self-confident enough to simply get better enough for the sake of getting better, than do NOT buy this game. It will take all the intrinsic motivation right out.
First thoughts:
I'm one of those people who has always wondered why each game in a series doesn't have every single option or gamemode the previous one had. It bothered me tremendously when halo 3 didn't have any variant of blood gulch.
I feel kind of the same with this game; Geometry Wars 3 seems to have omitted some things which I considered central to the second game.
As far as new content, Geometry Wars 3 has the 3-dimensional playing spaces, such as spheres or peanut shaped things of some sort. That's neat, and I'm interested to play them all. However, the game is trying to get some sort of campaign/unlock system implimented, which I honestly thoroughly despise. Instead of just having a menu where you choose which gamemode and which shape you want to play on, you need to progress one by one through various combinations of game type/shape in the "adventure mode." I used to be excited to play on these new shapes, but I in NO WAY wanted to ever have to unlock anything in a Geometry Wars game. Now I have to. I'll be playing the game anyway, but now it feels like a chore, and will probably take away a lot of the intrinsic value I originally got from simply playing.
Co-op options such as one player piloting and the other shooting are missing, and again, you need to progress through an adventure mode before you have any control at all over what game type/shape you play co-op on. I find this irritating because I have really always considered this franchise to be an arcade-style dual stick shooter, and now it feels more like a mobile game. It even implements the star system from angry birds or cut the rope.
It seems there's no way to do custom games modes of any kind, which is annoying considering that there's so many different factors now. Instead of just gamemode, you also have different geometric shapes to play on. When combined with the original 5 gamemodes, it seems like a no-brainer to just have a menu to select shape, select game, and get going. Granted, you can unlock many of these different combinations by playing through the main adventure mode, but working for it takes some of the joy out of it for me. You COULD play any of the 5 game modes from Geometry Wars 2 in "classic" mode, but you can only play on the classic rectangular playing field. So that's a waste of my time. I already own Geometry Wars 2 and frankly it works better.
The UI is clunkly and needlessly slow, and I think that the art style is a bit distracting. Honestly I don't like it, but that's just a personal thing. I miss the vector lines and the way I felt like I was in cyber space in the original two games. Everything is too blue now and the parts of the grid on the playing field change color to make it look like it's "reflecting" or something. It just clutters the screen.
TL DR: there's a progression system in a game I don't really think needs one, and the only step forward (3 dimensional playing fields) seems to have forced a step back in a few other areas. It's still geometry wars. But it's basically the same geometry wars I owned on xbox, with all my favorite features removed.
6/10 only because the elements it kept from the previous games are still fun.

The first thing I notice when starting up Geometry wars 3 for the first time are the stellar production values. The title screen alone with its swirling colored auras and a strange vector grid stretching out infinitely before you, the soothing electronic tones of the background music shimmering in and out like waves. Before even getting into the game I can already tell a tremendous amount of work has gone into the look, the feel, and the sounds of the game and have been focused on much stronger in this iteration of the series.
The progression of adventure mode is much more varied in levels than any of the classic games which will be a welcome addition to new players who craved a more content heavy experience. Across the adventure mode map you'll advance through levels of increasing difficulty and each with an important three star rating based on score. Aside from stars you'll earn points in order to purchase upgrades for your various drones, a newcomer to the Geometry Wars series that offers a number of abilities including back-up fire, mines, or magnetized pickups for the Geoms to keep your score multiplier going and let you focus on the action.
Each new level features a different mode ranging from classic 'Evolved' to new additions like 'Rainbow', with a variation of differently shaped 3D landscapes dotted with rotating pillars, red life stealing walls, and various other obstacles thrown into the mix. Aforementioned stars will be needed to access the various boss stages that break up adventure mode, and they can be quite hard to collect especially if you're not a diehard twinstick player. Bosses feel like a strange and not very Geometry Wars-like addition, but they are nonetheless very intense and flashy with their chaotic bullet hell-like patterns.
The classic enemies players will remember from the last games are adapted to this new 3D playstyle very well, and their movement patterns flow almost more naturally than before on the spherical landscapes you fight on. The straight-moving arrow enemies wrap around the globe-like levels and criss-cross past each other, while the quick and sporadic square enemies sneak up on you from either side of the rotating stages. In addition to the classic geometrical enemies we've come to love/hate, there are a couple new enemies with unique behavior that spice up your old strategies.
The shapely structure to the stages that changes with each one gives a more strategic and tactical approach to the twin-stick formula forcing you to adapt to the area and its hazards each time, keeping certain players more engaged than before. Old schoolers will likely miss the euphoric rush and focused score attacks missing in this new iteration, but I've more than warmed up to it, come to terms with the differences and have found new excitement in taking my place on the boards for what is a different kind of game.
Geometry Wars 3 has the variation, gamified progression, and massive content that some people felt was missing from the originals but older fans will more than likely miss the pure and calculated arcade action as well as the minimalistic neon visuals that the first two were known for. While GW3 may not bring the same-old-same-old that those fans were wanting,

It's worth sticking through and if you find yourself a little weary at first...well you're a Castlevania fan, deal with it and push on. If you're about halfway through and still don't like it then it may not be for you.
The combat is decent, and you'll learn a lot of new moves as you go along. You get side weapons, combos, light and dark magic forms and more. Combat is like god of war but there is more weight to dodging and such. Boss battles are enjoyable and some will make you think a tiny bit. There are some frustrating bits though.
Puzzles are fun, but entirely skippable if you hate them.
Overall I'd recommend the game! However the DLC...not so much. They aren't bad but they don't exactly add as much as you would hope and honestly I found them to be a bit stale and worse aggrivating with one of the end bosses of one. Still if you are a die hard fan...get them.

I wanted to like this game, I really did. Unfortunately, this could function as a case study on what's wrong with modern AAA action games. It's a tedious, boring, borderline insulting mess. It's a prime example of style over substance and spectacle over gameplay, which felt more like a standardized test than a game.
To give credit where credit is due, much of the artwork is beautiful and some of the voice acting is solid, particularly with Patrick Stewart. Which just makes it sadder that everything else is so awful.
This game is absolutely infested with quicktime events. They're everywhere. Apparently they'd rather not have those pesky players get in the way of their flashy spectacle. So instead of making, you know, gameplay, they'll just tell us when to press what button.
The combat is a dull experience. There's a system of earning points which you can spend special attacks made up of arbitrary button combinations, none of which are worth your time to commit to memory. Fights are boring and time consuming.
Camera angles are always fixed, there's no looking where you want to look or aligning your view to make platforming or combat more practical. The game just sort of herds you from one section to the next with the camera. There's nothing wrong with linear games, but this feels less like a linear path, and more like the a series of check boxes.
The story is mostly delivered through exposition dumps, and it isn't very interesting. I didn't care what happened to any of the characters.
The keyboard controls are poor, and I don't just mean the default bindings are bad, though they most assuredly are. I mean things like the game more than once expecting you to mimic the rotation of an analog stick with the directional keys, or the fact that the jump button won't work if you're moving diagonally by holding two directional keys. Controller support is sketchy, despite the description of "full controller support". Mine wouldn't work at all.
The whole thing is just such a tedious chore of a game. Don't waste your time, not even if it's on sale for cheap.

SteamWorld Dig is a phenomenal platformer that is more than the sum of its parts.
What I enjoyed most about this game was the conversation between designer and player that was happening. In the beginning, I quickly realized that the most efficient way of mining was to dig down two blocks and then go horizontal, in either the left or right direction. Okay, says the game, here's a block that falls down when you mine under it.
Later on, when you get a steampowered jump and drill, you have to balance out these tools, because water is actually very scarce. But then the game throws exploding enemies at you, that make it almost impossible to stick to a plan that maximizes output and that forces you to spend water on jumps...
This back-and-forth is tremendous fun!
On top of that, the UI is well-designed and beautifully drawn. The way the total dollar amount fades away after a few seconds on your inventory, how negative space is drawn opaque in your minimap. It's these details that make this an example of a great game done well!
My only gripe would be the weird double currency. Why lock upgrades behind this currency? And why are teleporters so expensive!
Get this game. It will charm your pants off.

Life of a slime rancher is pretty simple:
- Put slimes in corralsl
- Buy upgrades to keep slimes in corrals.
- Mantain slimes well fed, lest they get angry.
- Grow enough crops, and make sure you don't use all your food before you restart harvest.
- Create chicken coops.
- Make sure that there's not too many chickens, and make sure you don't take them all.
- Keep at least 1 Roostro
-Make sure slimes are fed their favorites.
- Don't accidentely give largos wrong plorts, resulting in Tarr.
- Sell your plorts.
- Keep track of ever fluxuating plort market.
- Remember where you are and don't get lost when exploring.
Like I said: very simple. Not much complexity behind it, still great game.

This game is a beautiful and rich take on the retro space shooter genre. With it's non-euclidian level design, geometry wars has you move around on the surface of many 3d shapes fighting enemies with a drone by your side for backup. There isn't much to say about the gameplay. It's a tried-and-true game type for sure with a wide variety of enemies of varying movement  and mechanics.
What I really want to talk about is the art style! Gorgeous geometric neon lines on a space background with levels that bend and warp as you or your bullets glide over them like the very fabric of reality. Every character has recieved a 3d remodel since the last game and every inch of this game makes you feel as though you're fighting it out in a retro rendition of cyberspace. Another upshot to this type of visual style is that it takes up next to no disk space (the game's only 86MB!).
Definitely worth your time and your money.

I do love me some music games such as this. Audiosurf, Symphony, Beat Hazard .etc are all worthy titles. Riff Racer is no different. I really like what this game is all about. Considering I do used to like driving out in long travels into the night with music playing, now I can do it with this game.
Beautiful visuals, driving through a futuristic city on a track that's based on the music you're playing. The tracks provide you a little light show for you to drive over and there's obstacles that are just as pretty too. You're locked into 60FPS, but then again the game isn't really that demanding when you look at it's requirements.
It appears the game does have a system where you earn enough in-game currency to buy different cars with. You'll have a lot of music to play, I hope, to earn enough to buy them!
There isn't a lot of music formats this game supports. There's only .MP3, .AAC and .M4A. So anyone with .OGG, .APE, .WMA .etc are going to have to convert.
There are no real other modes to contend with in this game either. It's just you, the music, your vehicle and the course of the track to drive on as well as the obstacles left for you to drive on and avoid. Like ramps and street posts.
Only few gripes with this game is that the controlling of the vehicle is a little too tight to barely make the turns in time. This affects some of the steering too including drifts. The other gripe is the ramps that could launch you a little ways where you'd fly off occasionally.
However, it's not exactly enough to be not fun and it's why I'm liking it and you might too.

SCP: Secret Laboratory is basically a multiplayer version of
where you can play as an SCP, class D, scientist or NTF. These different 'teams' have their own goals and don't necessarily work together, for example scientists and class Ds don't like each other but they can work together in order to survive. To put it simply you have three teams trying to escape the SCP facility but also trying to stop each other escaping. If you've ever played the Breach gamemode on
then you should know how this works.
- Escape. Avoid NTF. Avoid SCP. Can work with scientists.
- Escape. Avoid SCP. Work with NTF. Can work with Class D.
- Shoot SCP. Shoot Class D. Save scientists.
- Escape. Kill everyone!
- Avoid SCP. Kill NTF and scientists. Save Class D.
While this may sound confusing its actually not, the game gives you a lot of on-screen infomation and it even has some decent tutorials with voice acting.

Solid action, but Castlevania mostly in name. (This plays a bit more like Onimusha.)
This title has solid graphics, good sound, and good controls. The difficulty curve scales nicely - Knight difficulty requires running some engagements perfectly in order to advance. Whip combat is pretty decent. There's a system of "runes" that allow you to heal or do greater damage. Giant monsters can be tamed and ridden. If this is sounding a lot like God of War, unfortunately, it's several steps wide of the mark - but this IS very much like the feel of Onimusha. Expect lots of chamber-based combat, soul pickups, careful health management, and revisiting old maps to clear challenges or acquire pickups that you couldn't get earlier.
For: Fans of Onimusha, anybody who likes action games.
Not for: People expecting a 2D action/patformer (like Castlevania), or a 2D a/p with RPG elements (like Simon's Quest), or a 2D metroidvania (like SOTN), or a 3D exploration RPG with pets (like Curse of Darkness).

Castlevania: Lords of Shadow is pretty cool I guess.
Now, to get this out of the way. My experience with the actual Castlevania series is about as thin as the condom my parents used on the night of my conception. I played a little bith of Symphony, a little bit of Rondo of blood on
a Super Nintendo, and a little bit of Castlevania: Portrait of Ruin for this magical two screened device I found in the back of a dumpster.  This being said, I do like the series even if I haven't gotten around to playing them. I know who Simon Belmont is, and who Dracula is, and who Trevor Belmont and Richter Belmont are. I know the general lore and backstory behind the games, and I know just how deep and involving the series was, especially Symphony of the Night and onward.
This is Simon Belmont, right?
Anyway.
Castlevania: Lords of Shadow is a reboot to the long standing and venerated Castlevania series. Set in Southern Europe during events that totally happened. When Earth's ties with Heaven is severed, a bunch of bad things happen such as dead people walking and evil monsters knocking on your door and asking for a donation in human flesh. Knowing that the end of the world is upon us all, the Brotherhood of Light decides to send only their tallest and most handsome knights on a crusade to stop this evil and save the human race.

But the tallest and most handsome of them all is Gabriel Belmont, a newcomer to the series. Gabriel is seeking atonement for the sins of his past as well as vengeance for a love lost to him. He does this by grabbing what could possibly be one of the coolest weapons in video game history and punching the love of Christ into anything that looks like it came from a Bram Stoker novel.
What seperates Kings of Comfortable Shade from other Castlevania games is that it's a hack-n-slash brawler in the same vain like God of War, a big departure for the series but I feel like it did good in this regard, if not better than it's angry Greek man counterpart.
All of Gabriel's attacks have this meaty weight to them, the general crunch of his combat cross and the big flashyness of the impact give an impression that hits a little harder than your average human. Take this and add it to a simple yet versatile combo system, and you have room to make your enemies say "That was sick" right before their skulls are punched out the back of their heads.
But how does it play out?
Lords of Shadows is, to my knowledge, the first Castlevania game handled by a studio outside of Japan, though I'm probably wrong. But you can tell that Spanish based Mercury Studios put a lot of love into the world and lore of this game. Lords of Shadow has that advantage that many games of it's calibre lack, and that is that Lords of Shadow isn't afraid of explain things to the player. The way the world works, what does what, who is who, and what I'm punching in the head is all laid out and explained to Gabriel and, in turn, to the player.
What does this mean? It means I know that a guy called Gandolfi created the combat cross after playing with a yo yo and thinking "This could probably hurt somebody."
I know that the more human a vampire looks the more likely it is to go all Sith Lord on you with the lightning hands. I know that the Forgotten One is a huge prick, and I know that there probably aren't any cute lycan girls. They wouldn't date you anyways so it's okay.
Should you play Fortressmania: Dukes of flashlight?
Is it a good game? I would say so, it does many things better than it's competitors, It's world is unique and interesting enough to make you want to learn more, and Gabriel himself is a pretty cool protagonist for what it is. It also helps that the game's plot is narrated by Patrick Stewart. You can hear his bald, it's amazing.
But is it a good Castlevania game? I'm probably not the best person to ask. I like the series, don't get me wrong. It's just that I have never actually gotten around to sitting down with all of them. if you treat it for what it is, a reboot seprated from the main franchise, then you'll probably like it. But if you look at it as another piece in the main adventures of Belmont and pals, then it would probably leave a bad impression with you.  But I, personally, enjoyed the game and have a new respect for murdering the hell out of things with a crucifix.

Scrolling through the reviews, it appears to be the case that many people who pick this game up rapidly drop it.
I am one of those people.
As I understand it, the standard game (i.e. without DLC) has 12 chapters. I forced myself through the first of those, started in on the second and decided that the game was not worth my time.
What I experienced in the first chapter was the laziest possible recapitulation of a Hideki Kamiya-style brawler, complete with boss/level designs cribbed at total random from classic, non-Castlevania adventure/beat-em-up games. In terms of plot, the whole leaky boat is held together by a slap-happy, Epic Fantasy Mad Libs of one-dimensional characters, plowing through an plot that, even for a franchise game, makes the word "idiotic" seem either charitable or grossly insufficient, depending on how much warmed-over Judeo-Christian fan fiction is being forced through the pipe at the time.
The first bits of Castlevania: Lords of Shadow's second chapter promised no major changes to that formula, so I decided to walk away. A number of other Steam reviewers point that out as a common mistake and, acknowledging the possibility that I may have made that common mistake (i.e. that there may, in fact, be a great game hidden somewhere deep within in Castlevania: Lords of Shadow), I feel perfectly comfortable walking away after only a few wasted hours, based on the first chapter.
(Also, as a bit of a post-script, I will say that if you're a Castlevania fan, you already know this, but I feel compelled to write it here anyway: the damage that Koji Igarashi did to this once-great 8-bit/16-bit franchise over however-many successive generations of his erotic kawaii "Metroid-vania" drop farming games will obviously take generations to be undone, as the corporate rights-holders struggle to unravel the mystery of why the franchise no longer performs as it once did. Castlevania: Lords of Shadow does not, unfortunately, seem to take any meaningful steps in that direction.)

Although some may say the PC port of Dishonored 2 isn't as great as its console counterparts, Dishonored 2 is still a great game with some excellent new features.
Dishonored 2 is set around 12 - 15 years after its predecessor. Emily Kaldwin, the girl you had to protect in Dishonored, is now the Ruler of Empire of the Isles. The protagonist, Corvo Attano is now once again, the Lord Protector of the new Empress. But some folks who have played the 'Brigmore Witches DLC' from Dishonored will know who Delilah Copperspoon, or now know as Delilah Kaldwin is and will know that she is once again trying to steal the throne from Emily by using her magic. You, the player can either choose to play as Corvo Attano, Lord Protector and father of Emily Kaldwin, or you can choose to play as Emily herself.
The Dishonored Series is probably one of my favourite game franchises as it mixes in stealth and mass genocide with numerous ways to sneak or kill with a plentiful amount of weapons and a plethora of abilities like Blink, Far Reach, Bend Time and so forth. In Dishonored 2, no players will have the same path, the same Bone charms, or use the same weapons. Every playthrough is different in some way or another.
I believe Dishonored 2 is a excellent game, improving what Dishonored lacked in and what they didn't. I think Arkane Studios have done an excellent job and I applaud their actions and love this game with all my heart.

When I impulsively decided on buying this game I wasn't even aware it was in Alpha stage. Not that I bothered, because it was the sheerly amazing artstyle and mechanics I fell for. I didn't quite anticipate the fact that there were multiple planets to explore in one save until i had played this gem for about 4 hours.

Unfortunately though, since it's in early alpha, it's not even close to being complete. I estimate myself somewhere at 1/3 of what the game has to offer. There are, naturally, many things I haven't figured out yet, but the majority of mechanics and buildings I've learned about rather quickly. I predict the game will hit a great audiance once it's finished. For the future I hope to see more buildings and mechanics. One day a black vortex opened up in the middle of a farm in Manitoba. This vortex seemed innocuous at first. Nothing seemed to be happening. The farmer had made a small sum charging people to come see it, but people got bored. "Hey, that's a boring vortex." they would say. So they let it be, sitting there quietly humming.
It would be years before we discovered the horrifying truth. The vortex was in fact syphoning all colour from our video game entertainment. We didn't notice at first because the 1990's had brought a shameful bout of "Grimdarkness" to our media, and so we attributed this lack of colour in games to words like "gritty", and "Batman". We were fools. FOOLS!
Luckily someone did notice, and that person was Sierra, who is not actually a person. They are an old video game company that died and was mysteriously revived from the grave. It is a strange ghoulish version of Sierra, some would say it no longer has any humanity due to the lich lord that resurrected it, however the ghoul Sierra has seemingly brought with it a gift from beyond the grave. They brought with them a new game... a special game that contains All The Colours.
Yes, be warned, for while this game will finally let loose the missing colours thought destroyed by the Grimdarkness, your fragile mind may not be able to maintain sanity in the presence of such vibrance. Your dulled senses could fry when forced to interpret information such as red and orange. You may witness greens and blues. There will be pink.
A great gift has been bestowed upon us... but are we capable of handling it's power? Tune in next week to find out.
Case closed.

A really good game, you can't truly compare it to anything else. It's not like audiosurf. It's not like a real racing game. It's pure arcade madness accompanied by your music of choice. And here's where the game might fail: If your music of choice is not really suitable for the game style, it can become boring or 'uneventful'. It works very well with upbeat EDM. Some metal songs have really sick tracks too. If you play popular songs it gets very competitive, like for example, I often race to songs from the Initial D soundtrack and there's plenty of people playing them, getting to rank 1 was really hard on some tracks because there are some sick racers out there. Racing against a ghost is helpful, you can learn some techniques and stuff that other people do and you didn't even think about trying. It can become pretty technical, actually.
The cons would be the lack of content (there are lots of cars to play -some of them are really ugly though-, but only THREE backgrounds with minor variations), and the fact that every car runs the same, they're just skins... but I guess that balancing a ton of cars for a game based on fast paced stunts could be a nightmare. Also, it feels like the devs abandoned it a little bit: last update was on february and there has been complete silence since then. Another bad thing is that if you play from different computers (with the same account) the rank positions are not matched, meaning that if you play on a new device you can see your own nickname there but you start with 0 points, as if you never played that track before. I guess those things are stored locally, which makes little sense considering that this game is on Steam and designed to play online (because you can't run a new song if you have no internet access, that's another downside). But this last point should only be of concern if you get competitive and really like to be top ranked on your songs.
Leaving that aside the game is really enjoyable. It's fun, and that's the most important thing for a game to achieve.

Unfortunately, this game is no longer functional.
You need to frequently delete a hidden folder located under your User directory on your computer just to be able to create a new track, and when you finally make it to that point, the game no longer works with iTunes files, meaning that the majority of people can no longer play the majority of their music.
Long story short, the game sucks now and needs to be fixed before I ever consider recommending it.
