The best hardcore survival game I've ever played. Full of drama, often the good kind. Probably best to play with 2+ people as it can get really frustrating solo. Not that solo isn't super fun; but starting with a group is the nicest way to learn the game. The game has official servers and community ones; official ones are all well maintained and great. Game is still being updated like crazy too with big features every other patch.
If you like longterm world persistence, this game isn't for you (in its current state). 99% of servers completely wipe once a week or once a month to keep the server from being overrun with houses/max-geared characters. The game is also very skill based so if you like RPG style/level based gameplay then Rust probably won't be your cup of tea.
Other than that if you can accept a medium-to-high learning curve and hardcore experience this game is quite awesome! And if you have friends to play with already the game can be great even if your a more casual player as it has a lot of different activities (gathering, building, sorting, scouting/exploring, manipulating/befriending your neighbors) that aren't PVP-based. Good luck, and if you happen across me in a server... visit my shop! :D

Now we
have new curve to learn with ,which is a risky step if this got implement poorly it will ruin the gameplay for good (but fortunately it's fun effective and kind of "easy to learn but hard to master-ish".)
As for the Campaign mode, Futuristic Warfare plot help out a lot to supressed how unrealistic and unbelievable design. I can tell that they are going with not taking story too seriously and let it all be showcase of ideas and toys which they can't do in modern era which will suddenly making game far too cheesy.
But! (oh big big but) , the storyline and plot twists are predictable as steam sale list.for such a top notch acting performance and impressive motion capture. It's not so hard to predict where the plot gonna goes. Even if you are not a CoD series player it still easy to guess ( by giving too much obvious clue to the player). So except from introducing nice and fun gadgets this still same old Call of Duty style of story telling like "follow me player!" "do this player!" "wait for me to open the door, player!". First things first. The thing everyone is wondering, is it as good as past geometry wars? I would say yes, and in fact a lot better. It is perhaps the best geometry wars game out yet to date. *GASP*  I have played all of the geometry wars, from the first one to even the Wii and Ds games. Love the series. Many long time fans were worried  since this wasn't developed by the Bizzarre creations guys that it just wouldn't be the same. But fear not, much of the old staff has transitioned to the newly formed Lucid Games (after they disbanded from making Blur) which in turn created this masterpiece!
For any of you that wanted the classic gameplay, those modes are in with the updated snazzy visuals.  There are many classic modes to choose from, from pacism mode, to the tried and true three stock mode, to the waves mode just to name a few. So if you are an old time fan of the series, you will love the updated visuals paired with the classic gameplay.  Along with these modes is a local co-op mode for you and a buddy to tackle head on together!
On top of the geometry wars you have all grown to know and love, there is a new adventure mode, something similar to what you might have seen in the Wii version. There are a multitude of maps and different traps to conquer on Lucid Game's newly envisioned 3d playing field. The new and unique 3d playing field brings on for exciting gameplay challenges that haven't been seen in past iterations. No longer are you shooting on a flat surface, but now you are traversing through spheres or other geometrical shapes. Not only does each map have a leaderboard, but it also has a three star system for you to aim for if the top score is not your preference. You can ignore the star system just like the leaderboard scores, but as your point score racks up, you see the star meters guage fill up, just teasing you to three star each map. You are always left with the feeling, "One more run and I can finish that last star!" Another exciting addition inside the adventure mode are boss fights where you have to tackle a boss with its own unique set of traits.  These boss fights are not for the feint of heart and are quite difficult for even the seasoned veteran like myself.
One of the first things you notice about this game are the visuals. They are beautiful and have that eye popping look accompanied by bright neon explosions.  Along with the vibrant visuals, the soundtrack has a thumpy electro vibe that matches the fast and frenetic nature of Geometry Wars, a perfect fit!
Perhaps one of the coolest features I am really excited for and hopefully the Steam community for geometry wars gets big enough is the multplayer mode.  You might be asking, "What? Multiplayer in my Geometry Wars?" There is a matchmaking mode online where you can compete against other players.  You go around shooting, competing for ammo, upgrading your ship, and taking down bosses. Whoever can score the most points/take down the bosses wins. A nice challenging and new creative way to play Geometry Wars.
From the updated beautiful visuals, the new 3d playing field, adventure mode, to the classic and new matchmaking modes, for any old or new fan, Geometry Wars 3 will be an addicting game that will consume us for hundreds if not thousands of hours again. If Lucid games had just ported the classic modes without any of the graphical changes, that alone would have made it a great game, but there is a whole bunch more here than just that!
Brb, back to playing!

Ok the game actually has a back story, a pretty long one.  The game itself is fine as a casual game..  but survival mode is vastly INFERIOR to Orion Prelude.
The harvest version of survival seems oddly more fun but still lacking compared to orion prelude. Game load times are significantly slow compared to Orion Prelude.
This however does have a leader board so if you can play with friends you have bragging rights - but the game itself seems overly complicated when you consider the 3 basic play modes - Survival/Harvest,  PVP,  Space Dogfighting.
There is a 4th mode which is basically just walking around a static base and occaisionally an NPC will give you a mission.  It seems to serve more as a lobby to create fire teams before you hop into a server, and as a portal to the in game shop where you can buy crazy hats or player class add ons.
What I also find really ironic here is there are a bunch of character customisations that gives your player an Australian voice etc.. yet no actual servers exist in Australia.  The game handles lag very well however, I saw no significant handicap playing on a server full of non-Australians but the gameplay gets stale very quickly compared to Orion Prelude.
I love orion prelude, but this is not an upgrade from that game.  If anything its a downgrade gameplay wise, strategies that are mostly effective on prelude, work Brilliantly on this game.. but too brilliantly, you are basically invulnerable, while in prelude you have to keep dodging the flying enemies or thrown attacks. The maps seems more limited, and very few vs Orion prelude.
If I didn't need to compare this game to Orion Prelude I would recommend it, but it is marketed as a followup/upgraded version to Prelude, and against that measuring stick it sadly falls well short as of the writing of this review.
But Orion Prelude was considered a troubled game at the start too, so with time and improvements I have no doubt this can be a great game, but at this time it is not.  But really at 99 cents it is a great casual game which is likely to go places eventually and this review may get turned around then.  Don't be afraid to try the game, it still stands on its own merits as a 99 cent game, but dont come in with very high expectations.

Third, the rock slimes really hurt and they are my favorite, but their spikes hurt and walking in their bepens can mean death so I suggests an upgrade like armor. Also there is a weird light glitch near the end of the moss biome when your near the return pad. I also have a couple suggestions. I think the terrain for gardens with trees should be either dark or like you put a veggie in the sloy instead of fruit because it looks like sand. Tars have been spawning a lot more frequently when I am trying to explore and gather. Overall, if this is the last game you ever play, I would play this one. I love this game so much i would pay up to $35 for the game, but thankfully it's not. It has so much to do, you almost never get bored, you always have to do something, and come on look at it, the game style isn't just cute, it is creative, unique, and just gorgeous to look at. I don't want to spoil anything, but this is a fun, calm. intriging, adorable, exploration, farm game that I would recommend to anyone and everyone! It may not be a looker, it may not be as solid a port as we would like, but for those who could actually get the game to launch, it is unquestionably one of the greatest games ever released.

TL;DR for those who like that kinda thing.
Really good game, well done port, controls are a little shakey if you're using KB+M, there are a few more "cheap" segments than the first one.  8/10 game, would recommend.
On to the review.
I've been waiting for this game since it was announced to NOT be an easy to get into for new players marketing game, back in early 2013.
The release of Dark Souls 1: Prepare to Die Edition was...  not looked well upon, it was hard to open properly, a lot of the controls were bad unless you had a controller connected, and sometimes you had to have a work around to get those to work, it was terribly optomized, and it was capped at 30 FPS, regardless sometimes you still dropped frames.
Dark Souls 2 is NOT that port.
This game is extremely well optomized, better than a lot of only PC games, (Looking at you Guild Wars 2, which I also love) infact, I've never had it drop below 60 fps, regardless of the fact that there were around 6 enemies, 2 invaders, one using Flame Swathe and another using Soul Greatsword.  Based Belltower.  Umbasa.
I've heard of a few issues launching the game with AMD Cards, or with HDMI connections.  I didn't experience any of these and everything worked as intended out of the box.  Err...  Steam Client.
The game is VAC secured, it will be nearly impossible to get away with hacking safely, a massive improvement over both console versions and Dark Souls 1.
Now onto the actual game instead of the port.  The game is hard, this is still Dark Souls, not your grandma's game, (unless your Grandma is a BAMF, in which case, my apologies.) but there are a few more "cheap" segments in this game, which was a little dissapointing, compared to the first one.
Spoiler alert, continue reading at your own risk
I felt like Iron Keep, once of the places I was actually stuck, was keeping me there just by being cheap.  There were great bow archers at both corners of the room constantly firing arrows at you, that will knock you down if you're poiseless, or below 10, and stun you at anything above that.  The enemies in the area are extremely fast, way faster than anything you've fought previously, even if they do only have 2 attacks, it can be quite an adjustment.  Not to mention there are Iron Knights who will knock you off thin platforms, into lava, flat on your back/face depending and prevent you from circling behind them.  Please note that these mechanics aren't nessecarily bad, in fact there were situations like this in Dark Souls 1, it's just the frequency of them that bothers me.
Another area of the game, that I wouldn't call cheap, but can be annoying if you want to be human, is the Shaded wood Ruins.  There are jars that can curse you causing you to lose your humanity.  While they're a cool mechanic and easy enough to avoid if you simply break them, there is one area where theres a pot directly infront of you, and one dirctly above you in another room you can't directly see, but can still curse you.  I've never made it through there area with max health simply because of that pot.  Luckily that is an optional area, so I suppose I can let it pass.
Now on to the good.
Multiplayer connects nearly instantly (except in the Brotherhood of Blood arena T_T, where are my fellow Blood lovers?!), all the covenents, except Brotherhood of Blood, see above, are extremely active, and I've had great experiences with summoning and all the bosses.  A lot of the areas are well designed, even if a bit short, and theres a lot of cool stuff everywhere for you to find if you actually put forth the effort.  The only thing I can say about this game is if you know the path through everything it feels easier to run through than it is to kill stuff.  Even more so than Dark Souls 1.  This may be because of the multitude of enemies that are in a lot of areas.
There are a lot of things you can do, there are a pleathora of rings available to experiment with, and a lot of viable armours.  You can use rings from other covenants regardless of the fact that you're no longer in that covenant, and the whole world feels more vast and fun to explore than the first one did.
All the weapons are extremely good now thanks to infusion and magic buffs, if you so choose to use them.  You can powerstance if you have 150% of the stats required to wield the weapon in your right hand and your left hand, not together, both weapons stats.  It's complictated, I'm not gonna explain now.  You'll get a new moveset and theres a lot of fun things you can do.
Even bare vists are viable, and infact, stronger than the first weapon, if you choose to get a rather difficult to obtain ring from a covenant that makes the entire game harder.  Yes, that is real.  Yes, that is in the main hub.
Just experiment, have fun, play around with your builds, you can respec now if you jacked your build up, and you want to min-max (from your classes starting stats, not everything set to level 1, unfortunately) so go nuts and try out new things.
Overall I think this is a very solid game that I am going to be getting a lot of hours of play time on.  Since Games For Windows Live is shutting down, I'm probably done with Dark Souls 1.  It gave me a good 430 hours, and I'm predicting even more from this one.
I give this game an 8/10, I would reccomend the purchase.

For me, this game is just too tedious to play without a guide. I feel the designers did a terrible job on the level and boss designs. All the hidden items are off in some remote corner of an area. No puzzles to work out, its just off some abscure path that you missed somewhere. The items that aren't hidden often require an ability you don't have yet. Come back later when you have a grippier chain... Stupid. The bosses all have their scripted quirks and quicktime events. Requiring you to start back from the bottom (sometimes litterally) just to climb back up to take a shot at figuring out what you are doing wrong. Fall, rinse, repeat. Once you do figure it out, theres typically something dumb coming right after it. If you miss the QTE, the boss gets his health back. Meaning you have to beat him down again for your shot at the QTE...  The game could have been a million times better. They had the budget (patrick steward narrates between levels). It looks like they just threw a bunch of money at it, said, go make a game, and left it all in the hads of some yahoo. *sigh* I was so hopeful for this game that I'm actually mourning the loss.

This game has an amazing idea in play. The deaf leading the blind, and vice-versa in situations. For a free to play title, and despite its short length, I'm very impressed with this game. You choose either the deaf Soldier who can see, but cannot hear a thing (armed with a crossbow), or you choose the blind Oracle who can hear, but cannot see (armed with a spell-casting staff). The Soldier leads the Oracle through the level using a beacon that's mute to him, but emits a distinct sound to the Oracle. You solve puzzles together that involve the Soldier leading the Oracle to the puzzle to activate it together, but be wary as there are invisible monsters in the game that only the Oracle can hear to which they must zap it in order to reveal its location for the Soldier to kill. Upon death, the monsters drop gate keys only the Oracle can pick up that open gates to advance the level.
Like I said, this game is very short, but enjoyable in this concept. If they added random level generation, the replayability of this game would soar. However, I recommend this game to anyone who has a buddy to play with (over LAN/Hamachi, etc) that's intrigued by the game's mechanics. It's free, so there's really not a whole lot you can complain about. Glitches? Maybe some clipping issues in the level, but nothing game-breaking to be honest.
Well, what are you waiting for? Give this little gem a go!

I looove this game! I've played it nonstop since I bought it- and I was incredibly eager to pick it up once I got the money.
However, early access leaves a lot to be desired - as you find yourself accumulating a lot of money and needing more space. I can't wait for the next update. I can tell with the dedication of the team, this game will be well worth the money once it fully releases. I'd love to see it on a handheld platform. The aesthetic suits it.
Pros:
- Well-done ambient soundtrack. The music doesn't overwhelm gameplay, and you don't find yourself thinking "Wow, this is really annoying."
- Cute slimes! Of course! Each type of slime seems to have its own personality - not limited to favorite foods, but behaviors as well.
-Pretty (albiet small) places to explore. The textures and waterwork are amazing!
- Well-done mechanics. You'd really have to look to find ways to break the game as it is.
- Good time waster. I've been playing this game for. Approximately two days straight.
Cons:
-Anxiety for the next updates are driving me up the wall! I've accumulated so much money I don't know what to do next. You find yourself unlocking most of the areas and leaving crops to rot, as there's no more space to do much else.
-A lack of inventory slots. Carrying multiples of one item only gets you so far.
-A lack of narrative. You're a slime rancher, and that's basically it. You have a rival, but she's very cut and dry antagonistic - which doesn't drive me personally to fight against her. As the player, you feel very detached from other characters. They're narratives that are simplified to trading and occasional letters.
In summary, I loved this game, but as early access it leaves a little to be desired - but not enough where I wouldn't recommend it to those who can afford it. I wouldn't blame anyone if they'd like to wait.

Do you like the beat-em-up systems in God of War? And chosing skill chains to improve like Devil May Cry? How about giant mega-bosses ala Shadow of the Colossus? And what about climbing, swinging, jumping and scampering about like in Prince of Persia or the Uncharted series? How about a slightly overwritten origin story for the FIRST BELMONT EVER?!
If even a few of those concepts appeal to you, you're likely to really enjoy this game. A version of all those elements from other sources were pretty much lifted and used here, but the whole is really more than the sum of its pilfered parts. Those disparate elements and more modified from other games really come together and shine here in a fun beat-em-up that wil keep you entertained throughout, and likely keep you coming back to complete some of the wacky challenges it throws at you after you beat a stage.
It's easy to recommend, and I was surprisingly pleased by this little gem; so many new reboots fail to capture even some of the things that make their source great, but LoS does a fairly decent job in at least some of the boss fights, and by filling in some fun lore plot gaps in a tragic tale of bad decisions made for the right reasons. Also Patrick Stewart is there, so that's a big plus for this nerd.

I've gotten way more replayability out of this than I had anticipated. I was expecting this to be an MP-only sort of game, whether local or online (the latter of which has worked surprisingly well for early access), and although it definitely excels as a party game, there are a lot of pleasures that are easier to experience soloing: setting up fall traps with barrels, positioning propane tanks, screwing around with rolling blocks, experimenting with the various bros.
Also worth mentioning is the impressive amount of game modes I've only just begun to scratch the surface of. The standard campaign on and offline has been enough to keep me and my friends plenty occupied, but there are still several other attractive-looking game modes to keep me coming back. Considering how many games fall within the same price range but feature just a campaign, sometimes even a very short one, it's exciting to see an indie dev work in so much content.
Basically, whether you're looking for a chaotic, "YOOOOOOOOO!"-inducing party game to bro out over, or a fun single player experience with a sandbox worth of destructibility, environmental hazards, a ton of game modes and myriad characters and abilities, you can't go wrong with Broforce.

SteamWorld Dig is a very fun, increasingly addicting platformer with some steampunk and mining essence sprinkled in. Tight controls, sharp graphics and solid game progression make this a game I was always itching to get back to playing.
Starting off I was a little discouraged with how seemingly boring the gameplay was. Hit things a lot with my pickaxe, run out of light and/or storage space and be forced back up to the surface to cash in my findings and get more light. However, sticking with it, you’ll find yourself buying upgrades faster, mining faster, and getting new abilities which help you navigate the underground faster. Soon enough you’ll be a mining machine. It felt good to plow through areas where I had previously had to hammer away several times to remove one block.
The game is fairly short. Usually I don’t mind this but I wish it was a bit longer. Also, it’s a fairly easy game. Some harder rooms could have been implemented. I died the most from getting crushed by falling rocks I forgot to get out of the way fast enough.
Most enemies can simply be avoided. You are rewarded with a little more light, health or water if you do choose to fight them. I found myself generally avoiding them unless I was desperate for health or water. The light boost they give you doesn’t help too much when you’re low on that anyway.
There are a lot of upgrades that you can buy. Some of them are absolutely necessary, like upgrading your weapons. So the deeper you go in the mine, the less hits it takes to destroy a block. I found all of the upgrades helpful and never seemed like I wasted money on one.
+60fps
+Great game progression
+Great graphics and animation
+Nice game mechanics
+Tight controls
+Upgrades
+Fun!
+A little short
+Story is a little bare
+A little too easy
Definitely would recommend this one as I was always wanting to get back to playing after I stopped. That will always be a sign of a good game to me.

Firstly, image mindcraft. now add no man sky and the un-pixelated version of mindcraft and booom, you have astoneer! lol.. its a farming game with plenty potential and loads of fun in 2 ways. so that is why I am going to break this down in 2 reviews
First one being. The multiplay. anyone at any one time can join your game.
So the game goes alot faster and gets fun faster when you get through the basics of establishing your base. when you land on the planet, hunting for the upgrades becomes alot easier with a friend and in doing so makes the game go better in the short term. trust me, you want to jump in and out of planets and start new ones when you can and if you made mistakes with your digging etc.. its cool though, each new start gives you a different planet colouring and style and layout. the tunnels underneath vary between each new game you make too so once you find the perfect tunneling near your habitat (home/rocket), dont play around with it too much. just build yourself to get ready for making an underground network once you have unlocked the habitat upgrade from the shells.

the 2nd part of my review is. Playing by yourself.
well, unlike playing with a mate. the game goes alot slower and can potentially become boring fast if you dont have a good strategy. so i suggest you turn on your music and play it as if you are guna play for 5 hours or so. because its a grind. but becomes fun once you have sorted out your oxygen and power supply.

Okay, first things first, I think I got this game for around 9 Cent or so, as I used a Coupon.
Secondly, this is a game that totally fits my style as I'm a dude that got every single achievement in "Super Hexagon", a game with a similar premise.
The game in itself is totally okay for a 0.99€ game. You have a Square/Hexagon and flying orbs with a color of one side of your shape. The orbs must fly into the right color so you win a point and another orb spawns. Through time you unlock new gamemodes which are as followed:
These levels all give lots of content that can hook you for an hour or two. Totally fine there.
While I think the Gameplay is fluid and is mostly fair I do have some minor problems with the normal mode.
The normal mode is (as described in the game) a mode where all other modes are combined. That's totally ok and whilst I haven't seen the Trip mode up to this point I'm kinda ok with that.
The problem there lies in the switching times between modes. As an example when entering Hexagon Mode the Square has a short morphing time in which the next orb/ dot already comes flying at you but you cannot change the direction your (then Hexagon) is facing, therefore giving you more or less half the time you had beforehand for more spins.
Another problem there is, that the color that faced beforehand the top/bottom changes when morphing in and out of Hexagon-mode making it impossible to predict how often you'll need to spin afterwards.
But other than that I have only experienced one time while Hexagon-Mode switched off and Flip mode started in the same time that 3 orbs came at the same time with different colors... Not sure what went off there but with multiple tries I could not reconstruct that scenario after that one time...
The only other thing that I think could take some improvement are the different unlockable modes. While I did enjoy most of them (except Trip Mode, bc that's literally the worst thing or I'm just too stupid) I think that it would've been more enjoyable to input them so, that the player could choose which one of them he wants to play and also play MULTIPLE AT THE SAME TIME.
Personally I think that a Time+Hexagon-Mode would be perfect and up to this point it doesn't seem that there's a way to play a mode like that.
So tl;dr:
While the game isn't perfect it's totally worth 0,99€. If the developer implements a way to play multiple modes at the same time (while not putting all of them at random like in normal mode) I'd say I would like the game even more. But as it stands I can still recommend this game to people who crave some lil fun.

I looove this game! I've played it nonstop since I bought it- and I was incredibly eager to pick it up once I got the money.
However, early access leaves a lot to be desired - as you find yourself accumulating a lot of money and needing more space. I can't wait for the next update. I can tell with the dedication of the team, this game will be well worth the money once it fully releases. I'd love to see it on a handheld platform. The aesthetic suits it.
Pros:
- Well-done ambient soundtrack. The music doesn't overwhelm gameplay, and you don't find yourself thinking "Wow, this is really annoying."
- Cute slimes! Of course! Each type of slime seems to have its own personality - not limited to favorite foods, but behaviors as well.
-Pretty (albiet small) places to explore. The textures and waterwork are amazing!
- Well-done mechanics. You'd really have to look to find ways to break the game as it is.
- Good time waster. I've been playing this game for. Approximately two days straight.
Cons:
-Anxiety for the next updates are driving me up the wall! I've accumulated so much money I don't know what to do next. You find yourself unlocking most of the areas and leaving crops to rot, as there's no more space to do much else.
-A lack of inventory slots. Carrying multiples of one item only gets you so far.
-A lack of narrative. You're a slime rancher, and that's basically it. You have a rival, but she's very cut and dry antagonistic - which doesn't drive me personally to fight against her. As the player, you feel very detached from other characters. They're narratives that are simplified to trading and occasional letters.
In summary, I loved this game, but as early access it leaves a little to be desired - but not enough where I wouldn't recommend it to those who can afford it. I wouldn't blame anyone if they'd like to wait.

Welcome to Slime Rancher! You're a new farmer so to speak, an unusual one; yes you will be raising chickens, and growing crops...but not their harvest reaps your reward...It's what you feed those products to. Cute, cuddly, and sometimes deadly slimes. There's so many different types of them. And not only that, bud each of them can be combined with eachother. Right now I have cat and luminescent slimes, as well as exploding radioactive slimes. SERIOUSLY! This game has insane potential and it has an extremely large amount of content that it's worth anyone's purchase!! It sounds, feels, and looks amazing. The graphics are as great as the soundtrack, the game runs really smoothly (except for a few areas for me, where the framerate drops a little bit) and it's just an entertaining game!
This is all coming from a dude who mainly likes FPS and fast paced games...This game was the first game every where I wanted to stay awake, sacrificing hours of sleep for. I've never ever done that with another game, except perhaps a pokemon game or two.
I really hope my review helps you purchase this game; it's truly a piece of art and I can promise you you'll enjoy it. And if not, well...you have 2 hours of free play time thanks to Steam Refund! I sincerely hope you purchase this and help support the developers. It's an amazing game.
The only thing else that I'd like from this game is multiplayer, however they have said they have no plans to make it (as their team is very very small.) but we might see it in the future, not certain, don't quote me on it!!
Thanks for reading my review, and I hope you make some awesome, creative combinations of slimes on your ranch!

First, I'd like to state that this is my opinion, and only my opinion, so take it as you will. I've logged easily 1000hours into Demon's Souls on ps3, and another 1000 into Dark Souls on ps3; aswell as probly close to 500 for Dark Souls 2 on my ps3. The game is absolutely fantastic, all three of them. I, myself, didn't have a tremendous amount of trouble with any of them after I got the hang of it in the first few hours on Demon's Souls. I would like to state however, that I truly believe Demon's Souls offers the best experience, Dark Souls offers the best expansive, free roam kind of feel, and Dark Souls 2 offers... well... To say the least, I've found that in Dark Souls 2, instead of truly making the game more difficult, they simply broke some of the mechanics that made it possible to be made easier.
The first thing I noticed out of the gate was that the dodge mechanic was both slow and clunky, and the hit boxes for both players and enemies are... sketchy at best. This meaning, that where a perfectly timed dodge in Demons Souls or Dark Souls would have prevented you taking damage, you would still take damage in Dark Souls 2 because the player hit box either doesn't follow the dodge animation correctly, or they simply revamped it to make it far more clunky to make the game 'feel' harder.
Secondly, and this ties into my first point. The armor and resistances in Dark Souls 2 are practically laughable. Allow me to explain. There is a boss, a fair ways through the game that deals almost entirely fire based damage. Meaning, even if you block an attack, you still take damage, and you take a ton of damage if you do not block an attack. Where Demons Souls and Dark Souls would let you stack armor sets with high resistance to one element or another, it's almost pointless in DS2. Unless resitances are simply meant for PvP to negate pyromancy, in which case, PvP fans eat your heart out. But I noticed that wearing a suit of armor, that maximized fire resistance, and also had a higher physical defence then my normal armor, albeit at the expense of movement speed, I still took damage at relatively the same rate from the boss' fire based attacks. This being said, wearing lighter armor to move faster, is still not much of an option, as the dodge mechanic fails pretty badly.
The third issue I noted, was that the inability to farm a steady means of maintaining your humanity can quite literally stop a player in their tracks if they fail a boss fight multiple times in a row and end up hollow, with no effigy's. I can see that they made this change to prevent making the game too easy, but this can also completely halt a players ability to progress through the game if they are incapable for beating a certain boss by themselves. You might be thinking "Just get summoned and beat the boss." Doesn't work that way. As they removed that mechanic aswell. So it is, quite literally a possibility for a players humanity to... well, run dry, so to speak.
I think the most gamebreaking issue to note however, is that in early stages, finding summons signs is easy. Once I got into NG+ on my ps3, I noticed no summon signs, at all, I played through half of NG+ solo, and only saw 2 summon signs, both of which disappeared or were "already being summoned". A friend had told me that the main body on NG+ players were in the level ranges beyond 130... I got to level 148, solo of course, and still hadn't seen any summon signs. Joining the PvP covenant however yeilded plenty of PvP duels, where most players resort to dirty use of spells and lag to kill you through walls. I'm also given to understand that "soul memory" has something to do with summon range. If that is the case, then I most likely had too high of a soul memory, as I had only managed to lose maybe 45k souls by the time I hit level 148. That would in turn lead me to believe that the soul memory mechanic serves to encourage players to die, and do poorly, losing souls, so that they can maintain a proper connection with the main host of players on the game at later levels.
All this being said, it is by no means a bad game. Walkthroughs will be helpful, as you will get lost and not know where to go or what to do. Also, I'd recommend using an xbox controller or something to play, as using a mouse and keyboard is fairly clunky. Although.... if you wanted to use a controller, you might aswell just buy the console version, as it will likely present less bugs at this time and it is optimized to play on the ps3, so you won't need a beast of a pc to run the game. Just a thought =/
Anyways, that's my rant, I do recommend the game, but I highly recommend buying and playing it with a true desire to sit down and get into it, as none of the 3 Souls games are really for casual gamers and it takes a LOT of patience at times. Do your research though. Don't buy a game blindly based on a few reviews you read on Steam. Watch gameplay, ask friends, maybe even try the game out on console if one of your friends has it before you commit 50$ to a game you may regret buying if it proves to be too much for you. It's a good game, it will be buggy on PC for a while, and I, personally, recommend buying it for console over pc, to save oneself the hassle. Have a great day everyone, and if you do decide to buy the game, always remember, life is precious, cling to it with every fibre of your being. >=]

Lords of Shadow was to me a game made by people who seemed to have a good amount of care for the series but ultimately had too many badly executed ideas mixed in with inspired ones.
Performance an presentation :
The game actually ran more or less perfectly.  I had all settings on max on my 6850HD / 16gb / 3.2ghz * 6 system aside from AA on 8x instead of 16x.  The game maintained a steady 60fps even during most action scenes.  xbox360ce performed as expected and while controller binds can't be changed I felt like they all worked well.  I did not attempt to use KB+M controls.  Menus and saving and steam integration were pretty satisfactory (the game pauses when you open the steam overlay for instance) so it seems like the port was handled pretty well.
The environments of the game are really a mixed bag.  The opening third of the game is set in arbitrary country locales and ruins with vermin small and large, while the rest is very nicely designed and atmospheric.  Music is either generic gothic choir you've heard before, or occasionally very inspired remixes of classic CV songs with a completely different tone.  A browse of the concept art gallery shows a lot of amazingly imagined locales that don't always translate over well into a third-person action titles.  My take from this was like feeling the tantalizing cool breeze coming from somewhere in a stuffy room, refreshing and wonderful when you felt it but not lasting beyond brief moments or strong enough to make the complete package something special.
Story :
Story wise... its kind of hard to say.  The game's protagonist doesn't feel like he fits the story as narrated in the loading screens of every stage.  They say how tortured and tired and full of anger he is, but he just acts like a more toned-down stoic badass type stutting happily away in transitions and cinematics, barely showing the tortured soul he is supposed to be until the very end of the game.  He is toned-down from most stoic badasses in videogames though, and the lack of over-the-topness is appreciated,   The game's originating premise is actually genuinely interesting but then resolves in a much less epic or interesting conclusion, as gathering all the dark powers together doesn't make the protagonist any kind of interesting figure (for good or evil) but results in a last boss and villain who just happened to have orchestrated the whole thing but is more or less irrelevant to the story in any meaningful way.  The game starts our pretty badly with you fighting indigenous monsters and meeting throwaway characters in the opening third to being much more player-relevant with foes and faces in the middle third, then ending with a nicely atmospheric desolate finale chapter more devoid of life in the last third.  It makes the opening third of the game feel very throwaway and put there just to be gamey rather than planned.  The post-credits story cutscene feels like a typical movie sequel hook set farther in the future but leaves questions to be answered in the post-release DLC that ultimately feels like a cop-out rather than a meaningful progression from the game to its sequel hook.  Something that could have been solved had the original premise led to a more interesting conclusion than villain-out-of-nowhere.
Gameplay :
This is pretty much where the game doesn't shine.  The game doesn't really excel in any particular area and is bad enough in some to be bad.  Not atrocious, just bad.  Lets talk about a few.
The game holds your hand 95% of the time and then leaves you boggled for the other.  Every new area is camera-panned.  Ledges are highlighted with glows AND text telling you what to do in long text.    Enemy special attacks that allow for special contextual responses are zoomed, focused, and slow-mo'd... except when all of these aren't.  In those cases, you'll be left boggled by what exactly to do because the game wasn't designed in a way to SHOW, it was designed to TELL.  Hold R2 to grip!  Dodge that projectile!  But this one?  Nope you just get hit by the giant golem's hand that didn't really seem to touch you, and you fell off for some reason.  This is mitigated somewhat by gratuitous checkpoints, except at the end of the game where the game expects a sequence of actions performed across two paths with no checkpoint resets in between and doesn't inform you of the lost progress until you traverse one of the paths to find your progress wasn't kept.  The game isn't really hard because of this inconsistency, it just neither lets you feel clever or perceptive because it wasn't designed for you to think or try to solve it.  It was made to be spoonfed like applesauce, but then pours the applesauce on the table at a few points.
Combat is very fluid but doesn't really reward or challenge the player too much except if you get hit.  The only way to heal is via hitting enemies while using a resource-limited super mode, by finding a healing shrine in the stage, or having it restored to 1/2 if you die and reload a checkpoint.  The only way to restore this resource is find a resource shrine or by hitting enemies without taking any damage yourself to build up a meter, much like in Devil May Cry games except this gives you Devil Trigger instead of points towards a reward at the end of a level.  The meter doesn't reward super mode unless it is completely full, and keeping it full is either completely easy or annoyingly difficult depending on the enemy.  Bosses?  Easy.  Groups of large mobs?  Not easy.  Small enemies?  OHKO them one by one with the grab attack, because its easier than fighting them normally and no small enemy is immune to the grab attack.
Bosses are of two kinds.  Multi-phase bosses with predictable patterns, and Shadow of the Colossus style bosses that are completely uninteresting to fight.  You can't restore health on these bosses except by game over, which leads to having to watch choreographed 'look out for this attack' slow mo moments or waiting for attacks to cycle until you can actually do anything sooner than if you were able to manage your health like in normal combat.  Platforming on these bosses is not interesting, and they aren't even real puzzle bosses like they can be in SotC.  There is no gimmick or thought or variation in how you have to defeat them.  Its a script you just learn and follow, and this isn't helped by the fact that the ledge platforming can be a modest amount unresponsive at times.  Only one of the three in the game is actually meaningful to the story purely in that it is a reference Death's skeletal monster forms in the rest of the series.  Developers need to learn why Shadow of the Colossus was fun and not just try to copy the game's scale with sequences like these that are in no way fun to play.
This is what I want to call a  'console-style game'.  The game is made for people who don't care to do much beyond pop the disc into the xbox and have the flashy cool gothic monster fighting show up on screen.  Irrelevant QTEs abound and show your character doing cool things rather than you doing them yourself.  Puzzles are all simple logic puzzles that don't require any thought and all of them give you the option to skip them.  Platforming and level progression are linear and there is no meaningful exploration, despite the illusion of it by divergent paths that converge again only a minute or so later in the stage.  Combat is quirky but more or less button mash friendly and half the enemy types are meaningless due to the grab move OHKO.  Constant checkpointing means you never get too stuck on any part of the game.

Castlevania: Lords of Shadow Ultimate Edition came to PC after a successful debut on Xbox 360 and PS3. Although a re-release, this version is special in a few ways that make it a good buy. However, there was a specific purpose that was in mind with this edition.
The story follows Gabriel Belmont, a member of the Brotherhood of Light, in his quest to revive his murdered wife. With the help of the mythical God, Pan, Gabriel journeys through various lands to kill the Lords of Shadow; three powerful demons responsible for a spell that has cut off God's connection to the world. After defeating each member of the Lords of Shadow and some lesser bosses, Gabriel gains various armours and medallions that grant extra moves and powers while also upgrading his Combat Cross, a weaponized chain whip – the main weapon. There are twists and turns with plenty of cinematics and dialogue which keep Castlevania very much story orientated. Gameplay is very similar to titles such as God of War and Dante's Inferno, with a third person view and jumping, dodging, blocking and parrying, grabs and button mashing and timing grapples, all playing their respective roles in combat and level progression that is smooth and intense. Base enemies vary in difficulty and tactics, with each enemy type having their own signature moves and fighting styles so there is no 'upgraded bad guy with the same moves as the last one' going on. Each area has its own minions who will not likely appear anywhere else, so combat is kept fresh. There are lots of combos that can be learned, some of which can only be used when certain extra abilities are activated. These combos also help to keep things fresh as many enemies will not be affected the same way by the same combo or move; where as one is stunned by a ground-pound, another will shrug it off. There are such a large number of combos and moves that a player will likely find the few they like the most and stick to those. A complaint from some, the large volume of moves at least gives wiggle room for alternative play styles.
Boss fights focus on a cinematic approach rather than straight forward smash 'n slash beat downs. As with the previously mentioned titles, the aim is to take down a small amount of health with standard fighting then, when the boss becomes vulnerable, tired, or fooled into running headlong in to a wall, must be grabbed or will recover most, if not all, of the health that had been taken away. When grabbed, a series of timed inputs, or rapid mashing, will take the player through a preset sequence of blows and recapitulates that, if successful, will break down the boss bit by bit until, finally, a longer and more engrossing sequence will play out for the ending death blows. These sequences are well planned out and show some imaginative choreography, however, the player will most likely miss many of the subtleties in these sequences as the inputs will be the main focus. Environment design is an important part in the immersion of any visual art. Castlevania has some of the best level and environment design out at the moment. Large, sweeping castles, forests, tundras, and canyons, titantic towers, spires, mountains, cliffs, huge and dilapidated stone warriors strewn about in aimless deaths, all and more immerse the player in a world of gigantic beings and powers. The sheer size of many places shows the great feats that Gabriel will have to overcome both physically and mentally if he is to succeed.
Castlevania also demands the player climb and jump through the level in order to progress. Many, if not all, of the environments have obstacles and areas that can only be surpassed and reached, respectively, by climbing. Ledges, of course, are the primary mode of this form of transportation. The Combat Cross also comes in to play as convenient branches of wood and stone, embedded rungs in walls, and broken turrets can be latched on to and used as an anchor to ascend, descend, and swing on.
Set in to the level design is the regular appearance of puzzles that must be solved in order to continue. These puzzles are usually story relevant with only a rare few being put simply to confound the player with abstract riddle. These puzzles can be simple manoeuvring challenges which rely on the players quick and nimble controller movements, to logical conundrums and riddles that must be understood first before the pieces may be moved in to their correct places. There is a wide variety of these puzzles that occur on a regular basis and whose completion gains experience. These puzzles can be solved instantly if a scroll on which a hint and description of the puzzle is found. The side-stepped puzzle does not give out an experience bonus, though, so the challenges are well worth the time they take while also giving an out for the particularly stubborn ones.
What this re-release offers as extras in its Ultimate Edition is reason enough to buy. Lords of Shadow is now soaked in magnificent drawn and painted representations of every enemy type, boss, and character. Once met, a notification will show and the games menu will direct the player to the amazingly detailed pencil portraits depicting the enemy or friendly along with a description and a visual representation of its defences and weaknesses, where applicable. Points can also be saved and spent in an Extras menu in which concept art, storyboards, and painted level designs can be accessed after the completion of their respective chapter. These drawings and paintings are indeed works of art and any fans of the Castlevania series, dev team, or any aspiring and established artists will find these pieces both beautiful and technically sound.
The jewel of the proverbial crown, however, is the DLC. Reverie and Redemption, two extra chapters that lead through the aftermath of the Lords of Shadow storyline, take us to the desolate castle of the defeated vampiric Lord of Shadow where more events unfold that inevitably set up the story for Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2. This Ultimate Edition does not just give what was already given, but adds to it with upgraded graphics and beautiful and interesting additional content. The foundation of such a strong revamp of a classic series to the modern action-adventure genre quiets most complaints and comments right off the bat. Those who have played or are interested in Lords of Shadow know what they will be getting. If one was looking forward to the sequel, this Ultimate Edition brings the player up to speed all for one price. On a personal note, I very much enjoyed this Castlevania and am looking forward to finishing the next one!

Should you play this game? Yes. Though I would caution fans of the original series to keep an open mind. The Lords of Shadow games are not connected to the main storyline in any way. You will see familiar names, quotes and story elements from past titles in the original canon but ultimately this reimagining is its own animal. Think of it as a short and sweet break from the patterns and pace of the original.
The environments are beautiful and the character designs are detailed. The game can become a bit of a rage fest when the QTE sequences start and there is no way to turn them off (Something to smile about in LoS2). Though once you get into the rhythm of the gameplay it should be smooth sailing for the most part.
The story is centered on Gabriel Belmont and the journey that sends a man with noble intentions down a cruel dark path. Looking back on the three games as a whole there is some parallel to the Legacy of Kain series. Lords of Shadow shows the beginning of a dark road, Mirror of Fate is the outcome of the events in LoS as seen from another point of view and Lords of Shadow 2 are the two perspectives coming together for the end game.
If you're the type that enjoys seeing a video game character fall from grace only to rise up and make the darkness within their own, I highly recommend the Castlevania: Lords of Shadow series, starting with this Ultimate Edition.

I dunno, as much as i love the castlevania series as a whole, this game feels like the creators forgot how to make games fun. If your idea of fun is walking down hallways with an ALWAYS FACING FORWARD CAMERA you cannot control, and absurdly long and unintuitive fights then i guess this could be your thing.
I usually play all my 3d fighters games (god of war/dmc/bayonetta/darksiders/kingdoms of amaulr/ect) on hard mode and usually enjoy the challenge it provides. And while the game provides challenges... it didn't feel fun. It was a series of short combo and dodging a very obvious attack. You can never actually do attack combo's long enough to do the cool combo's in the game before an enemy is about to strike (you cannot interrupt them from attacking you) so you're never actually ever able to do anything than a few short strikes and repeat. Fairly simple, but since enemies have SO much health it quickly loses an appeal and becomes a chore. After becoming bored with this, i put the game difficulty down to easy just so i could blaze through and still... it was more or less the same feeling, only now i didn't take dmg when i got hit.
As for the platforming /exploration, its garbage. There are some secrets in levels that you have to get upgrades down the line and come back to, but its not like typical backtracking in metroidvania type games, you have to pick the stage and run through the linear halls to simply get back to where that thing was. It doesn't feel like you're making intelligent choices on how to use your upgrades, its just remembering where the item was and walking down those same hallways again to use the item on the door. It's not much but really the aspect of exploring is non existent and it makes a huge impact on how you as a player view the world.
I got through probably around 25% of the game and quit because i just wasn't having fun with this.  And as many things they do right (voice acting/ visuals / story /ect/ some bosses were kinda cool) the core gameplay fails to entertain and thus the whole experience falls flat.

There isn't much of a difference between this game and the original Half-Life. If you're deciding which to buy, it honestly doesn't matter. The water is nicer in this game and there are ragdolls and better physics. Other than that, it's essentially the same game. Don't worry about not getting the "pure" experience of HL1 because this is essentially it. Lower resolution water and people who just lay down and die without leaving a ragdoll for you to smack with a crowbar weren't the cornerstones of the Half-Life. Playing HL is an experience, regardless of trivialities such as this.
I wouldn't get this by itself personally; if you really wanna pick it up, get it via one of the packs in the Store and/or wait for a sale.
One interesting note though, you can load up the content from this game in Garry's Mod. If you have Gmod, this might give you some fun stuff to play around with.
Play the original. When you try playing a game on a physics engine it wasn't originally designed for, bad things happen.
A graphical update, that's all. If you liked Half Life, you will enjoy this cleaner version.
